title: The synergy of generative AI and inquiry-based learning: transforming the landscape of English teaching and learning
authors: Hui-Chin Yeh
summary: This qualitative study investigates the integration of AI tools, like ChatGPT, into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teacher education through an inquiry-based learning (IBL) framework. Conducted over a semester with thirteen in-service teachers, the research found that AI technologies empowered them to design interactive, personalized, and adaptive learning materials, such as picture books and karaoke exercises. This fostered a more dynamic, student-centered learning environment and significantly improved students' listening and speaking skills. The findings advocate for the strategic incorporation of AI in EFL teaching to support innovative pedagogical approaches that cater to diverse learner needs.

title: Beyond traditional classrooms: CALL as a catalyst for autonomous EAL learning
authors: Haohao Zhang, Yan Xia, Haowei Chen, Sathiamoorthy Kannan
summary: This study investigates the impact of Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) tools, including ChatGPT, on the learner autonomy and English proficiency of 100 undergraduate English as an Additional Language (EAL) learners in China. Through an 8-week intervention comparing a CALL-based experimental group with a traditional textbook-based control group, the study employed a mixed-methods design using pre/post-tests, digital analytics, and interviews. Quantitative results showed that the CALL group achieved significantly higher autonomy scores. Qualitative analysis revealed increased motivation, metacognitive awareness, and a preference for self-directed learning among participants using CALL tools. Despite challenges like technical barriers and the need for self-regulation skills, the findings support the integration of CALL tools within a structured framework to enhance learner autonomy and optimize language learning outcomes.
APA_reference: Zhang, H., Xia, Y., Chen, H., & Kannan, S. (2025). Beyond traditional classrooms: CALL as a catalyst for autonomous EAL learning. Acta Psychologica, 260, 105497. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2025.105497

summary: This mixed-methods study investigated the attitudes of Chinese graduate students in foreign languages towards Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI)-assisted academic paper writing. The study also identified four types of GAI users: Collaborative Innovative Users, Technology-Oriented Users, Professionally Guided Users, and Novice Exploratory Users. title: An AI-assisted critical thinking intervention to enhance undergraduate EFL learners' writing proficiency
authors: Xue Yin, Kun Dou
summary: This study investigates the effects of an AI-assisted critical thinking (CT)-oriented writing intervention using ChatGPT with 250 undergraduate EFL learners from three Chinese public universities. Using a pretest-posttest design, the research measured changes in students' writing proficiency and their acceptance of ChatGPT. Data were collected via writing tests, an acceptance questionnaire based on the UTAUT2 model, and semi-structured interviews. The results indicated that the intervention significantly improved students' critical thinking as reflected in their writing. Additionally, students' acceptance of ChatGPT, particularly in performance expectancy, effort expectancy, trust, and behavioral intention, showed positive shifts. The study demonstrates ChatGPT's potential as a scaffolding tool for CT-oriented writing in EFL contexts when guided by a structured framework. Limitations include a single-group design and a short experimental period.
APA_reference: Yin, X., & Dou, K. (2025). An AI-assisted critical thinking intervention to enhance undergraduate EFL learners' writing proficiency. Studies in Educational Evaluation, 86, 101480. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stueduc.2025.101480

title: ChatGPT: The catalyst for teacher-student rapport and grit development in L2 class
authors: Mohammad Ghafouri
summary: This study investigated the effectiveness of a four-stage ChatGPT-based rapport-building protocol (CGRBP) on enhancing teacher-student rapport and L2 grit among Iranian EFL learners. In a 16-week experimental study involving 30 intermediate-level learners divided into an experimental and a control group, data was collected through a pre-test post-test design. The experimental group, whose teachers used the CGRBP to inform their instruction, showed a significant outperformance in L2 grit compared to the control group. The results suggest that a structured application of ChatGPT can mediate the development of L2 grit by fostering an emotionally supportive learning environment and enhancing teacher-student rapport. The study provides non-correlational evidence for L2 emotion studies and links artificial intelligence with positive psychology, offering practical implications for language teaching.
APA_reference: Ghafouri, M. (2024). ChatGPT: The catalyst for teacher-student rapport and grit development in L2 class. System, 120, 103209. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2023.103209

title: The effects of generative AI on initial language teacher education: The perceptions of teacher educators
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse, Lucas Kohnke
summary: This study investigates the perceptions of English language teacher educators in Hong Kong regarding the effects of generative AI tools, like ChatGPT, on initial language teacher education (ILTE). Through in-depth interviews with thirteen educators from four universities, the research explores their familiarity with GenAI, its perceived impact on ILTE curriculum, instruction, and assessment, and the skills they believe are necessary in this new technological era. The study highlights a critical need for training and support for teacher educators to help them adapt ILTE to the influence of generative AI.

title: Understanding EFL students' use of self-made AI chatbots as personalized writing assistance tools: A mixed methods study
authors: Kai Guo, Danling Li
summary: This mixed-methods study explored how 69 Chinese undergraduate EFL students used self-made Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbots, created on the Poe platform, to support their argumentative writing. Data from student-built chatbots, essays, questionnaires, and reflections showed that students created chatbots for various purposes, including idea generation, outlining, and error correction, tailoring them with specific knowledge bases like scoring rubrics and course materials. Interactions with the chatbots involved requests for assistance, customization, and translation. The study found that using these personalized chatbots significantly improved students' writing motivation, specifically enhancing their performance and avoidance goals, writing confidence, writing beliefs, and positive attitudes toward writing. The findings support empowering students to create their own AI tools to foster personalized learning, autonomy, and motivation.

title: Developing language teachers' professional generative AI competence: An intervention study in an initial language teacher education course
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse, Yuwei Wan, Chenze Wu, Lucas Kohnke, Tsz Ying Ho, Theresa Kwong
summary: This mixed-method intervention study, conducted in an initial language teacher education program at a Hong Kong university, explored the effects of explicit training on pre-service language teachers' professional generative AI competence (P-GenAI-C). Fifty-four M.Ed students participated in an 11-week course intervention designed to enhance five aspects of the P-GenAI-C framework. Analysis of pre- and post-intervention questionnaires and follow-up interviews revealed that the intervention effectively improved all aspects of the participants' P-GenAI-C. The most significant gains were observed in pedagogical competence and critical awareness of GenAI tools. However, there was less development in their capacity to guide future students in using GenAI tools effectively, a gap attributed to the course content. The study discusses implications for integrating P-GenAI-C into teacher preparation programs.

title: Exploring ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback in the EFL context
authors: Jining Han, Mimi Li
summary: This study investigates an innovative AI-aided writing pedagogy in a Chinese tertiary EFL context, where teachers use ChatGPT to support the provision of writing feedback. Four instructors and 102 undergraduate students participated. The instructors used ChatGPT with specific prompts to generate corrective and rhetorical feedback on two student essays (argumentative and expository). They then adapted this AI-generated feedback before sharing it with students. The study analyzes the types and features of this 'AI + Teacher' feedback and how students incorporate it into their revisions. Findings show that the ChatGPT-supported feedback was diverse and helpful, addressing both grammatical errors and rhetorical aspects. Students demonstrated high engagement by incorporating a majority of the feedback into their revised essays. The study advocates for an 'AI + Teacher' model, which leverages AI's analytical power to reduce teacher workload and provide detailed feedback, while maintaining the essential element of teacher guidance and interaction.
APA_reference: Han, J., & Li, M. (2024). Exploring ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback in the EFL context. System, 126, 103502. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2024.103502

RQ2: How do students incorporate ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback into their revisions regarding two writing tasks?

title: Cognitive and sociocultural dynamics of self-regulated use of machine translation and generative AI tools in academic EFL writing
authors: Yijen Wang
summary: This study investigates the self-regulated use of AI tools (ChatGPT, Google Translate) by 79 Japanese university learners in an English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing course. Using a mixed-methods approach with pre- and post-surveys and writing journals over one semester, the research examines the interplay between students' cognitive processes and sociocultural interactions. title: ChatGPT as a tool for self-learning English among EFL learners: A multi-methods study
authors: Nguyen Hoang Mai Tram, Tin Trung Nguyen, Cong Duc Tran
summary: This study investigates the factors influencing the acceptance and use of ChatGPT for self-directed English language learning among EFL learners. Using a multi-methods approach that includes a systematic review, a quantitative survey of 344 learners, and 19 semi-structured interviews, the research proposes an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The findings indicate that interactivity, enjoyment, trust, and subjective norms positively affect continued use via perceived usefulness, while human-likeness, self-efficacy, and technology anxiety are linked to perceived ease of use. The study also explores how learners use ChatGPT for various language skills like reading, writing, vocabulary, and grammar, engaging in both active and passive learning for primary (language study) and secondary (work/study tasks) purposes. The results offer guidance for AI developers and educators on enhancing and integrating AI chatbots in language learning.
APA_reference: Tram, N. H. M., Nguyen, T. T., & Tran, C. D. (2024). ChatGPT as a tool for self-learning English among EFL learners: A multi-methods study. System, 127, 103528. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2024.103528

title: The grass is not always greener: Teacher vs. GPT-assisted written corrective feedback
authors: Shiming Lin, Peter Crosthwaite
summary: This study compares the written corrective feedback (WCF) provided by human teachers with that generated by ChatGPT (GPT-4). The findings indicate that teachers typically use a consistent mix of direct and indirect feedback, addressing both local (grammatical) and global (content) issues, though sometimes with inaccuracies. In contrast, ChatGPT-assisted WCF predominantly consists of metalinguistic feedback and text reformulation. A key finding is ChatGPT's inconsistency; it often provides different feedback on the same text with the same prompt across different sessions. It also produces grammatically accurate but sometimes redundant or over-corrected feedback. The study discusses the implications of these differences for second language (L2) writing instruction and the integration of AI tools in pedagogical practices.
APA_reference: Lin, S., & Crosthwaite, P. (2024). The grass is not always greener: Teacher vs. GPT-assisted written corrective feedback. System, 127, 103529. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2024.103529

title: The impact of different conversational generative AI chatbots on EFL learners: An analysis of willingness to communicate, foreign language speaking anxiety, and self-perceived communicative competence
authors: Chenghao Wang, Bin Zou, Yiran Du, Zixun Wang
summary: This study investigates the impact of different conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) chatbots on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' willingness to communicate (WTC), foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA), self-perceived communicative competence (SPCC), and speaking performance. The study involved three groups of Chinese undergraduate students: a control group (teacher-led interaction), an experimental group using a text- and voice-based GenAI chatbot (Typebot), and another experimental group using a GenAI chatbot with text, voice, and a human-like avatar (D-ID Agent). Quantitative analysis showed that the avatar group experienced significant improvements in WTC and SPCC and a notable reduction in FLSA compared to the control group. However, speaking performance did not significantly differ across the groups. Qualitative data from interviews indicated that the human-like avatars provided an immersive learning experience and emotional support, fostering a more engaging and supportive environment.
APA_reference: Wang, C., Zou, B., Du, Y., & Wang, Z. (2024). title: Investigating the capabilities of large language model-based task-oriented dialogue chatbots from a learner's perspective

summary: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Model (LLM)-based task-oriented dialogue (TOD) chatbots from the perspective of second language (L2) learners. The researchers developed two TOD conversational agents using Poe AI, a platform with easy-to-use LLM-based chatbot-building tools. South Korean undergraduate L2 students were tasked with engaging in two distinct chatbot-based linguistic activities and subsequently completed a survey on their perceptions. The findings indicated that the chatbots' language was perceived as highly natural and contextually appropriate. The chatbots demonstrated a strong ability to understand dialogue context and maintain conversational flow. Overall, learners rated the chatbots positively as a useful resource for L2 learning, noting that they felt motivated and interested in the interactions, which could maximize learning effects.

title: ChatGPT affordance for logic learning strategies and its usefulness for developing knowledge and quality of logic in English argumentative writing
authors: Ruofei Zhang, Di Zou, Gary Cheng
summary: This study developed a GPT-4-based logic learning bot to explore its affordances for logic learning strategies and its effectiveness in developing logical knowledge and writing quality. Forty EFL university students participated in the study, which employed a mixed-methods approach involving the analysis of learner-bot conversations, pre-post knowledge tests, essay writing tasks, and semi-structured interviews. The findings revealed that ChatGPT afforded 12 sub-strategies of logic learning, with 'Gathering' and 'Exercising' strategies being the most frequently used. These strategies significantly improved participants' knowledge and quality of logic in English argumentative writing. The study identifies key features of ChatGPT that influence the effectiveness of these strategies and provides implications for its implementation in logic learning.

title: The educational affordances and challenges of generative AI in Global Englishes-oriented materials development and implementation: A critical ecological perspective
authors: Alfred W.T. Lo
summary: This study explores the use of Generative AI (GenAI) for developing and implementing Global Englishes (GE)-oriented teaching materials from the perspective of secondary school teachers in China. Adopting a critical ecological perspective, the research used qualitative methods, including reflective journals, classroom observations, and interviews, to analyze teachers' experiences. The findings indicate that GenAI enhances efficiency in material creation, supports student-centered design, integrates with other digital tools, and increases student engagement. However, challenges were identified, such as rigid curricula, inaccuracies in AI-generated content, technical problems, and the inability of AI to replace the unique insights and 'human touch' of teachers. The study concludes that while GenAI is a promising tool for GE-oriented materials development, the teacher's role remains essential in Global Englishes Language Teaching (GELT).
APA_reference: Lo, A. W. T. (2025). The educational affordances and challenges of generative AI in Global Englishes-oriented materials development and implementation: A critical ecological perspective. System, 130, 103610. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2025.103610

title: GenAI as a translation assistant? A corpus-based study on lexical and syntactic complexity of GPT-post-edited learner translation
authors: Ho Ling Kwok, Yining Shi, Han Xu, Dechao Li, Kanglong Liu
summary: This corpus-based study investigates the impact of using Generative AI (specifically GPT-3.5) as a post-editing tool on the translations of second language (L2) learners in Hong Kong. It compares the lexical and syntactic complexity of translations produced by students with and without GPT post-editing. The findings show that GPT post-editing significantly improved lexical complexity (density, diversity, and sophistication). However, its effect on syntactic complexity was inconsistent: while it led to longer clauses and more complex nominals, it also resulted in less subordination and fewer verbal structures compared to the non-edited translations. The study suggests that while GenAI is a promising tool for enhancing translation, it also introduces a distinct 'AI footprint' and highlights the need for critical AI literacy in translation education.
APA_reference: Kwok, H. L., Shi, Y., Xu, H., Li, D., & Liu, K. (2025). GenAI as a translation assistant? A corpus-based study on lexical and syntactic complexity of GPT-post-edited learner translation. System, 130, 103618. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2025.103618

title: When Al meets source use: Exploring ChatGPT's potential in L2 summary writing assessment
authors: Haeyun Jin
summary: This study investigates ChatGPT's ability to score L2 summary writing compared to human raters, focusing on differences in rating results across writing criteria and decision-making in assessing source use. Using Many-Facet Rasch Measurement (MFRM) analysis, ratings of 90 student essays by an original GPT, a calibrated GPT, and two human raters were analyzed. Results showed the original GPT was the strictest rater, while the calibrated version aligned more closely with human raters but still showed significant gaps in assessing source-use. Qualitative analysis of raters' think-aloud protocols revealed ChatGPT's detailed, rule-based approach but also its lack of contextual flexibility and over-reliance on surface-level cues. The findings highlight ChatGPT's potential as a supplementary rating tool but underscore its limitations, pointing to the need for L2-specific training to better align its judgments with human standards.
APA_reference: Jin, H. (2025). When Al meets source use: Exploring ChatGPT's potential in L2 summary writing assessment. System, 133, 103737. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2025.103737

title: A word to the wise: Crafting impactful prompts for ChatGPT
authors: Myunghwan Hwang, Ki-Ho Lee, Hee-Kyung Lee
summary: This study examines 238 learner-generated prompts from ten Korean EFL graduate students to understand their linguistic features, prompt engineering strategies, and content-related issues, and how these factors impact the quality of ChatGPT's responses, as measured by learner satisfaction. The findings indicate that learners typically used concise, minimally strategic prompts, with prompts in English receiving higher satisfaction ratings. High-satisfaction prompts were characterized by clear, interconnected strategies such as contextualization and specifying text style, tone, and length. Conversely, low-satisfaction prompts often featured fragmented strategies and repetition. The study identified six primary problems in prompts that negatively affected response quality: lack of context, unclear feedback, dual requests, grammatical errors, abstract vocabulary, and excessive constraints. The authors conclude that effective interaction with ChatGPT requires clear, contextually rich, and strategically designed prompts, highlighting a need to equip EFL learners with specific prompting techniques for AI-assisted learning.

title: EFL learners' perceptual perezhivaniya and actual writing revision behaviors mediated by GenAI: A sociocultural theory perspective
authors: Lili Qin, Jingjing Dong
summary: The study investigates the relationship between 19 Chinese university EFL learners' perceived experiences (perezhivaniya) and their actual behaviors when using Generative AI (GenAI) for L2 writing revision tasks. Using a mixed-methods approach including Q-methodology, interviews, and screen-recording (Translog), the research identifies three learner profiles: active content-focused agents, passive language-focused perceivers, and multidimensional-focused participants. A key finding is the general consistency between learners' perceptions and behaviors, particularly regarding content. However, inconsistencies were noted, such as a subconscious focus on text alignment that was not perceptually prioritized. The study, framed by Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, highlights the need for individualized pedagogical strategies and policies to foster learner agency and mitigate overreliance on AI.

title: Exploring the efficacy of ChatGPT-4 feedback in second language Spanish writing
authors: Dimaris Barrios-Beltran
summary: This qualitative study investigates the use of ChatGPT-4 to provide feedback on the writing of advanced Spanish second language (L2) learners. Through thematic analysis of questionnaires, writing revisions, and student reflections, the study explores how AI-generated feedback compares to traditional instructor input. Participants received feedback from both their instructor and a custom ChatGPT-4 on a formal writing task. Findings indicate that while ChatGPT-4 delivered detailed, rubric-aligned, and efficient feedback that helped with revisions, students consistently preferred the personalized, context-sensitive feedback from their instructor. The study highlights AI's potential for enhancing early-stage drafting but also reveals student concerns about overreliance, data privacy, plagiarism, and the lack of clear institutional policies. The author concludes that integrating AI literacy into education is crucial for ensuring these tools are used critically, ethically, and effectively, preferably in a hybrid model that complements human instruction.

title: Generative AI tools and empowerment in L2 academic writing
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse, Yuwei Wan, Chenze Wu, Meixin Wu, Tsz Ying Ho
summary: This qualitative study explores how 21 postgraduate L2 writers in Hong Kong perceive and use Generative AI (GenAI) in their academic writing during their first month of study. Using the frameworks of critical digital literacies (CDL), agency, and empowerment, the research conducted focus group interviews to understand how these students position themselves relative to GenAI and their instructors' policies. Findings indicate that students integrate GenAI for tasks like linguistic support, summarizing, and structuring, which they perceive as empowering. However, this may be a 'false empowerment' as they lack a deep critical awareness of the tools' workings. title: Automated scoring in the era of artificial intelligence: An empirical study with Turkish essays
authors: Burak Aydın, Tarık Kışla, Nursel Tan Elmas, Okan Bulut
summary: This study empirically evaluates the performance of OpenAI's GPT-4o for automated scoring (AS) of Turkish essays written by second language learners. Using a zero-shot approach with a rubric based on the Common European Framework of Reference, the study compared AI-generated scores with those from professional human raters for a dataset of 590 essays. The results indicate a strong alignment between human and AI scores, with a Quadratic Weighted Kappa of 0.72 and a Pearson correlation of 0.73. The analysis also explored rater effects, finding that factors like rater experience and gender had modest influences on score discrepancies. The findings support the potential of AI for scoring in under-represented languages like Turkish but also highlight sources of disagreement, such as the AI's stricter penalization of certain errors. The study concludes that while promising, AI should be used as a complementary tool to human raters.
APA_reference: Aydın, B., Kışla, T., Elmas, N. T., & Bulut, O. (2025). Automated scoring in the era of artificial intelligence: An empirical study with Turkish essays. System, 133, 103784. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2025.103784

summary: This study aimed to develop and validate a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) literacy scale specifically for the Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) context. title: Development and validation of the PA-SDA Scale: Measuring personal attributes in AI-integrated self-directed language learning
authors: Belle Li, Zhuo Zhang, Victoria Lowell, Chaoran Wang, Curtis J. Bonk
summary: This study introduces the Personal Attributes for Self-Directed AI Learning (PA-SDA) Scale. This 44-item instrument measures key personal attributes of language learners who use generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT. An initial pool of items was constructed through an extensive literature review, pilot testing, and expert review. We validated the scale with 699 global language learners, and the sample was divided into two independent subsamples for exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses to achieve cross-validation of the factorial structure. The final scale comprises five primary constructs: Attitude (perceived usefulness, ease of use, understanding limitations), Strategy Use (behavioral, cognitive/meta-cognitive, overall), Motivation, Self-efficacy, and Resource Use. Each primary construct contains subconstructs. The PA-SDA scale represents the first validated instrument for measuring personal attributes in AI-integrated SDL contexts, advancing theory by operationalizing qualitative insights, providing researchers with a reliable assessment tool, and offering educators means to evaluate learners’ AI-learning readiness.
APA_reference: Li, B., Zhang, Z., Lowell, V., Wang, C., & Bonk, C. J. (2025). Development and validation of the PA-SDA Scale: Measuring personal attributes in AI-integrated self-directed language learning. System, 133, 103793. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.system.2025.103793

title: Enhancing translation accuracy and learning outcomes for low-resource languages: AI fine-tuning and learner adoption factors

summary: This study investigates optimizing AI models for translating low-resource languages (LRLs) and the factors influencing student adoption of these tools. The research consists of two parts. authors: Seungjin Hong, Yu Kyoung Shin
summary: This study investigates the impact of three different levels of ChatGPT integration (Restricted, Guided, and Free use) on the academic writing skills of 103 L2-English learners in South Korea. Through a quasi-experimental design comparing three groups in English essay writing courses taught by the same instructor, the study found that both groups with AI access (Guided and Free) significantly outperformed the group with no access (Restricted). An interview with the instructor provided qualitative insights, suggesting that structured guidance is vital for content development, whereas greater autonomy may be beneficial for other writing aspects. The findings advocate for a strategic and balanced integration of AI in L2 writing instruction.

title: Doctoral students' use of Generative AI and their engagement in English for Research Publication Purposes writing: An activity theory perspective
authors: Chenxi Du, Yingli Yang
summary: Drawing on Activity Theory, this multiple-case study investigated how and why three Chinese doctoral students used Generative AI (ChatGPT) for English for Research Publication Purposes (ERPP) writing. Data from GenAI dialogue histories, interviews, and reflective journals were thematically analyzed. Findings revealed that students used GenAI for language, content, and format-related tasks, driven by contradictions within their academic activity system (e.g., workload vs. time). While GenAI use resolved these initial contradictions and enhanced writing engagement, it also introduced new contradictions related to academic integrity and the need to validate AI output, which in turn could lead to disengagement. The impact of GenAI was idiosyncratic, influenced by individual factors like AI literacy and self-efficacy.

summary: This mixed-method study investigates the factors influencing Chinese university students' intention and application of Generative AI (GAI) in both their first (L1 Chinese) and second (L2 English) language writing, across formal and informal contexts. authors: Behice Ceyda Cengiz, Zeynep Bilki, Amine Hatun Ataş, Berkan Celik
summary: This study investigates how B1-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in Türkiye engage with ChatGPT-generated feedback on their opinion essays. summary: This mixed-method study investigated the metacognitive awareness of 452 undergraduate EFL students in a semester-long writing course in China as they used ChatGPT for academic writing feedback. title: Impacts of GenAI-assisted collaborative prewriting on university EFL students' interactions with GenAI, outline quality, and task motivation
authors: Jun Wang, Kai Guo
summary: This study investigated a novel approach, GenAI-assisted collaborative prewriting (GACP), comparing it with GenAI-assisted individual prewriting (GAIP) among 69 Chinese undergraduate EFL students. Using a within-subjects design, the study analyzed chat histories, writing outlines, and post-task questionnaires. Findings revealed that while brainstorming was the primary use of GenAI in both conditions, peer collaboration in the GACP group led to more effective prompting, higher quality content in outlines, and reduced misuse of the tool (i.e., ghostwriting). Students in the GACP condition also reported greater confidence in their writing outcomes. However, no significant differences were found in the organizational or linguistic quality of the outlines, or in overall task motivation between the two conditions. The study suggests that collaborative use of GenAI can enrich student learning experiences in EFL writing.

title: University EFL instructors' engagement with generative AI: A cross-cultural analysis
authors: Safaa M. Abdelhalim, Asma A. Alsahil, Clare Baek, Mark Warschauer
summary: This study investigates the integration of Generative AI (GenAI) by university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instructors in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Mexico, and Turkey. Using a framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with Sociocultural Theory (SCT), the research analyzes survey data from 307 instructors. The findings reveal significant cross-national differences in pedagogical beliefs and perceived institutional support. While Mexican and Turkish instructors leaned towards constructivist approaches, their Saudi and Egyptian counterparts favored transmissive methods. Constructivist beliefs were positively correlated with higher perceived utility and ease of use of GenAI. Attitude towards GenAI was the strongest predictor of intention to use, which, along with perceived usefulness, predicted actual use. However, perceived trust and institutional support did not directly drive usage, indicating a gap between intention and practice. The study highlights the need for culturally responsive policies and professional development to effectively integrate AI in language education.

title: Investigating students' cognitive processes in generative AI-assisted digital multimodal composing and traditional writing
authors: Meilu Liu, Lawrence Jun Zhang, Christine Biebricher
summary: This qualitative study explores the cognitive processes of two groups of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) undergraduate students over two weeks. One group completed a traditional argumentative essay, while the other created a multimodal PowerPoint (PPT) presentation, both using generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Bing Chat. Data were collected through screen recordings with think-aloud protocols, the final texts, and interviews. The study found different patterns in text production between the groups. The PPT group focused more on creating bridge texts and hierarchical examples, and tended to directly use summarized search results from Bing Chat. In contrast, the essay group delved deeper into the source materials. For image generation, students in the PPT group used text descriptions from ChatGPT as prompts for Bing Image Creator, refined the AI-generated images, and evaluated them based on criteria such as relevance, reasonability, and style. The study discusses the pedagogical implications of using generative AI for multimodal composing.
APA_reference: Liu, M., Zhang, L. J., & Biebricher, C. (2024). Investigating students' cognitive processes in generative AI-assisted digital multimodal composing and traditional writing. Computers & Education, 211, 104977. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104977

title: Improving elementary EFL speaking skills with generative AI chatbots: Exploring individual and paired interactions
authors: Tzu-Yu Tai, Howard Hao-Jan Chen
summary: This study investigated the impact of a GAI chatbot, CoolE Bot, on the English speaking skills of 85 elementary school EFL learners in Taiwan. Over a three-week summer program, participants were divided into three groups: individual interaction with the chatbot (I-Bot), paired interaction (P-Bot), and a control group with conventional classroom interaction (No-Bot). Quantitative analysis of pre- and post-speaking tests revealed that both chatbot groups significantly outperformed the control group, with no significant difference between the I-Bot and P-Bot groups. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews indicated that learners perceived the chatbot as enjoyable, motivating, and supportive. Key positive features included its coherent conversational ability, human-like voice, diverse topics, and its role in reducing speaking anxiety and building confidence. The study found that individual interactions fostered personalized, self-directed learning, while paired interactions promoted social learning and collaborative problem-solving.
APA_reference: Tai, T.-Y., & Chen, H. H.-J. (2024). Improving elementary EFL speaking skills with generative AI chatbots: Exploring individual and paired interactions. Computers & Education, 220, 105112. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105112

title: Self-assessment accuracy in the age of artificial Intelligence: Differential effects of LLM-generated feedback
authors: Lucas W. Liebenow, Fabian T.C. Schmidt, Jennifer Meyer, Johanna Fleckenstein
summary: This study investigates the effect of LLM-generated feedback on students' self-assessment accuracy (SAA) in the context of writing an argumentative essay in English as a foreign language. Through a randomized control experiment with 459 upper secondary students, the researchers examined whether feedback from GPT-3.5-turbo could improve SAA, and whether this effect was moderated by students' initial performance or SAA levels. The results showed no overall main effect of the feedback on SAA. However, a significant interaction effect was found: students with lower initial SAA (i.e., less accurate self-assessors) significantly improved their SAA after receiving feedback compared to a control group. Conversely, exploratory analyses suggested that students who were already highly accurate did not benefit and their SAA even decreased. The study concludes that LLM-generated feedback can be a targeted, beneficial tool for lower-calibrated students but requires careful design to avoid being counterproductive for more accurate students.
APA_reference: Liebenow, L. W., Schmidt, F. T. C., Meyer, J., & Fleckenstein, J. (2025). Self-assessment accuracy in the age of artificial Intelligence: Differential effects of LLM-generated feedback. Computers & Education, 237, 105385. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105385

RQ2. Does feedback have differential effects depending on students' performance and SAA levels?
H1. Students receiving LLM-generated feedback improve their SAA more compared to students who do not receive feedback.
H2a. Lower-performing students can improve their SAA more with LLM-generated feedback compared to higher-performing students.
H2b. Students with lower SAA improve their SAA more with LLM-generated feedback compared to students with higher SAA.

benefits_affordances: LLM-generated feedback significantly improved the self-assessment accuracy (SAA) of students who were initially less accurate (lower-calibrated).
The feedback acted as a targeted aid, helping students who initially overestimated their performance to reduce this overestimation and improve their accuracy.
The feedback provided diagnostic cues that lower-accurate students could use to adjust and correct their self-assessment.
drawbacks: On average, there was no significant main effect of LLM-generated feedback on students' SAA.
For students who were already highly accurate, the feedback did not provide a benefit and may have even decreased their SAA.
The purely formative feedback, lacking a holistic score, might have caused highly accurate students to focus on minor flaws and underestimate their overall performance.
study_limitations: The study used only one type of feedback (elaborated, formative feedback without a holistic score), which may have limited its effectiveness, particularly for high-performing students.
The intervention was brief, conducted in a single 90-minute session, which limits understanding of long-term effects.
The control group received no feedback, making it difficult to assess the relative effectiveness of LLM feedback compared to other types of feedback (e.g., from teachers).
The findings are specific to GPT-3.5-turbo and may not be generalizable to newer or different LLMs.

students: Lower-calibrated students can benefit from LLM feedback to improve their self-assessment skills, a key component of self-regulated learning.
Higher-calibrated students may be negatively impacted by feedback that focuses solely on areas for improvement, suggesting a need for adaptive feedback design.
teachers: LLM-generated feedback offers a time-saving, cost-effective, and scalable method to provide individualized support for students' SAA.
institutions: Educational institutions can leverage LLMs to provide scalable, real-time feedback to support student learning and self-regulation.

policy_guidance: A careful implementation of LLM-generated feedback in classrooms is recommended.

emergent_themes: Differential effects of feedback: The impact of LLM feedback is not uniform and depends significantly on students' initial self-assessment accuracy.
The 'Robin-Hood effect': The intervention primarily benefits students who are most in need of support (lower-calibrated), redistributing the educational benefit to them.
Feedback as an anchor: LLM-generated comments can serve as an anchoring reference point, helping less-calibrated students to adjust their self-perceptions of performance.
emergent_issues: A significant emergent issue is the potential for well-designed LLM feedback to be detrimental to high-performing or well-calibrated students, disrupting their already accurate self-assessment processes if it only highlights flaws without affirming overall quality.

title: On the role of engagement in automated feedback effectiveness: Insights from keystroke logging
authors: Ronja Schiller, Johanna Fleckenstein, Lars Höft, Andrea Horbach, Jennifer Meyer
summary: This study investigates the role of learner engagement in the effectiveness of automated feedback on writing tasks. In a classroom experiment with 453 English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) learners, the researchers compared a group receiving feedback from a large language model (GPT-3.5 Turbo) with a control group receiving no feedback. Using keystroke logging, the study analyzed both behavioral engagement (e.g., number of keystrokes, typing time) and cognitive engagement (e.g., writing pauses) during text revision. The findings show that automated feedback increased behavioral engagement, which in turn mediated improvements in both revision and transfer task performance. While feedback influenced pausing behavior, these measures of cognitive engagement did not significantly mediate performance outcomes. The study concludes that behavioral engagement is a key mechanism through which automated feedback works and highlights the utility of keystroke logging for gaining insights into the feedback process.
APA_reference: Schiller, R., Fleckenstein, J., Höft, L., Horbach, A., & Meyer, J. (2025). On the role of engagement in automated feedback effectiveness: Insights from keystroke logging. Computers & Education, 238, 105386. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105386
research_h_q: RQ1. Do the edit distance and the total time on task, as indicators of behavioral engagement during text revision, mediate the expected effect of automated feedback on learners' revision performance and their performance on a transfer task?

RQ2. Do online measures obtained from keystroke logging (i.e., the total number of keystrokes and the typing time as indicators of behavioral learning engagement, and the total pausing time, the mean pause length, and the number of pauses) mediate the expected effect of automated feedback on learners' revision performance and their performance on a transfer task?
RQ3. Do the indicators of behavioral engagement differ in how much variance they explain in learners' performance?

The paper states the prompt instructed the LLM to provide feedback on content, structure, and language for upper secondary EFL learners, using a tabular format with hints and examples.
sample_size: N = 453 EFL learners in the 10th grade
duration: The maximum duration of a test session was 90 minutes. The revision task itself had no time limit.
learning_perceptions: N/A

benefits_affordances: Automated feedback significantly increased learners' behavioral engagement during text revision (measured by edit distance, time on task, keystrokes, and typing time).
Behavioral engagement fully mediated the positive effect of automated feedback on revision performance.

Higher levels of behavioral engagement during revision were associated with better performance on a subsequent transfer task, indicating a significant indirect effect of feedback on transfer performance.
drawbacks: The direct effect of automated feedback on transfer task performance was not significant.
Measures of cognitive engagement (writing pauses) did not significantly mediate the effect of feedback on either revision or transfer performance.
study_limitations: The accuracy of the automated scoring for text quality is limited and may contain measurement errors.
The quality of the LLM-generated feedback was not analyzed, so the possibility of hallucinations or incorrect information cannot be excluded.
The study design did not allow for a differentiated analysis of how learners engaged with specific aspects of the feedback (content, structure, language).
Methodological limitations in defining writing pauses, as thresholds were based on an initial writing task rather than a neutral copy task.
The interpretation of time-related process measures (e.g., typing time, total time on task) is ambiguous, as they could include off-task behavior.

The quantitative operationalization of engagement may not fully capture the complexity of the construct, and distinguishing between behavioral and cognitive dimensions is challenging with the methods used.

students: Students who receive automated feedback tend to engage more behaviorally in revision tasks, which is associated with improved writing performance on both the immediate task and subsequent tasks.
teachers: N/A
institutions: N/A

policy_guidance: Future research and development of educational tools should combine automated feedback systems with process measures (like keystroke logging) to better explain learners' responses and improve feedback effectiveness.
The inclusion of learners' behavior in the investigation of learning effects is increasingly relevant and should be considered in future research, especially given the rise of AI-generated feedback.
emergent_themes: Behavioral engagement as a key mediator for feedback effectiveness, suggesting the process of engagement is as important as the feedback content itself.
The distinction and differential utility of 'online' process measures (from keystroke logging) versus 'offline' measures (from log files/text comparison) in capturing learning engagement.

The complexity of measuring cognitive engagement through process data like writing pauses, whose meaning varies by context (e.g., revision with vs. without feedback) and does not consistently predict performance.
emergent_issues: The methodological challenge of interpreting process data, as behaviors like pausing or time on task can signify either productive cognitive engagement or off-task behavior, requiring more advanced or multimodal validation methods (e.g., eye-tracking).
The difficulty in using process data to clearly distinguish between the behavioral and cognitive dimensions of learning engagement, as they are often intertwined during complex tasks like writing.

title: Using ChatGPT to bring non-player characters to life: Effects on students' storyline-driven game-based writing learning
authors: Ya Xiao, Danling Li, Kai Guo
summary: This study investigates the integration of ChatGPT into non-player characters (NPCs) within a storyline-driven, game-based learning environment for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction. Using a quasi-experimental design with two classes of Chinese undergraduate students, the research compared the effects of interacting with ChatGPT-powered NPCs (n=42) versus conventional NPCs (n=43) on students' affective factors (intrinsic motivation, situational interest), cognitive factors (cognitive load, effort regulation), and argumentative writing performance. Quantitative data from questionnaires and essay evaluations were supplemented with qualitative analysis of students' chat histories with the AI-powered NPCs. The findings indicate that the ChatGPT-enhanced NPCs significantly improved students' intrinsic motivation, situational interest, and effort regulation without increasing cognitive load. Furthermore, students in the experimental group produced argumentative essays that were clearer, more elaborated, persuasive, and better at addressing opposing views. The study also identified various conversational strategies students employed, demonstrating a deeper and more interactive engagement with the learning content.

title: The more the merrier? Examining the effects of a conversational agent on EFL learners' speaking in three conditions
authors: Yao Ma, Zhuo Wang, Hui Pang
summary: This study investigates the impact of a generative AI conversational agent, TalkFriend, on the oral English proficiency of 45 EFL university students in China. Using a multi-modal approach including oral tests, questionnaires, interviews, and EEG brainwave data, the research compares students interacting with the AI individually versus in pairs ('Lead' and 'Assisting' roles). The findings indicate that while all participants showed significant gains in fluency, the paired learning groups demonstrated superior improvements in communicative confidence. The 'Lead' learners in pairs also showed a marked increase in learning interest. The study, interpreted through Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), proposes a four-quadrant 'emotional ZPD' model that emphasizes the interplay of cognitive support from AI and socio-emotional support from peers for optimizing AI-assisted language learning.
APA_reference: Ma, Y., Wang, Z., & Pang, H. (2025). The more the merrier? Examining the effects of a conversational agent on EFL learners' speaking in three conditions. Computers & Education, 239, 105442. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105442

title: Self-regulation plus individual interests? A design-based study on the development of a GenAI-empowered platform for self-directed out-of-class reading
authors: Mengru Pan, Chun Lai, Kai Guo, Jing Huang
summary: This study employed a design-based research (DBR) methodology over three semesters to develop and refine a GenAI-empowered online platform for self-directed out-of-class reading. It compared three approaches for supporting English as a Foreign Language (EFL) university students in China: a conventional method with a preset reading pool and human-delivered Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) training (Cycle 0), a platform with GenAI-recommended materials and chatbot-supported SRL (Cycle 1), and a refined platform that also incorporated students' personal interests for material recommendation (Cycle 2). Using a mix of quantitative and qualitative data, the study found that the final design, which combined interest-based reading recommendations with personalized, interactive SRL support via a ChatGPT-powered chatbot, was most effective in enhancing students' self-regulated reading strategy use and self-directed reading behaviors. The findings led to the development of design principles for creating effective GenAI-supported tools for self-directed learning.
APA_reference: Pan, M., Lai, C., Guo, K., & Huang, J. (2026). Self-regulation plus individual interests? A design-based study on the development of a GenAI-empowered platform for self-directed out-of-class reading. Computers & Education, 241, 105474. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105474

RQ2: How effective is the GenAI chatbot-supported online reading platform in improving students' self-regulated reading strategy use?
RQ3: How effective is the GenAI chatbot-supported online reading platform in improving students' self-directed reading?

The criteria for reading level are as follows: A1: I can understand familiar names, words/signs and very simple sentences, for example on notices and posters or in catalogues. A2: I can read very short, simple texts. summary: This study examines the implications of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in English language teacher education in Türkiye, focusing on the perceptions and responses of teacher educators. title: Unpacking the role of motivation and enjoyment in AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE): A mixed-method investigation in the Chinese context
authors: Guangxiang Leon Liu, Ron Darvin, Chaojun Ma
summary: This study investigates how Chinese university students' second language (L2) motivation, specifically their 'ideal L2 self' and 'ought-to L2 self', and their sense of enjoyment influence their engagement in AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE). Using an explanatory sequential mixed-method design with 690 survey participants and 12 interviewees, the research found that the ideal L2 self significantly predicts both enjoyment and AI-IDLE participation. In contrast, the ought-to L2 self only predicts enjoyment directly. The study reveals that enjoyment is a crucial mediator, partially channeling the effect of the ideal L2 self and fully channeling the effect of the ought-to L2 self on AI-IDLE. Qualitative data further illustrates that promotion-focused motives (ideal L2 self) drive autonomous AI use for personal language goals, while prevention-focused motives (ought-to L2 self) are linked to using AI for formal coursework. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between motivation and enjoyment in shaping learners' engagement with generative AI for language learning.

title: Unleashing pre-service language teachers' productivity with generative AI: Emotions, appraisal and coping strategies
authors: Hongbiao Yin, Chan Wang, Zhijun Liu
summary: This study investigates the emotional experiences of 1,683 pre-service language teachers with generative AI and how these experiences relate to their AI-enabled productivity. It explores the mediating roles of cognitive appraisal (viewing AI as a challenge or hindrance) and coping strategies (approach-oriented vs. avoidance-oriented). The findings indicate that positive emotions like achievement and challenge are linked to higher productivity, primarily through the pathway of appraising AI as a challenge and adopting positive reinterpretation as a coping strategy. Conversely, negative emotions like loss and deterrence are associated with hindrance appraisal and avoidance coping, which do not enhance productivity. The study concludes that challenge appraisal and positive reinterpretation are key sequential mediators, offering insights for supporting teachers in effectively integrating AI into language education.

title: Flow in ChatGPT-based logic learning and its influences on logic and self-efficacy in English argumentative writing
authors: Ruofei Zhang, Di Zou, Gary Cheng, Haoran Xie
summary: This study investigates the concept of 'flow'—a state of full engagement—in a ChatGPT-based learning environment designed to teach logic in English argumentative writing. The researchers developed a GPT-4-based bot and studied 40 Chinese university EFL students using questionnaires, eye-tracking, knowledge tests, writing tasks, and interviews. Findings indicate that the ChatGPT environment strongly supports the antecedents of flow, particularly skill-challenge balance and playability. Students who experienced a deeper state of flow demonstrated a better understanding of argumentative logic. However, their writing self-efficacy decreased, possibly due to a heightened awareness of the complexities involved. The study provides insights into how AI can influence learning experiences and outcomes in language education.

title: Demystifying large language models in second language development research
authors: Yan Cong
summary: This study introduces and operationalizes 'LLM-Surprisal'—a numeric representation of the interplay between lexical diversity and syntactic complexity—as a metric for automatic writing assessment. The author develops an LLM-based pipeline to compute Surprisal scores for English writing samples from Chinese L2 learners and L1 speakers. The study finds that LLM-Surprisal can effectively distinguish between L1 and L2 writing, track developmental stages in L2 learners, and predict proficiency scores assigned by human raters. By comparing Surprisal with classic L2 writing indices, the research demonstrates that LLMs are promising tools for enhancing L2 development research, offering a more nuanced, computational approach to assessing and understanding the process.

title: Towards LLM-assisted move annotation: Leveraging ChatGPT-4 to analyse the genre structure of CEO statements in corporate social responsibility reports
authors: Danni Yu
summary: This study investigates the feasibility of using ChatGPT-4 to automate the annotation of rhetorical moves in a professional genre: CEO statements from corporate social responsibility (CSR) reports. The research proceeded in two phases: first, a prompt was designed and optimized using a corpus of 30 CEO statements. Second, the efficacy of the prompt was tested on a larger corpus of 50 CEO statements. The assessment found that ChatGPT-4's annotations achieved an accuracy of 87.14%. However, a double-annotation process revealed an intra-model inconsistency rate of 32.87%, highlighting the need for human verification in ambiguous cases. The study concludes that LLMs can significantly reduce the workload in developing move-annotated corpora, which are valuable pedagogical resources for ESP practitioners. Furthermore, integrating LLMs into genre analysis can prompt researchers to refine their theoretical frameworks.

title: Rhetorical distinctions: Comparing metadiscourse in essays by ChatGPT and students
authors: Feng (Kevin) Jiang, Ken Hyland
summary: This study investigates the use of metadiscourse in argumentative essays generated by ChatGPT compared to those written by British university students. Using Hyland's (2005) framework, the analysis of interactive and interactional metadiscourse reveals significant rhetorical and linguistic differences. The findings show that ChatGPT's essays, while structurally coherent and logical, have a markedly lower frequency of interactional metadiscourse (e.g., hedges, boosters, attitude markers), resulting in a more impersonal and expository tone. In contrast, student essays display greater rhetorical engagement through nuanced stance markers and personalized expressions to foster reader interaction. The study concludes that these differences highlight the complementary roles of AI and human authorship in academic writing, suggesting that while AI can model structural coherence, it currently lacks the nuanced, audience-aware engagement characteristic of human writing.
APA_reference: Jiang, F. (Kevin), & Hyland, K. (2025). Rhetorical distinctions: Comparing metadiscourse in essays by ChatGPT and students. English for Specific Purposes, 79, 17-29. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esp.2025.03.001

title: Graduate students' use of ChatGPT for academic text revision: Behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement
authors: Svetlana Koltovskaia, Payam Rahmati, Hooman Saeli
summary: This study examined how six Iranian graduate ESL students in STEM fields engaged with ChatGPT for revising their academic research proposals. Using a tripartite framework of behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement, the research analyzed students' texts, screencasts, stimulated recall comments, interviews, and surveys. Findings indicate that students used ChatGPT behaviorally for lower-order concerns, particularly style and paraphrasing, while demonstrating high cognitive engagement by critically evaluating and often rejecting inaccurate feedback. Affectively, students were highly satisfied, viewing ChatGPT as a tool to enhance professionalism. The study concludes that students can engage with AI feedback responsibly and critically, and offers insights for integrating ChatGPT into L2 writing instruction.

title: Conceptualising and cultivating Critical GAI Literacy in doctoral academic writing
authors: Amy Wanyu Ou, Baraa Khuder, Sindija Franzetti, Raffaella Negretti
summary: This study addresses the need for L2 writers, particularly at the doctoral level, to develop critical skills for using Generative AI (GAI) ethically and effectively. The researchers conceptualize 'Critical GAI Literacy' (C-GAI-L) and develop a micro-curriculum based on self-regulated learning theory to foster these skills. The study was conducted with 60 PhD students at a Swedish university, examining their perspectives and strategies for using GAI in academic writing. Findings indicate that students began with varied attitudes and limited knowledge but, through the self-directed learning process, developed a more nuanced understanding of GAI's ethical issues, improved their prompting methods, and increased their awareness of text ownership. title: AI or student writing? Analyzing the situational and linguistic characteristics of undergraduate student writing and AI-generated assignments
authors: Larissa Goulart, Marine Laísa Matte, Alanna Mendoza, Lee Alvarado, Ingrid Veloso
summary: This study explores the extent to which AI-generated assignments can replicate the situational and linguistic features of student-authored assignments in an English as a Foreign Language (EFL) context. Using a corpus of undergraduate assignments (essays, critiques, personal narratives), the researchers compare student responses with outputs from ChatGPT for the same prompts. The study employs a register approach, following Biber and Conrad's (2019) framework, which includes situational analysis, linguistic analysis (Multi-Dimensional Analysis), and functional interpretation. The findings indicate that while AI can mirror personal narratives, it struggles to replicate the complex interplay of communicative purposes and situational features (like use of recent sources) found in student essays and critiques. Linguistically, AI-generated texts were found to be more informationally dense, explicit, less involved, and more homogenous than student writing. The study aims to inform writing instructors about the strengths and limitations of AI tools to better guide students in using these technologies.

title: Translanguaging with generative AI in EFL writing: Students' practices and perceptions
authors: Wanli Yang, Chenming Lin
summary: This qualitative study explores how six lower to intermediate proficiency EFL students in China use a generative AI, ERNIE Bot, in their writing process. Through a translanguaging lens, the study analyzes semi-structured interviews and artefacts (interaction logs, essays) to understand students' practices and perceptions. Findings show that students used their native language (Chinese) for problem-solving, idea generation with semiotic resources, and iteratively transforming ideas into English. While students appreciated the AI's support and feedback, they also experienced mixed emotions, including anxiety and a fear of overreliance. The study concludes that while generative AI can support translanguaging and enhance writing skills, its integration requires careful pedagogical guidance to foster self-directed learning and address potential drawbacks.

title: Collaborative writing based on generative AI models: Revision and deliberation processes in German as a foreign language
authors: Marije Michel, Iryna Bazhutkina, Niklas Abel, Carola Strobl
summary: This study investigates how generative AI (GenAI) influences collaborative revision and deliberation processes among second language (L2) learners of German. In a classroom-based intervention, four pairs of university students (N=8) revised a synthesis text they had co-authored, based on a guided comparison with two model texts generated by ChatGPT. The study analyzed screen recordings and dialogues to identify collaboration patterns and assessed changes in text quality using the Functional Adequacy framework. Findings show that pairs exhibiting truly collaborative patterns engaged in more language-related episodes (LREs) and achieved greater improvements in text quality. The intervention successfully triggered critical discussions about both language and task-related aspects, highlighting GenAI's potential as a pedagogical tool for L2 writing when implemented with clear guidance and tasks that foster critical engagement.

title: The need for critical digital literacies in generative AI-mediated L2 writing
authors: Ron Darvin
summary: This article argues for the necessity of critical digital literacies (CDL) when using generative AI (GenAI) in L2 writing. Drawing from a case study of secondary school students in Canada, the paper examines their dispositions towards GenAI tools, the influence of platform design, and material inequalities affecting their use. It proposes materiality, indexicality, and ideology as key constructs for developing CDL. These constructs help learners and educators understand how platform designs, resource access, and algorithmic processes can steer users towards specific interactions and reproduce societal biases. The paper suggests that by critically analyzing how GenAI privileges certain ways of thinking and writing, L2 writers can better comprehend how these technologies shape their authorial identities.

title: Investigating L2 writers’ critical AI literacy in AI-assisted writing: An APSE model
authors: Chaoran Wang, Zhaozhe Wang
summary: This qualitative case study investigated how L2 writers in two first-year US writing classes used ChatGPT and the critical AI literacy (CAIL) they demonstrated. Findings show students used AI for various writing stages, from brainstorming to sourcing. The study proposes an APSE model of CAIL based on four identified dimensions: (1) critical Awareness of AI, (2) critical Positionality, (3) critical Strategies for interaction, and (4) critical Evaluation of AI affordances. The model highlights the specific challenges L2 writers face in critically leveraging AI's resources. Pedagogical implications include the need for explicit CAIL instruction and developing students' AI feedback literacy and self-directed learning skills.
APA_reference: Wang, C., & Wang, Z. (2025). Investigating L2 writers’ critical AI literacy in AI-assisted writing: An APSE model. Journal of Second Language Writing, 67, 101187. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jslw.2025.101187
research_h_q: How do L2 students use ChatGPT, a popular generative AI technology, to assist with their writing?
How are the L2 student writers' CAIL (or lack thereof) evidenced in their interactions with ChatGPT and their linguistic and rhetorical decision-making?

title: University students' engagement with generative AI-supported automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback
authors: Steven Yeung
summary: This study examines the behavioural, cognitive, and affective engagement of four undergraduate engineering students in Hong Kong with feedback from a generative AI-powered automated writing evaluation (AWE) platform called Learnalytics. Using a qualitative, multiple-case study approach, data was collected through student drafts, screen recordings, stimulated recall sessions, and interviews. The findings reveal that the forms and levels of student engagement were mediated by individual differences, including writing proficiency, and various aspects of their writing process and experiences. The study aims to contribute to the research on the intersection of generative AI and L2 writing by providing insights into how students engage with GAI-generated AWE feedback.
APA_reference: Yeung, S. (2025). University students' engagement with generative AI-supported automated writing evaluation (AWE) feedback. Journal of Second Language Writing, 68, 101203. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jslw.2025.101203

title: Generative AI is useful for second language writing, but when, why, and for how long do learners use it?
authors: Haerim Hwang, Xingyu Chang, Jiaxin Sun
summary: The study investigates how L2 English learners use ChatGPT during a timed argumentative writing task by analyzing screen recordings and their perceptions from a post-task survey. Using frequency, time-series, and semantic network analyses, the research finds that learners primarily use ChatGPT for idea generation, especially in the initial stages, and less frequently for word/grammar checks, polishing, and example generation later on. While participants viewed ChatGPT positively for content creation and time management, they also raised concerns about accuracy and overreliance. The findings highlight ChatGPT's potential in L2 writing and underscore the need for digital literacy education.
APA_reference: Hwang, H., Chang, X., & Sun, J. (2025). Generative AI is useful for second language writing, but when, why, and for how long do learners use it? Journal of Second Language Writing, 69, 101230. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jslw.2025.101230

title: From algorithms to annotations: Rethinking feedback practices in academic writing through AI-human comparison
authors: Hadi Kashiha
summary: This study compares the feedback provided by ChatGPT and human instructors on 200 academic introductions written by Malaysian L2 students. It analyzes two key dimensions: epistemic strategies (assertiveness vs. mitigation) and delivery methods (monologic vs. dialogic). The findings indicate that while both sources use mitigation, instructors are more assertive and employ more dialogic feedback, reflecting their authoritative and interactive pedagogical role. In contrast, ChatGPT provides predominantly monologic feedback that is grammatically sound but static and less adaptive. The study concludes that AI feedback can complement human expertise by handling surface-level issues, but it lacks the interpersonal depth and contextual adaptability of instructor feedback, advocating for a blended feedback model.
APA_reference: Kashiha, H. (2025). From algorithms to annotations: Rethinking feedback practices in academic writing through AI-human comparison. Journal of Second Language Writing, 70, 101254. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jslw.2025.101254

title: Detecting and assessing AI-generated and human-produced texts: The case of second language writing teachers
authors: Loc Nguyen, Jessie S. Barrot
summary: The study investigates how second language (L2) writing teachers assess and differentiate between essays written by humans and those generated by ChatGPT. Six Vietnamese university instructors graded five essays from various authors (native and non-native students and lecturers, and ChatGPT-3.5) and were interviewed about their assessment process and detection strategies. Findings show that essays by a native English-speaking lecturer and ChatGPT received the highest scores, making them difficult to distinguish. Teachers struggled to consistently identify AI-generated texts, relying on their familiarity with L2 learner errors, exposure to native writing, and prior engagement with AI tools. The study concludes that distinguishing advanced AI writing from proficient human writing is a significant challenge, with implications for teacher training, assessment practices, and academic integrity policies.
APA_reference: Nguyen, L., & Barrot, J. S. (2024). Detecting and assessing AI-generated and human-produced texts: The case of second language writing teachers. Assessing Writing, 62, 100899. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asw.2024.100899

title: The impact of self-revision, machine translation, and ChatGPT on L2 writing: Raters' assessments, linguistic complexity, and error correction
authors: Minjoo Kim, Yuah V. Chon
summary: This study investigated the effectiveness of three proofreading methods—self-proofreading (SP), machine translation-assisted proofreading (MAP) using inverse translation, and ChatGPT-assisted proofreading (CAP)—on the L2 English writing of South Korean high school students. In a controlled experiment, 79 learners revised their texts using each method. Findings revealed that both MAP and CAP significantly improved overall writing quality compared to SP. Specifically, CAP led to longer texts with greater lexical diversity and syntactic complexity, although it reduced verb cohesion. Both AI tools were effective in reducing grammatical, mechanical, and sentence structure errors but failed to correct prepositional errors. The study provides practical recommendations for integrating these AI tools into L2 writing pedagogy, highlighting their distinct affordances and limitations.
APA_reference: Kim, M., & Chon, Y. V. (2025). The impact of self-revision, machine translation, and ChatGPT on L2 writing: Raters' assessments, linguistic complexity, and error correction. Assessing Writing, 65, 100950. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asw.2025.100950
research_h_q: How do SP, MAP, and CAP compare in terms of improving the holistic scores of L2 writing?
How do these proofreading tools impact linguistic complexity measures in L2 writing?
How do these tools affect language accuracy in the texts produced by L2 learners?

title: Investigating a customized generative AI chatbot for automated essay scoring in a disciplinary writing task
authors: Ge Lan, Yi Li, Jie Yang, Xuanzi He
summary: The study investigates the correlation between writing scores from a customized GenAI chatbot (powered by Claude-3-Opus) and English teachers for 254 technical progress reports written by engineering students in Hong Kong. A custom chatbot was built to mimic the teachers' marking procedures. The findings show a moderate positive correlation for the total score (r = 0.424) but weaker correlations for analytical domains. The chatbot performed better at assessing language (r = 0.364) and organization (r = 0.316) than task fulfillment (r = 0.275) and formatting (r = 0.186). The study concludes that while GenAI has limited capacity for overall automated assessment, it shows more promise for evaluating linguistic and structural features than content-related or multimodal aspects of disciplinary writing.
APA_reference: Lan, G., Li, Y., Yang, J., & He, X. (2025). Investigating a customized generative AI chatbot for automated essay scoring in a disciplinary writing task. Assessing Writing, 66, 100959. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asw.2025.100959

title: Challenges and opportunities of automated essay scoring for low-proficient L2 English writers
authors: Vanessa De Wilde, Orphée De Clercq
summary: This study investigates the feasibility of using Automated Essay Scoring (AES) for writing samples from 3,166 low-proficiency, young L2 English learners with L1 Dutch. The researchers compared a traditional feature-based machine learning approach with a deep learning approach that involved fine-tuning three large language models (RoBERTa, XLM-RoBERTa, and the Dutch model RobBERT). They also examined the impact of spelling errors by testing the models on both original and spell-checked versions of the texts. The results indicate that the deep learning approach, particularly the fine-tuned Dutch LLM (RobBERT), performed best, achieving a reliable agreement with human raters (QWK > .70). Interestingly, all models performed better on the original, uncorrected texts, suggesting that spell-checking is not necessary and may even be detrimental to AES performance for this learner group. The study concludes that AES is a promising tool for assessing beginner L2 writers, potentially saving teachers time and enabling more frequent assessment.
APA_reference: De Wilde, V., & De Clercq, O. (2025). Challenges and opportunities of automated essay scoring for low-proficient L2 English writers. Assessing Writing, 66, 100982. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asw.2025.100982

AES models perform more accurately on original, uncorrected texts than on spell-checked texts, which saves time and effort.

drawbacks: Feature-based AES models struggled to perform reliably with this dataset.

title: Integrating move analysis and sentence reconstruction in automated writing evaluation for L2 academic writers
authors: Bo-Ren Mau, Hui-Hsien Feng
summary: This study proposes and evaluates GURUS, a genre-based automated writing evaluation (AWE) system designed to assist L2 writers with academic abstracts. Grounded in second language acquisition (SLA) theories, GURUS provides both indirect corrective feedback (CF) on rhetorical moves using an ensemble learning model (XGBoost) and direct CF through sentence reconstruction using a transformer-based LLM (T5). The system was trained on over one million sentences from medical abstracts. The evaluation, using automated metrics (F1-score, Brier score, BERTscore) and human assessment, showed that GURUS effectively classifies sentence moves and reconstructs sentences while maintaining semantic meaning. The study discusses the system's potential to enhance learners' genre awareness and proficiency in move-based academic writing, contrasting its specialized approach with the limitations of general-purpose LLMs like ChatGPT.
APA_reference: Mau, B.-R., & Feng, H.-H. (2025). Integrating move analysis and sentence reconstruction in automated writing evaluation for L2 academic writers. Assessing Writing, 66, 100984. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.asw.2025.100984

title: Effects of an AI-supported approach to peer feedback on university EFL students' feedback quality and writing ability
authors: Kai Guo, Mengru Pan, Yuanke Li, Chun Lai
summary: This study investigated the impact of an AI-supported peer feedback system on the feedback quality and writing ability of English as a foreign language (EFL) university students. The researchers developed an online platform, EvaluMate, with an integrated AI chatbot named Eva (powered by GPT-3.5 Turbo) to assist students in generating peer feedback. In a quasi-experimental study involving 124 Chinese undergraduate students, an experimental group (n=64) used the AI-assisted platform, while a control group (n=60) did not. Pre- and post-tests measured feedback quality and writing performance. The results indicated that the AI intervention significantly enhanced the quality of students' peer feedback and improved their own writing ability, demonstrating the potential of AI technology in EFL writing instruction.

summary: This study investigated the effect of a GenAI chatbot (powered by ChatGPT 3.5) providing interactive, personalized self-regulated learning (SRL) support to 61 Chinese university EFL students in a 12-week reading program. title: Generative AI in dissertation writing: L2 doctoral students' self-reported use, AI-giarism, and perceived training needs
authors: MohammadHamed Hoomanfard, Yaser Shamsi
summary: This qualitative study explores the perspectives of 54 L2 doctoral students at a public university in the American Central South regarding their use of Generative AI (GenAI) for dissertation writing. Through semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, the research found that students utilize GenAI for three main purposes: exploration, confirmation, and execution. The study highlights two major themes concerning AI-induced plagiarism ('AI-giarism'): students' uncertainty about the boundary between legitimate use and plagiarism, and their dilemma over acknowledging GenAI use in their work. Participants expressed a clear need for training on selecting appropriate GenAI tools, effective prompting, understanding plagiarism concerns, and managing data privacy.
