title: Human-AI collaborative reading in academic contexts: An exploratory case study
authors: Dayoung Joo, Diane Belcher
summary: This exploratory case study examines how an international graduate student uses Generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, to support academic reading in a second language (L2). Grounded in sociocultural theory and the Direct and Inferential Mediation (DIME) model, the study collected data over six weeks through screen recordings, chat logs, and interviews. Findings indicate that ChatGPT served as a translator, knowledge facilitator, and strategic partner, helping to reduce reading anxiety and improve comprehension of vocabulary, background knowledge, and reading strategies. The student's reading approach evolved from a reliance on translation to more strategic methods like summarization. However, challenges were noted, including the AI's questionable reliability and overly detailed responses, which led to user fatigue. The study provides an in-depth look at human-AI interaction in academic reading, contributing to the literature on GenAI's role in L2 education.
APA_reference: Joo, D., & Belcher, D. (2025). Human-AI collaborative reading in academic contexts: An exploratory case study. Journal of English for Academic Purposes, 78, 101571. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeap.2025.101571
research_h_q: How does ChatGPT support the reading process of an international graduate student engaging with discipline-specific texts in a second language?
What are the learner-perceived benefits and drawbacks of using ChatGPT as a means of scaffolding discipline-specific L2 reading?

title: Students' self-determination in using machine translation and generative AI tools for English for academic purposes
authors: Hao Tran, Peter Crosthwaite, Quy Huynh Phu Pham
summary: This study uses Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to investigate the motivations (autonomy, competence, relatedness) of English for Academic Purposes (EAP) students for using machine translation (MT) and generative AI (GAI) in academic writing. Through a mixed-methods approach involving a survey of 416 students and interviews with 17 students in Australia (ESL context) and Vietnam (EFL context), the study explores how learning context and academic discipline influence these motivations. Findings indicate a complex relationship between MT/GAI use and students' needs, with Australian students showing lower relatedness. The study highlights the need for context-specific teaching strategies and institutional collaboration to effectively integrate MT/GAI into EAP, bridging research and practice.

title: Zone of proximal creativity: An empirical study on EFL teachers' use of ChatGPT for enhanced practice
authors: Saadet Korucu-Kış
summary: This study investigates how ChatGPT can be used to foster creativity among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. Through an inductive content analysis of data from twenty-nine postgraduate teachers—including ChatGPT inquiry threads, lesson plans, written reflections, and survey responses—the research found that teachers utilized ChatGPT for creative ideation (seeking novel perspectives, exploring multiple ideas) and as a knowledge resource (for information, tools, and materials). Key challenges identified were the need for precise user input and the generation of repetitive content by the AI. Based on these findings, the study proposes a conceptual model framing ChatGPT as a tool that, contingent on teacher expertise, facilitates progression towards a 'Zone of Proximal Creativity'.
APA_reference: Korucu-Kış, S. (2024). Zone of proximal creativity: An empirical study on EFL teachers' use of ChatGPT for enhanced practice. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 54, 101639. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2024.101639

title: Exploring the use of ChatGPT to foster EFL learners' critical thinking skills from a post-humanist perspective
authors: Weijun Liang, Yanjun Wu
summary: This study investigates the impact of a structured, ChatGPT-based pedagogical program on the critical thinking skills of 58 university EFL learners in Macau. Using a post-humanist perspective, the study collected data through pre- and post-tests and student reflection journals. While quantitative test results showed no significant change in critical thinking skills, qualitative findings from journals revealed a more nuanced impact. Students reported that ChatGPT helped them become 'spatially advised critical thinkers' by expanding their knowledge, aiding in analysis, and constructing arguments. However, they also expressed concerns about overreliance, cognitive laziness, and the tool's limitations. The study concludes that ChatGPT can be a tool for cognitive enhancement but requires a balanced integration of technology and human cognition, emphasizing the need for students to critically engage with the AI.
APA_reference: Liang, W., & Wu, Y. (2024). Exploring the use of ChatGPT to foster EFL learners' critical thinking skills from a post-humanist perspective. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 54, 101645. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2024.101645

summary: This study investigated the effect of combining ChatGPT and teacher feedback on the argumentative writing skills of 68 intermediate Iranian EFL learners. title: The impact of chatbots based on large language models on second language vocabulary acquisition
authors: Zhihui Zhang, Xiaomeng Huang
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of a chatbot based on Large Language Models (LLMs) for second language (L2) vocabulary acquisition. 52 foreign language students were randomly assigned to two groups: an experimental group using the chatbot and a control group using other digital resources. Both groups learned the same vocabulary over eight weeks. Assessments conducted immediately after and two weeks later showed that the chatbot group significantly outperformed the control group in both receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge. The findings indicate that LLM-based chatbots not only aid in vocabulary acquisition but also enhance long-term retention of productive vocabulary and facilitate incidental learning. The study concludes that LLM-powered chatbots are valuable tools in language education and encourages educators to integrate them into their teaching strategies.
APA_reference: Zhang, Z., & Huang, X. (2024). The impact of chatbots based on large language models on second language vocabulary acquisition. Heliyon, 10(4), e25370. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e25370

title: Exploring the impact of the use of ChatGPT on foreign language self-efficacy among Chinese students studying abroad: The mediating role of foreign language enjoyment
authors: Si Xu, Pengfei Chen, Ge Zhang
summary: This study surveyed 712 Chinese students studying abroad to examine the relationships between the use of ChatGPT, foreign language self-efficacy (FLSE), and foreign language enjoyment (FLE). Using structural equation modeling, the research found that using ChatGPT has a significant positive impact on both FLSE and FLE. Furthermore, FLE was found to positively influence FLSE and serve as a mediator in the relationship between ChatGPT use and FLSE. The findings suggest that ChatGPT is a valuable tool for international students, helping them adapt to new language environments and improve their language proficiency by fostering enjoyment and confidence.

title: Uncovering personalized L2 motivation and self-regulation in ChatGPT-assisted language learning: A hybrid PLS-SEM-ANN approach
authors: Amir Reza Rahimi, Mahshad Sheyhkholeslami, Ali Mahmoudi Pour
summary: This study investigates the factors that determine the cognitive behaviors, particularly self-regulation, of language learners in a personalized learning environment using ChatGPT. Data was collected from 133 Iranian EFL learners who used ChatGPT for personalized language learning. Using a hybrid Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) approach, the researchers analyzed the relationship between the learners' personalized L2 motivational self-system (PEL2MSS) and their personalized self-regulation (PESRL). The findings indicate that learners' current L2-self, digital self-authenticity, and ought-to L2-self were the most significant motivational factors affecting their self-regulation. The study found that learners were more motivated to learn with ChatGPT compared to previous environments, leading to increased self-evaluation and goal-setting. The study proposes a new conceptual framework for personalized language learning and suggests that ChatGPT can serve as a co-teacher to supplement classroom instruction.

summary: This study investigates the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI), specifically ChatGPT, on the language learning engagement and creativity of Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in a higher education setting. title: Evaluating ChatGPT's effectiveness in enhancing argumentative writing: A quasi-experimental study of EFL learners in Pakistan
authors: Musarat Yasmin, Walees Fatima, Isra Irshad
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of ChatGPT in improving the argumentative writing skills of Secondary School Certificate (SSC) students in Pakistan learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL). Using a quasi-experimental, one-group pre-test/post-test design over three months, the research assessed changes in students' writing abilities. The findings suggest that ChatGPT is a useful tool for enhancing writing skills and supporting error correction in EFL education.

title: Identifying ChatGPT-generated texts in EFL students' writing: Through comparative analysis of linguistic fingerprints
authors: Atsushi Mizumoto, Sachiko Yasuda, Yu Tamura
summary: This study investigates the distinguishability of essays written by Japanese EFL learners from those generated by ChatGPT. 140 first-year university students wrote essays and completed a survey on their use of the tool. A comparative dataset of 125 student essays, 13 student essays using ChatGPT for proofreading, and 125 essays fully generated by ChatGPT was created. These 263 essays were analyzed using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (random forest). The results revealed significant linguistic differences between human-written and ChatGPT-generated essays, with the latter being easily identifiable. The study highlights the need for clear guidelines on the ethical use of AI in L2 writing and emphasizes fostering a mutual understanding of responsible AI integration in academic work.

title: More human than human? Differences in lexis and collocation within academic essays produced by ChatGPT-3.5 and human L2 writers
authors: Mengxuan Zhang, Peter Crosthwaite
summary: This study conducts a comparative corpus analysis of academic essays produced by human L2 writers and ChatGPT-3.5. Using quantitative methods to examine lexis and collocations, the research finds that ChatGPT-3.5 generates texts characterized by formal, complex, and technical vocabulary, focusing on broad societal and technological themes. In contrast, L2 writers' essays are more centered on personal and social issues, employing more varied and context-rich vocabulary that reflects their personal experiences. summary: This study examines the factors influencing acceptance and intention to use ChatGPT among Yemeni pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. title: Training an AI-based Writing Assistant for Spanish Learners: The Usefulness of Chatbots and the Indispensability of Human-assisted Intelligence
authors: Ángel Huete-García, Sven Tarp
summary: This article examines the relationship between human and artificial intelligence within an ongoing project to develop a Spanish Writing Assistant. It details how ChatGPT is used for key development tasks, such as training the language model and preparing user communication, through a collaboration between lexicographers and IT experts. Based on the analysis of 35,000 reviewed sentences, the study describes the interaction process between humans and the chatbot across different tasks: creating parallel corpora with induced errors, generating validation material, and writing grammatical explanations. The authors conclude that the nature of the human-AI relationship changes depending on the task and that human knowledge, skills, and linguistic intuition are crucial for the chatbot to function effectively.

title: Using Generative AI to Provide High-Quality Lexicographic Assistance to Chinese Learners of English
authors: Qian Li, Sven Tarp
summary: This paper reports on a research project that aims to explore how and to what extent generative AI can be used to produce different types of explanations that can be activated in writing assistants for Chinese learners of English. It first places the project in a lexicographic context and describes the general methodology used, including the limited usefulness of a learner corpus as an empirical basis and the need to use ChatGPT as a supplement to determine the error sub-categories to be explained. As a result, 26 error sub-categories are identified within the main category of subject-verb disagreement. The paper then compares two generative AI chatbots, Baidu's Ernie Bot and OpenAI's ChatGPT, and describes how the latter was found to be more efficient and therefore prompted by lexicographers with experience in second-language teaching to write long explanations for each of the error sub-categories, with several examples demonstrating both the chatbot's remarkable performance and the constant need for human supervision and intervention. At the same time, the paper argues for the integration of generative AI directly into writing assistants to produce short default explanations for errors found in learners' texts. Finally, the paper summarises the findings, including the complex relationship between human and artificial intelligence.
APA_reference: Li, Q., & Tarp, S. (2024). Using Generative AI to Provide High-Quality Lexicographic Assistance to Chinese Learners of English. Lexikos, 34, 397–418. https://doi.org/10.5788/34-1-1944
research_h_q: To explore how and to what extent generative AI can be applied to produce different types of explanations that can be activated in writing assistants for Chinese learners of English.
Hypothesis: Generative AI technology can increase productivity, at least without compromising quality, but probably improving it as well.

I need the text to have the following structure 1) an introduction to the problem, 2) an example sentence with an error, 3) the same example sentence with the error corrected and 4) a brief explanation of the incorrect and correct examples. The example sentences must be at least 12 words long.

drawbacks: Baidu's Ernie Bot performed poorly, providing nonsensical and unhelpful explanations for English grammar issues.
ChatGPT's generated explanations often contain 'noise' such as excessive verbosity, superfluous wording, and minor inaccuracies that require human editing and removal.
ChatGPT can be 'sloppy' in its formulations, requiring human intervention to clarify concepts (e.g., specifying that subject-verb agreement is in 'number').
study_limitations: The method of using deduction and generative AI to identify error sub-categories may overlook less frequent errors compared to a purely empirical analysis of a tagged corpus.
The test of ChatGPT's ability to explain 26 sub-categories of errors is not statistically sufficient to draw a definitive conclusion, although results are strongly suggestive.

students: The proposed writing assistant provides instant, multi-layered grammatical explanations, enhancing opportunities for both incidental and intentional learning.
Learners can receive direct, clear explanations about specific errors in their own writing, connecting universal grammar rules to their individual mistakes.
teachers: The study provides a methodology for teachers and material developers to use generative AI to increase productivity in creating high-quality, didactic content for language learners.
institutions: N/A
other: For lexicographers, the study demonstrates how generative AI can be a powerful tool to speed up the creation of glosses and explanations for modern, problem-centred databases, shifting their role towards supervision and prompt engineering.

policy_guidance: A key principle for practice is that humans (experts, lexicographers) should always have 'the last word' when working with generative AI, as the tools are not entirely reliable.
Effective use of generative AI requires a combination of user skills (learning how to write good prompts) and deep domain knowledge (e.g., English grammar and typical learner errors).
emergent_themes: The 'necessary symbiosis' between human intelligence and artificial intelligence is crucial for creating high-quality educational tools.
The application of a dialectical framework (individual error, particular short explanation, universal long explanation) as a design principle for effective pedagogical explanations in a digital tool.
The evolving role of the lexicographer from content creator to a prompter, supervisor, and editor in an AI-assisted workflow.

title: Integrating critical corpus and AI literacies in applied linguistics: a mixed-methods study
authors: Pascual Pérez-Paredes, Niall Curry & Pilar Aguado Jiménez
summary: This study examines the integration of corpus literacy and critical AI literacy in language education. In a sequential mixed-methods design, 37 undergraduate learners from a southern European university participated in structured workshops using the corpus analysis software Sketch Engine and the generative AI tool ChatGPT for vocabulary and grammar learning. Data from pre-workshop surveys, workshop activities, and a post-workshop focus group revealed that while learners were initially unfamiliar with corpus tools, they grew to recognize their value in developing linguistic awareness. Conversely, ChatGPT, though widely used, received mixed evaluations regarding its reliability. The findings suggest that corpus literacy fosters critical engagement with language data, which can serve as a foundation for developing critical AI literacy. The study argues for the value of corpus approaches in language learning and the necessity of explicit training in AI tools to mitigate challenges like over-reliance and a lack of true personalization.
APA_reference: Pérez-Paredes, P., Curry, N., & Aguado Jiménez, P. (2025). Integrating critical corpus and AI literacies in applied linguistics: a mixed-methods study. Computer Assisted Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2025.2569351

Confidence: Some learners perceived ChatGPT as a confidence-building tool, as it allowed them to practice language without fear of making mistakes.

ChatGPT can provide quick explanations, correct grammar, expand vocabulary, and offer personalized feedback.
ChatGPT can serve as a confidence-building tool for language practice.
drawbacks: Learners found corpus tool interfaces complex and data interpretation challenging.
ChatGPT's reliability was a concern, with risks of over-reliance and a lack of truly personalized learning.
The non-deterministic nature of ChatGPT's responses poses pedagogical challenges for teachers.
study_limitations: The use of purposive sampling may introduce biases and limit the generalisability of the findings.
The study does not aim for generalisability.

students: Developing corpus literacy can serve as a foundation for critical AI literacy, enhancing overall language learning.

policy_guidance: Advocates for a research agenda focused on the contribution of corpus literacy to the development of Critical AI Literacy (CAIL).
Calls for a 'radical turn in language education' that emphasizes the role of educators as promoters of knowledge and critical thinking.
Recommends an integrated approach to teaching corpus and AI literacies to help learners transfer critical skills between tools.
Urges that any implementation of LLMs in education must ensure clear benefits for all learners and be weighed against potential costs and adverse impacts.
emergent_themes: Synergy of Corpus and AI Literacies: The study posits that the skills developed through corpus literacy—such as data reasoning and language awareness—are transferable and foundational for building critical AI literacy.

Process vs. Product in Learning: A key contrast is drawn between the difficult 'process' of using corpus tools, which promotes critical inquiry, and the streamlined 'product'-oriented output of ChatGPT, which may inhibit deeper learning.

The ELIZA Effect: Learners' confidence in ChatGPT's convincing outputs may be partly due to the ELIZA effect, where human-like interaction fosters a sense of intelligence and reliability, which needs to be tempered with critical literacy.
emergent_issues: Pedagogical challenges of non-determinism: The unpredictable and varied nature of AI-generated responses creates significant difficulties for teachers in structuring lessons, managing classroom activities, and ensuring consistent learning outcomes.

The illusion of personalization: The study critically questions whether the 'individualized' responses from GenAI tools constitute genuine 'personalized' learning, arguing that true personalization must be based on specific learner needs and pedagogical goals, not just the tool's inherent randomness.

title: A Comparative Study on the Effectiveness of AI Chatbots and Dictionary Apps for Lexical Tasks and Retention
authors: Yuzhen Chen
summary: This study compared an AI chatbot (Kimi) and a bilingual dictionary app (NCD) in supporting vocabulary tasks among Chinese junior English majors. Sixty-six participants used either Kimi or NCD to complete both receptive and productive lexical tasks. Questionnaires gathered user feedback on tool use, and a surprise retention test assessed long-term vocabulary retention one week later. Results showed that Kimi significantly outperformed NCD in vocabulary comprehension, collocation production, and productive knowledge retention. Additionally, Kimi demonstrated more consistent performance than NCD across all test items, highlighting its reliability. The study underscores the potential of AI chatbots to address language-related queries and enhance vocabulary acquisition. It also advocates for aligning technological advancements with pedagogical goals to optimize language learning tools and create a sustainable learning environment.
APA_reference: Chen, Y. (2025). A comparative study on the effectiveness of AI chatbots and dictionary apps for lexical tasks and retention. Lexikos, 35, 157–182. https://doi.org/10.5788/35-1-2027

title: Wrong Answers Only: Distractor Generation for Russian Reading Comprehension Questions Using a Translated Dataset
authors: Nikita Login
summary: This study explores the development of an effective distractor generation solution for Russian exam-style reading comprehension questions. The author fine-tunes two pre-trained Russian large language models, RuT5 and RuGPT3, on a large English multiple-choice question dataset that was automatically translated into Russian. The models were trained on two specific question types: selecting the best title and true/false statement selection. The performance of these models was evaluated against baselines and on an independent set of questions from the Russian state exam (USE). The results indicate that models fine-tuned on the translated dataset outperformed baselines and models trained on an existing native Russian dataset. Specifically, the RuT5 model showed superior performance, highlighting the viability of using translated datasets for this task and the importance of matching the domain (e.g., language examination) and question type of the training data to the target task.
APA_reference: Login, N. (2024). Wrong answers only: Distractor generation for Russian reading comprehension questions using a translated dataset. Journal of Language and Education, 10(4), 56-70. https://doi.org/10.17323/jle.2024.22244
research_h_q: RQ#1: Whether a distractor generation model can be effectively fine-tuned on an English dataset, that was automatically translated to Russian?

RQ#2: Is there a need for a specific Russian multiple-choice reading comprehension question dataset for efficient exam-style distractor generation or is an existing non-exam-style dataset MuSeRC appropriate for this task?
RQ#3: Can fine-tuning on a specific type of questions result in better performance of distractor generation model on standardised exam data?

assessment/grading

For RuT5 (sequence-to-sequence): Input included a reading passage, a question, and a right answer, demarcated by the same Russian phrases as RuGPT3. The target output consisted of distractors enclosed in double quotes and separated by semicolons.
sample_size: The study utilized several datasets: Ru-RACE-TITLE (4575 training, 219 test, 242 dev items), Ru-RACE-TF (3288 training, 175 test, 187 dev items), MuSeRC (12,805 questions), and USE-TF (55 questions).
learning_perceptions: N/A

benefits_affordances: A translated English examination dataset proved more effective for fine-tuning distractor generation models for Russian than an existing native Russian dataset.
Fine-tuning models on specific question types (e.g., true/false statements) leads to better performance on standardized exam data with the same question format.
The T5-based model (RuT5) demonstrated generally better results than the GPT3-based model (RuGPT3) for the distractor generation task.
drawbacks: Models trained on a general-purpose Russian reading comprehension dataset (MuSeRC) performed poorly on specific exam-style tasks, indicating a lack of transferability due to differences in domain and complexity.
The autoregressive RuGPT3 model performed substantially worse than the sequence-to-sequence RuT5 model, suggesting architectural disadvantages for this specific generation task.

teachers: Can benefit from tools that automatically generate distractors for multiple-choice questions, reducing the time and cost of creating assessment materials.
institutions: Exam organizers can use the developed models for automatic and continuous replenishment of test item banks, which helps ensure test variability and prevent cheating.

title: Can ChatGPT make reading comprehension testing items on par with human experts?
authors: Dongkwang Shin, Jang Ho Lee
summary: Given the recent increased interest in ChatGPT in the L2 teaching and learning community, the present study sought to examine ChatGPT's potential as a resource for generating L2 assessment materials on par with those created by human experts. To this end, we extracted five reading passages and testing items in the format of multiple-choice questions from the English section of the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) in South Korea. Additionally, we used ChatGPT to generate another set of readings and testing items in the same format. Next, we developed a survey made up of Likert-scale questions and open-ended response questions that asked about participants' perceptions of the diverse aspects of the target readings and testing elements. The study's participants were comprised of 50 pre- and in-service teachers, and they were not informed of the target materials' source or the study's purpose. The survey's results revealed that the CSAT and ChatGPT-developed readings were perceived as similar in terms of naturalness of the target passages' flow and expressions. However, the former was judged as having included more attractive multiple-choice options, as well as having a higher completion level regarding testing items. Based on such outcomes, we then present implications for L2 teaching and future research.

authors: Dongkwang Shin, Jang Ho Lee
summary: This study investigates the use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based chatbot-building platforms (ChatGPT, Poe AI, Pi) for second language (L2) learning. title: Comparing individual vs. collaborative processing of ChatGPT-generated feedback: Effects on L2 writing task improvement and learning
authors: Da 'Alex' Yan
summary: This study investigated the effects of different feedback processing modes (individual, teacher-scaffolded, peer-scaffolded, and combined teacher-peer-scaffolded) on L2 writing development among 117 Chinese university EFL learners using ChatGPT. Over seven weeks, the study measured writing task improvement and learning progression. Findings indicate that while individual processing of ChatGPT feedback led to the most significant immediate task improvements, collaborative processing, especially with teacher involvement, resulted in the most substantial long-term learning gains. title: The potential advantages of using an LLM-based chatbot for automated writing evaluation for English teaching practitioners
authors: Kyungmin Kim, Jang Ho Lee, Dongkwang Shin
summary: With the ever-increasing demand for assessing large amounts of student writing, Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) has emerged as an efficient system to satisfy this demand. However, it has also been suggested that applying it in teachers’ writing classes may offer limited results. Given this, the present study developed an AWE chatbot based on ChatGPT 4.0-turbo, designed as an automated rater. A total of 465 narrative essays written by Korean high school EFL students were scored according to three criteria by the developed tool; these were then compared with the scores administered by two professional raters using various analytic measures. The results showed that the AWE chatbot’s scoring was strongly correlated with that of the human raters. Meanwhile, the many-facet Rasch model’s result indicated that the two human raters’ statistics demonstrated an excellent fit, whereas those of the developed AWE chatbot were slightly lower. The Coh-Metrix analysis suggested that the human raters’ scoring tendencies and GPT are largely aligned, indicating that both raters scored the essays similarly. Based on our findings, we suggest that the Large Language Model (LLM)-based AWE chatbot has great potential to assist teachers in EFL writing classrooms.
APA_reference: Kim, K., Lee, J. H., & Shin, D. (2025). The potential advantages of using an LLM-based chatbot for automated writing evaluation for English teaching practitioners. Language Learning & Technology, 29(1), 1–12. https://hdl.handle.net/10125/73628

teachers: A well-developed AWE chatbot can serve as a reliable assistant for instructors in the time-consuming task of assessing student essays.

institutions: AWE chatbots could be integrated into educational platforms like online learning management systems to provide students with on-demand writing assessment tools.

policy_guidance: Teachers developing AWE chatbots should accurately identify the target audience's proficiency level.

emergent_themes: The study revealed a close alignment in the 'scoring tendencies' of the AWE chatbot and human raters, as both weighted similar textual features (e.g., essay length, temporal cohesion, lexical sophistication) when assigning scores.

title: Integrating ChatGPT for vocabulary learning and retention: A classroom-based study of Saudi EFL learners
authors: Safaa M. Abdelhalim, Raniya Abdullah Alsehibany
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating ChatGPT into classroom instruction for vocabulary learning and retention among Saudi EFL learners, comparing it to traditional teacher-led methods. Using a quasi-experimental, explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, 71 female learners were divided into an experimental group (EG) using ChatGPT and a control group (CG) with traditional instruction. Data were collected through vocabulary knowledge tests (pre-, post-, and delayed post-test) and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative results showed the EG significantly outperformed the CG in productive vocabulary knowledge and overall scores, though not in receptive knowledge. Qualitative findings revealed positive student perceptions, highlighting ChatGPT's role in enhancing engagement, motivation, and contextual vocabulary use through scaffolded, interactive tasks. The study, grounded in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, concludes that a structured, theory-informed integration of ChatGPT can effectively support productive vocabulary development.

title: Bringing Cinderella into spotlight: GenAI-assisted grammar acquisition in academic writing
authors: Shu Zhou, Gerhardus D. Du Preez
summary: This study investigates the effects, perceptions, and experiences of using a generative AI (GenAI) tool combined with pedagogical theory to improve grammar acquisition in academic writing. Conducted as a six-week mixed-methods experiment with 20 first-year Chinese undergraduates in an EAP course, the research used pre-/post-essay tests and reflective journals. Quantitative results showed a significant improvement in students' grammatical performance. Qualitatively, a four-stage developmental trajectory in student engagement was identified: Enthusiastic Discovery, Critical Engagement, Empowered Mastery, and Reflective Personalisation. The study proposes a pedagogical model that integrates GenAI into EAP curricula, using an interactive workflow to operationalize Grammar Learning Strategies (GLS) and help learners move from simple grammar correction to autonomous grammar acquisition.

title: Exploring AI-assistance in L2 Chinese writing with standardized assessment tasks
authors: Dan Song, Alexander F. Tang
summary: This mixed-methods study investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) on the Mandarin Chinese writing skills of 26 university-level foreign language students. Participants completed four writing tasks from the AP Chinese Language and Culture Exam over two days, with permission to use ChatGPT for assistance on one task per day. Writing samples were evaluated by two professional raters. The results showed that using ChatGPT consistently led to higher writing scores, particularly improving performance in vocabulary and translation. The study also analyzed student perceptions of using GAI, finding it to be a helpful tool but also noting concerns about overreliance and information retention. The research aims to provide empirical data on how GAI tools can support L2 writing development in the Mandarin Chinese context.

title: GPT-3.5 for ELE Leveling in a University Environment: A Comparative Study of Zero-shot Learning and Fine-tuning
authors: María Victoria Cantero-Romero, María Estrella Vallecillo-Rodríguez, Ana María Ortiz-Colón, Salud María Jiménez-Zafra
summary: This study explores the use of GPT-3.5 to automate the leveling of Spanish as a Foreign Language (ELE) students' written texts in a university setting. Two approaches are compared: Zero-shot Learning (ZSL) with explicit instructions, and a supervised method involving fine-tuning the model on the CAES corpus. title: The Effect of Feedback on Informative Text Writing: AI or Teacher?
authors: MEHMET ALI BAZ, SEVIL HASIRCI AKSOY
summary: This study was conducted to examine the effects of feedback provided by a generative AI chatbot trained by the researcher and feedback given by a teacher on students' achievement and retention in informative text writing. In this context, a convergent parallel mixed-methods approach was adopted. The research was conducted with two groups at the fifth-grade middle school level, comprising experimental and control groups. For eight weeks, the chatbot provided feedback on the texts of students in the experimental group through the researcher, while the teacher provided feedback on the texts of students in the control group. To measure students' informative text writing performance, the Informative Text Writing Performance Assessment Scale developed by Hamzadayı and Dölek (2022) was utilized. Findings indicated that feedback provided by both the AI chatbot and the teacher contributed to improvements in students' informative text writing performance. However, it was determined that such improvement persisted significantly only within the teacher-feedback group. Based on this finding, it was concluded that while chatbot feedback was as effective as teacher feedback in improving writing performance, it did not exhibit comparable long-term retention effects. When comparing the content of feedback provided, it was observed that the chatbot's feedback was quantitatively more extensive than that of the teacher. Conversely, teacher feedback was superior regarding affective components and question-oriented feedback. Consequently, generative AI tools hold significant potential for reducing teachers' cognitive workload in writing instruction by providing supplementary and innovative feedback methods.
APA_reference: Baz, M. A., & Hasirci Aksoy, S. (2025). The Effect of Feedback on Informative Text Writing: AI or Teacher? Open Praxis, 17(3), pp. 611-631. DOI: https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.17.3.871

title: Exploring the Feasibility and Efficacy of ChatGPT3 for Personalized Feedback in Teaching
authors: Irum Naz and Rodney Robertson
summary: This study explores the feasibility and effectiveness of using ChatGPT-3 to provide reliable, meaningful, and personalized feedback in language learning. Through an analysis of AI-generated feedback on mock student writing samples, framed by Social Cognitive Theory and Krashen's Second Language Acquisition theory, the study investigates the benefits, limitations, and reliability of this technology. The findings indicate that while AI can offer timely, personalized support that enhances student motivation and independence, it is also prone to errors, hallucinations, and vagueness, particularly with complex tasks. The study concludes that for effective integration, educators must use carefully constructed rubrics and prompts, and that significant teacher oversight remains essential. AI is positioned as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human teachers.

title: EFL Students' Perspectives on ChatGPT in Translation: Exploring Al Assistance, Motivation, and Learning Outcomes
authors: Cao-Tuong Dinh
summary: This study investigates how 62 junior English majors at a Vietnamese university perceive and use ChatGPT in translation classes. Using a mixed-methods approach guided by the Expectation-Value Theory, the research collected data through surveys, reflective journals, focus group interviews, and course grades. Findings indicate that students view ChatGPT as a valuable tool for improving translation accuracy, efficiency, and vocabulary, which boosted their motivation and confidence. The tool also facilitated collaborative learning. However, students noted significant limitations, particularly ChatGPT's difficulty with cultural nuances and idiomatic expressions, necessitating careful human review. The study concludes that while AI tools can effectively support translation education, they cannot replace human judgment and effort. It highlights the importance of balancing AI assistance with traditional methods and maintaining critical engagement to foster both linguistic and analytical skills.

title: Does AI Simplification of Authentic Blog Texts Improve Reading Comprehension, Inferencing, and Anxiety? A One-Shot Intervention in Turkish EFL Context
authors: Ferdi Çelik, Ceylan Yangın Ersanlı, and Goshnag Arslanbay
summary: This experimental study investigates the impact of ChatGPT-simplified authentic texts on university students' reading comprehension, inferencing, and reading anxiety levels. A within-subjects design was employed, and 105 undergraduate English as a foreign language (EFL) students engaged in both original and ChatGPT-simplified text readings, serving as their own controls. The findings reveal a significant improvement in reading comprehension scores and inferencing scores following ChatGPT intervention. However, no significant change in reading anxiety levels was observed. Results suggest that ChatGPT simplification positively influences reading comprehension and inferencing, but its impact on reading anxiety remains inconclusive. This research contributes to literature on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education and sheds light on ChatGPT's potential to influence language learning experiences within higher education contexts. The study highlights the practical application of ChatGPT as a tool for helping students engage in authentic text readings by making text more comprehensible. Based on the findings, several multifaceted implications that extend to various stakeholders in the field of language education are provided.

title: “ChatGPT for intercultural pragmatic learning? Potentially, but not yet” – The question of using AI to develop students’ intercultural pragmatic competence
authors: István Kecskés, Hanh Dinh
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of ChatGPT in developing the intercultural pragmatic competence of Japanese learners of English, using Kecskes' sociocognitive framework. Analyzing over 10,000 responses from interactions between ChatGPT and 45 university students of diverse nationalities, the research examines the AI's role in meaning negotiation and repair strategies in simulated social scenarios. Findings indicate that while ChatGPT can model some cooperative communication aspects and boost student confidence, it struggles with maintaining relevance, lacks human-like repair strategies, provides repetitive responses, and has a limited contextual understanding. Students were observed to initiate self-repair more often than receiving interactive feedback from the AI. The study concludes with a recommendation for the cautious use of ChatGPT in pragmatic learning, emphasizing the need for more advanced frameworks to effectively integrate AI into intercultural communication education.
APA_reference: Kecskés, I., & Dinh, H. (2025). “ChatGPT for intercultural pragmatic learning? Potentially, but not yet” – The question of using AI to develop students’ intercultural pragmatic competence. Intercultural Pragmatics, 22(2). https://doi.org/10.1515/ip-2025-2008
research_h_q: RQ1: How effectively does ChatGPT help students learn about self-initiated and other-initiated repairs in intercultural communication breakdowns during simulated social interactions and meaning negotiation?

RQ2: In what ways does ChatGPT facilitate students' intercultural pragmatic competence by modeling appropriate co-construction strategies in interactions with students from diverse cultural backgrounds?
RQ3: According to students' evaluations, what are the perceived advantages and challenges of using ChatGPT as a tool to enhance intercultural pragmatic competence?

title: Language Teaching in Transition: Educator Perspectives on Integrating Machine Translation Tools in Tertiary Contexts
authors: Antonie Alm, Yuki Watanabe
summary: This qualitative study explores the perspectives, experiences, and attitudes of four tertiary language educators (teaching French, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese) in New Zealand regarding the integration of AI-based tools, particularly Machine Translation (MT) and ChatGPT. Through semi-structured interviews analyzed using Knowles' ADAPT framework and thematic analysis, the study finds that while teachers generally accept MT as a learning tool, they harbor concerns about student over-reliance, loss of motivation, and superficial learning. The educators demonstrated limited familiarity and skepticism towards generative AI like ChatGPT. The findings reveal a transitional phase where teachers are reactively adapting their pedagogical practices, such as amending assignments and discussing MT use, but feel unprepared to formally train students or systematically assess with AI in mind. The study highlights a significant need for teacher professional development, peer collaboration, and flexible, context-sensitive frameworks for technology integration.
APA_reference: Alm, A., & Watanabe, Y. (2025). Language teaching in transition: Educator perspectives on integrating machine translation tools in tertiary contexts. In D. Coulson & C. Denman (Eds.), Translation, Translanguaging and Machine Translation in Foreign Language Education. Springer Nature Switzerland AG. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-82174-5_22

title: Generative AI in Reshaping Higher Education: Human Sciences Master Students at FLDM-USMBA as a Case Study
authors: Marwa Eljai, Yassamine Eljai, Khaoula Asmar
summary: This case study explores the impact of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, on the engagement and academic performance of 87 Human Sciences master's students at the University of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah in Fes, Morocco. Using a mixed-methods approach involving questionnaires and semi-structured interviews, the study found that AI tools enhance academic performance, writing quality, motivation, and confidence among students. title: Grammatical Error Correction and Explanation for Learners of Chinese Using Large Language Models
authors: Zhao-Ming Gao
summary: This study provides a quantitative and qualitative assessment of three state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs)—GPT 4.0, Bard, and Claude 2—for Chinese grammatical error correction (GCE), identification, and explanation. The study compares these general-purpose conversational AI tools against BART CGEC, a model specifically designed for GCE. Using a curated set of 25 sentences with various error types, the research evaluates the LLMs' performance with different prompts. Findings indicate that general-purpose LLMs outperform the specialized model, with Claude 2 showing the highest accuracy in error correction. The study also demonstrates that prompt engineering significantly enhances the performance of all models across all tasks, improving accuracy in error correction, identification, and explanation. The paper concludes that as of November 2023, Claude 2 is the most effective tool for Chinese GCE among the models tested, highlighting the potential of LLMs to revolutionize second language acquisition.
APA_reference: Gao, Z.-M. (2025). Grammatical Error Correction and Explanation for Learners of Chinese Using Large Language Models. In S.-H Teng et al. (eds.), Handbook of Chinese Language Learning and Technology. Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-5930-9_13
research_h_q: RQ 1. How effectively do the three LLMs perform in error identification, error correction, and error explanation when given simple and straightforward prompts?
RQ 2. What impact does prompt engineering have on these three tasks?
RQ 3. Which model is best suited for developing a Chinese grammar checker as of November 20, 2023?

study_limitations: The study is based on a small set of 25 representative samples, which may not be generalizable to all error types.

title: Comparing the effects of teacher- and AI-mediated corrective feedback on accuracy, complexity, and quality in L2 written narratives
authors: Mahmoud Abdi Tabari, Ali Kushki, Yizhou Wang
summary: This study investigates the comparative effects of teacher-mediated versus AI-mediated written corrective feedback (WCF) on the accuracy, complexity, and quality of L2 narrative writing. Participants were 166 upper-intermediate ESL undergraduates at a U.S. university, divided into two groups: one receiving teacher feedback (n=80) and the other receiving AI feedback from ChatGPT-4 (n=86). Both groups wrote an initial narrative, received feedback, and submitted a revised draft. The analysis revealed that while both groups significantly improved in accuracy and lexical complexity, the teacher-feedback group showed greater gains. Conversely, syntactic complexity declined in both groups, but the decline was less pronounced in the AI-feedback group. Overall writing quality improved for both, with no significant difference between the groups except for word choice, where the teacher group improved more. The findings suggest that AI-mediated WCF is a promising complement to traditional teacher feedback, each having distinct effects on different linguistic aspects of writing.
APA_reference: Abdi Tabari, M., Kushki, A., & Wang, Y. (2025). Comparing the effects of teacher- and AI-mediated corrective feedback on accuracy, complexity, and quality in L2 written narratives. Computer Assisted Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2025.2561608

RQ3: How do AI-mediated and teacher-mediated WCF affect quality scores in L2 narrative writing?

title: A comparative analysis of human and GenAI-generated feedback on EFL students’ argumentative writing performance
authors: Mine Yıldız, Arif Cem Topuz, Hamza Polat, Elif Taşlıbeyaz, Engin Kurşun & Savaş Yeşilyurt
summary: This study investigated the impact of feedback from a human tutor (HT) versus Generative AI (GenAI) on the argumentative writing of 59 L2 learners in Turkey. Using a counterbalanced quasi-experimental design, students received feedback from either the HT or GenAI on two separate writing tasks. The results, analyzed via mixed-ANCOVA, showed that while both feedback sources led to improved final drafts, they had different effects. Human-generated feedback resulted in significantly greater improvements in overall writing scores, particularly in language and mechanics. In contrast, GenAI-generated feedback, like human feedback, effectively enhanced argumentation, evidence, and organization, but did not significantly improve language, mechanics, or overall scores. The study suggests that a balanced, hybrid approach, combining the strengths of both human and AI feedback, would be most effective for promoting EFL learners' writing skills and reducing teacher workload.

title: A corpus-based approach to developing vocabulary curriculum materials for Indigenous youth: AI-generated versus human-created content
authors: Jia Li, Todd Cunningham, Esther Geva, Catherine Snow, Andrew Biemiller, Novera Roihan
summary: This exploratory study uses corpus analysis to examine the vocabulary in verbal narratives of Indigenous high school students in a remote Canadian First Nation community. It compares their vocabulary use (specifically high-frequency and academic words) with two sets of curriculum materials: one created by a research team based on the students' narratives, and another generated by an AI (NotebookLM) using the same source material. The study found that students' narratives had a significant gap in less frequent (K2) and academic words. The human-created materials effectively increased the percentage of K2 words, while the AI-generated materials significantly increased both K2 and academic words. The findings suggest that a data-driven, culturally responsive pedagogy combining human oversight and AI efficiency can effectively develop vocabulary materials for Indigenous youth, leveraging their oral storytelling traditions.

summary: This mixed-methods study investigated the effects of ChatGPT-generated feedback compared to teacher-generated feedback on the writing skills and perceptions of 102 Saudi EFL university students. title: To disclose or not to disclose: Exploring the risk of being transparent about GenAI use in second language writing
authors: Xiao Tan, Chaoran Wang, Wei Xu
summary: This study investigates the impact of disclosing generative AI (GenAI) use on the assessment of second language (L2) writing. Using a mixed-method design, the research measures statistical differences in grades for the same essays under disclosure and non-disclosure conditions and explores the reasons for these differences through interviews with teachers. The quantitative findings reveal that teachers tend to assign lower scores when they are aware of GenAI involvement. The qualitative data suggests that this is due to teachers making negative assumptions about the student's writing ability and holding biases against GenAI use. The study provides empirical evidence for the concerns L2 writers have about disclosure policies and offers suggestions for fostering trust and rethinking writing assessment in the context of GenAI.
APA_reference: Tan, X., Wang, C., & Xu, W. (2025). To disclose or not to disclose: Exploring the risk of being transparent about GenAI use in second language writing. Applied Linguistics, XX, 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amae092

title: Advanced multi-lingual writers' self-directed use of generative AI in academic writing: Rethinking writing, authorship, and learning
authors: Chaoran Wang, Wei Xu, Xiao Tan
summary: This study investigates the self-directed use of Generative AI (GenAI) for academic writing by three advanced L2/multilingual (post)doctoral writers. Through multiple case studies, it explores how these writers use GenAI to address specific writing challenges. The findings reveal a spectrum of approaches, from prescriptive (AI as a tool) to dialogic (AI as an interactive participant), influenced by their disciplinary backgrounds and views on AI. The study challenges traditional notions of authorship and learning, proposing a post-structuralist perspective that views authorship as a distributed practice and AI as part of a writer's evolving semiotic repertoire. It calls for more nuanced ethical considerations regarding AI use to avoid stigmatizing multilingual writers and to foster a more productive relationship with AI technology in academic contexts.

title: An autoethnographic study of ESL academic writing with ChatGPT: from psychological insights to the SUPER framework
authors: Hsiao-Ping Hsu
summary: This autoethnographic study examines how English as a Second Language (ESL) higher education (HE) students use ChatGPT to address psychological challenges in academic writing. Guided by Maslow's hierarchy of needs and the concept of Escapism, the author reflects on their lived experience as an ESL doctoral student in the United States and an assistant professor in Ireland. Data sources included a personal diary, work logs, and annotated drafts. Findings indicate that ChatGPT can help fulfill a range of psychological needs, from physiological and safety to belonging, self-esteem, and self-actualization. However, the study also highlights concerns about overreliance and potential breaches of academic integrity. In response, the study proposes a user-friendly SUPER framework (Support not a Substitute, Unique Perspective, Prompt Engineering, Ethical Use, and Reflection) to guide students and writers in the ethical and effective use of ChatGPT.
APA_reference: Hsu, H.-P. (2025). An autoethnographic study of ESL academic writing with ChatGPT: from psychological insights to the SUPER framework. Cogent Education, 12(1), 2543113. https://doi.org/10.1080/2331186X.2025.2543113

summary: The study explored the adoption of ChatGPT in argumentative writing among students using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model as a framework. title: An Investigation of Applying Large Language Models to Spoken Language Learning

summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs) in spoken language learning, covering phonetics, phonology, and second language acquisition. The results offer insights into the strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs for spoken language learning applications.

title: A qualitative exploration of pre-service English teachers' integration of generative artificial intelligence in corpus-based language pedagogy
authors: Gökçe Kurt
summary: This qualitative case study examines the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into corpus-based language pedagogy (CBLP) by Turkish pre-service English teachers (PTs). Despite the established benefits of data-driven learning (DDL), its mainstream adoption is hindered by the complexity of corpus tools and inadequate pedagogical training. GenAI presents a potential solution to these challenges, but its role within CBLP is not well-understood. Using Shulman's pedagogical reasoning model as an analytical framework, the study investigated how PTs designed and implemented GenAI-supported CBLP lessons during their practicum. Findings indicate that PTs successfully developed and applied GenAI-supported CBLP, with their decisions on tool selection being influenced by a combination of cognitive, pedagogical, and affective factors. The study provides valuable insights into the practical implementation of this integrated approach and offers implications for future teacher education and research.

authors: Abdulelah Alkhateeb, Abdulrahman Mokbel Mahyoub Hezam & Athari A. Almuraikhi
summary: This study examines the adoption of AI tools by 61 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers for exam preparation in two Saudi universities, using the TPACK and UTAUT theoretical frameworks. Through an online survey, the research explores the applications, perceived benefits, and challenges of using AI. Findings indicate that tools like ChatGPT are commonly used for creating lower-order questions (e.g., multiple-choice), offering significant gains in efficiency and time-saving. However, teachers face challenges such as the inaccuracy of AI-generated content, difficulties in customizing it to meet curriculum standards, a lack of institutional training, and ethical concerns. title: Automated analysis of common errors in L2 learner production: Prototype web application development
authors: Atsushi Mizumoto
summary: This research report presents the development and validation of Auto Error Analyzer, a prototype web application designed to automate the calculation of accuracy and its related metrics for measuring second language (L2) production. Building on recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI), Auto Error Analyzer introduces an automated accuracy measurement component, bridging a gap in existing assessment tools, which traditionally require human judgment for accuracy evaluation. By utilizing a state-of-the-art generative AI model (Llama 3.3) for error detection, Auto Error Analyzer analyzes L2 texts efficiently and cost-effectively, producing accuracy metrics (e.g., errors per 100 words). Validation results demonstrate high agreement between the tool's error counts and human rater judgments (r = .94), with microaverage precision and recall in error detection being high as well (.96 and .94 respectively, F1 = .95), and its T-unit and clause counts matched outputs from established tools like L2SCA. Developed under open science principles to ensure transparency and replicability, the tool aims to support researchers and educators while emphasizing the complementary role of human expertise in language assessment. The possibilities of Auto Error Analyzer for efficient and scalable error analysis, as well as its limitations in detecting context-dependent and first-language (L1)-influenced errors, are also discussed.
APA_reference: Mizumoto, A. (2025). Automated analysis of common errors in L2 learner production: Prototype web application development. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 47, 867–884. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263125100934

title: Complementing but Not Replacing: Comparing the Impacts of GPT-4 and Native-Speaker Interaction on Chinese L2 Writing Outcomes
authors: Zhaoyang Shan, Zhangyuan Song, Xu Jiang, Wen Chen, Luyao Chen
summary: This study investigated the effectiveness of GPT-4 versus a human language partner in supporting Chinese L2 learners' writing during the pre-writing phase. Through a within-subject experiment with 23 learners under three conditions ('without interaction', 'interaction with GPT-4', 'interaction with a language partner'), the study found that interacting with a human partner significantly improved overall writing scores, organization, and language more than the other conditions. Both GPT-4 and human interaction enhanced learners' topic familiarity and writing confidence while reducing perceived task difficulty. However, for the GPT-4 group, increased topic familiarity correlated with better writing, whereas for the human partner group, increased confidence was negatively correlated with content scores. The findings suggest that LLMs like GPT-4 should serve as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human interaction in the L2 pre-writing process.
APA_reference: Shan, Z., Song, Z., Jiang, X., Chen, W., & Chen, L. (2025). Complementing but not replacing: Comparing the impacts of GPT-4 and native-speaker interaction on Chinese L2 writing outcomes. Behavioral Sciences, 15(4), 540. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs15040540
research_h_q: Q1: How do the overall writing score and its sub-dimensions (i.e., content, organization, language, and vocabulary) differ under different interaction conditions (GPT-4, human language partner, and without interaction)?

H1: Drawing on empirical evidence that interactive collaboration (peer-to-peer and teacher-student interactions) positively impacts L2 writing by enhancing accuracy and fostering learner autonomy, while LLMs have demonstrated their capacity to improve collaborative writing outcomes by providing contextually relevant feedback and optimizing interaction quality, we hypothesize that L2 learners’ writing scores will be higher under interactive conditions compared with without interaction, with the scores from interaction with GPT-4 and human language partner being comparable, and potential variations across its sub-dimensions.

Q2: What are the relationships between writing outcomes and factors such as topic familiarity, writing confidence, and perceived difficulty under the three interaction conditions (GPT-4, human language partner, and without interaction)?

H2: Building on prior research indicating that individual learner factors such as topic familiarity, writing confidence, and perceived difficulty are significantly related to L2 writing performance, and recognizing that these factors may interact differently with varying forms of writing support including AI-mediated and human-mediated feedback, we hypothesize that under different interaction conditions, writing outcomes will be differentially associated with learners’ topic familiarity, writing confidence, and perceived difficulty in L2 writing.

title: Profiles of Approaches to Writing and Their Links to Self-Efficacy and LLM Acceptance in L2 Academic Writing
authors: Fei Sun, Laura Mendoza, Junju Wang, Hongbin Li
summary: This study investigated the writing approaches of 578 Chinese graduate students in an L2 academic context. Using latent profile analysis, it identified three distinct profiles: 'unorganized', 'dissonant', and 'deep and organized', with the dissonant profile being the most prevalent. The research also examined the predictive roles of writing self-efficacy and large language model (LLM) acceptance on profile membership. Findings from multinomial logistic regression analysis showed that both writing self-efficacy and LLM acceptance were significant positive predictors. authors: Wei Xu, Xiao Tan
summary: This study investigates the perceptions, knowledge, and experiences of 122 second language (L2) writing teachers regarding the use of ChatGPT in their classrooms. Through a qualitative online survey and follow-up interviews with 13 teachers, the research explores their understanding of ChatGPT's capabilities, their views on the ethical issues involved, and their perceptions of its pedagogical affordances and potential risks. The findings indicate that while most teachers have some experience with ChatGPT, they express uncertainty about student usage and pedagogical integration. Key themes include the importance of AI literacy, ethical concerns surrounding academic integrity and teacher workload, and the dual nature of ChatGPT as both a tool for empowerment (e.g., brainstorming, linguistic support) and a source of risk (e.g., reduced critical engagement, perpetuating biases). The study provides insights into how L2 writing teachers are navigating the integration of generative AI and offers implications for pedagogy and institutional policy.

title: Harnessing the Power of ChatGPT for Mastering the Maltese Language: A Journey of Breaking Barriers and Charting New Paths
authors: Jacqueline Żammit
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of ChatGPT for learning the Maltese language among 41 international adult students. Using a mixed-methods approach involving a survey and a focus group over a two-week period, the research explores participants' experiences and perceptions. The findings indicate that ChatGPT is largely ineffective for learning Maltese, providing inaccurate information, non-existent words, and struggling to comprehend Maltese questions. Participants rated their experience poorly, citing limitations in grammar, vocabulary, translation, and conversational practice, especially compared to its effectiveness for learning English. While ChatGPT showed some utility in providing basic cultural information, its performance was hampered by a limited training dataset for the Maltese language. The study concludes that significant improvements in training data and collaboration with language experts are necessary to make ChatGPT a viable tool for learning low-resource languages like Maltese.

summary: This study investigates the effectiveness and acceptance of ChatGPT-4 for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing skills among undergraduate students in Algeria. title: From recorded to AI-generated instructional videos: A comparison of learning performance and experience
authors: Tao Xu, Yuan Liu, Yaru Jin, Yueyao Qu, Jie Bai, Wenlan Zhang, Yun Zhou
summary: This study investigates whether AI-generated instructional videos (AIIV) are as effective for learning as traditional recorded videos (RV). Seventy-six university students were randomly assigned to learn English vocabulary through either an AIIV or an RV. The AIIV was created using a pipeline involving a customized GPT for script generation, text-to-speech, and lip synthesis. Learning performance was measured by retention and transfer tests, while learning experience was assessed through subjective measures of cognitive, emotional, motivational, and social factors. The results showed that the AIIV group performed as well as the RV group, achieving significantly higher retention scores but showing no difference in transfer scores. While the RV was perceived as having a stronger social presence and the AIIV was rated slightly less favorably on subjective measures, the AI-generated teacher was still found to be attractive, avoiding the uncanny valley effect. The study concludes that AI-generated content is an effective tool for learning with practical implications for education.

students: AI-generated videos can provide an effective learning resource that allows students to focus more on the content due to reduced social pressure.
teachers: AI-generated content can alleviate the burden and cost of producing instructional videos, allowing teachers to focus more on instructional design.

title: Utilizing large language models for EFL essay grading: An examination of reliability and validity in rubric-based assessments
authors: Fatih Yavuz, Özgür Çelik, Gamze Yavaş Çelik
summary: This study investigates the reliability and validity of ChatGPT and Google's Bard for grading EFL student essays using a detailed analytical rubric. Fifteen experienced EFL instructors and the two LLMs graded three essays of varying quality across five domains (grammar, content, organization, style & expression, mechanics). The results showed that a fine-tuned ChatGPT model achieved very high reliability (ICC = 0.972), outperforming the default ChatGPT (ICC = 0.947) and Bard (ICC = 0.919). LLMs demonstrated strong alignment with human raters in objective domains like grammar and mechanics but showed divergence in subjective areas like content and organization, where they tended to score more generously. The study concludes that while LLMs have significant potential as reliable grading assistants, further fine-tuning is necessary for a more nuanced assessment of subjective criteria.
APA_reference: Yavuz, F., Çelik, Ö., & Yavaş Çelik, G. (2025). Utilizing large language models for EFL essay grading: An examination of reliability and validity in rubric-based assessments. British Journal of Educational Technology, 56, 150–166. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13494

RQ4: In what domains do the scores assigned by LLMs align with those given by human raters?

title: Optimizing self-regulated learning: A mixed-methods study on GAI's impact on undergraduate task strategies and metacognition
authors: Ping Wang, Tianle Liu, Yingying Yang, Xingyu Xiang
summary: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in education has shown the potential to improve learning outcomes, yet its impact on self-regulated learning (SRL) in second language (L2) writing remains underexplored. This mixed-methods study investigated the effects of a GAI chatbot tool on task strategy diversity, metacognitive awareness and writing performance among 40 undergraduate students in Eastern China over an 8-week intervention. Participants were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=20) using the GAI chatbot platform Tongyi.ai or a control group (n=20) relying on traditional resources. Data were collected using the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI), Strategy Inventory for Language Learning (SILL), writing performance assessments, participant interaction logs, reflective journals and semi-structured interviews. Quantitative analysis revealed that the experimental group showed greater improvements in task strategy diversity, metacognitive awareness and writing performance than the control group. Qualitative analysis further indicated that GAI tools could facilitate task planning, promote adaptive strategy use and deepen metacognitive reflection. Despite these benefits, participants expressed concerns about the potential of over-reliance on GAI and the accuracy of its generated content. The present study highlights the potential of GAI to enhance SRL in L2 writing by fostering adaptive task strategies and promoting metacognitive development, offering valuable implications for integrating GAI into L2 writing instruction.
APA_reference: Wang, P., Liu, T., Yang, Y., & Xiang, X. (2025). Optimizing self-regulated learning: A mixed-methods study on GAI's impact on undergraduate task strategies and metacognition. British Journal of Educational Technology, 00, 1–20. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.70018

title: Parent-led vs. AI-guided dialogic reading: Evidence from a randomized controlled trial in children's e-book context
authors: Feiwen Xiao, Ellen Wenting Zou, Jiaju Lin, Zhaohui Li, Dandan Yang
summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effectiveness of a large language model (LLM)-powered bilingual conversational agent (CA) compared to traditional parent-led reading for promoting engagement and improving learning outcomes among young children (aged 5-8) learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL). The study developed an interactive e-book with an embedded CA for dialogic reading. 67 children were randomly assigned to an AI-led group or a parent-led control group. Findings showed that the AI-led group significantly outperformed the control group in reading comprehension, with both groups showing comparable gains in vocabulary acquisition and story retelling. The study also identified different engagement patterns: children reading with the CA demonstrated higher global engagement and visual attention, while those reading with parents showed greater affective engagement and more narrative-relevant vocalizations.

summary: This study compares the effects of Bing and ChatGPT environments against traditional instruction on interpersonal emotion regulation (IER), behavioural emotion regulation strategies (BERS), hopelessness, and vocabulary retention among 458 upper-intermediate Chinese EFL learners. Using a mixed-methods design with pre/post-tests and interviews, the study divided participants into three groups: Bing, ChatGPT, and a control group. title: Can We Reliably Score Meaning Recall Vocabulary Tests Using AI? A Comparison of Human vs. AI Scoring
authors: Jeffrey Stewart, Laurence Anthony, Aaron Olaf Batty, Keita Nakamura, Christopher Nicklin, Stuart McLean, Kanako Tomaru
summary: Recent years have seen increasing calls to test L2 vocabulary knowledge under a meaning recall modality, where learners write the meaning of words in their L1, as such tests have stronger correlations to reading proficiency than meaning recognition multiple-choice tests. However, a drawback of meaning recall tests is that they are difficult for teachers to score, particularly if they are not fluent in learner L1s. Online tests scored by AI may mitigate this challenge because large language models (LLMs) can represent multiple languages in a single, nuanced, and context-dependent space. In this study a 150-item meaning recall test was taken by 611 Japanese university students and scored by two native Japanese researchers and three LLMs (Llama 3B-8, GPT4o and Gemini 1.5) to determine whether correlations, internal reliability, and mean scores between humans and LLMs were comparable. This was found to be the case for GPT4o and Gemini 1.5. Finally, many-facet Rasch measurement was used to isolate cases where LLMs rated responses differently than humans. The findings are discussed and recommendations are given for improving AI scoring.
APA_reference: Stewart, J., Anthony, L., Batty, A. O., Nakamura, K., Nicklin, C., McLean, S., & Tomaru, K. (2024). Can We Reliably Score Meaning Recall Vocabulary Tests Using AI? A Comparison of Human vs. AI Scoring. Unpublished manuscript.
research_h_q: Are LLM ratings stricter, more lenient, or statistically indistinguishable from human ratings of the same data?
Does scoring meaning-recall vocabulary tests affect test reliability relative to scoring by human raters?
Are correlations between human and LLM ratings acceptable under standards of inter-rater reliability in the field of language testing?
When and why do LLM and human raters differ in judgments?

teachers: N/A

prompts_used: System_prompt = ```You are a helpful, smart, kind, and efficient AI assistant. You always fulfill the user's requests to the best of your ability.```
user_prompt = ```For the English word "{target_word}", is the word/phrase "{response}" a good Japanese translation? Only answer with either "YES" or "NO".```
sample_size: 611 Japanese university students, two human raters, and three LLMs.
learning_perceptions: N/A

benefits_affordances: Leading commercial LLMs (GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5) can grade meaning-recall tests in a manner highly comparable to human raters in terms of mean scores, internal reliability, and score variance.
AI scoring can greatly simplify and expedite the grading of meaning-recall tests, making their adoption more feasible for educators and researchers.
LLMs facilitate the use of meaning-recall tests in contexts where educators are not fluent in the learners' L1s.
For research and low-stakes educational contexts, LLMs can provide a convenient method of scoring.
drawbacks: The open-weight, smaller model (Llama 3-8B) showed significant differences from human raters across multiple metrics, including lower mean scores, restricted variance, and lower reliability.
LLMs can make categorical errors, such as Llama marking a comma as a correct translation.

LLMs may exhibit different levels of leniency compared to human raters, sometimes accepting translations that are only loosely associated with the target word's meaning or are grammatically incorrect.
Discrepancies in scoring can arise from LLMs lacking specific contextual information that human raters might possess or infer.
study_limitations: The study used one of the simplest variants of the Llama model; more sophisticated versions might perform better.
The prompts used were minimal and did not attempt to mirror the complex thought processes of human raters.
The dichotomous (yes/no) nature of the scoring task may have simplified the process, potentially inflating agreement levels.
LLMs were used to score unique responses to create an answer key rather than scoring all 91,650 individual responses, which means the consistency of the LLMs on identical inputs was not tested.
Human raters were inadvertently exposed to non-defining context sentences that the LLMs were not, which may have influenced their judgments on certain items and affected the comparison.

students: The use of AI for scoring could enable faster feedback on vocabulary tests, allowing for more timely learning interventions (inferred).
teachers: AI scoring mitigates the difficulty and time-consuming nature of manually grading meaning-recall tests, especially for teachers not fluent in their students' L1.
institutions: Enables the scalable implementation of meaning-recall tests, which are considered more valid measures of vocabulary knowledge for reading proficiency than multiple-choice formats.
other: Researchers can use LLMs to reliably score vocabulary test data, reducing the cost and logistical challenges associated with employing multiple human raters.

policy_guidance: Caution must be exercised before using LLMs for vocabulary test scoring in high-stakes contexts.
To improve AI scoring, a voting system could be adopted where multiple LLMs score responses and the majority decision is used.
Disagreements between LLMs could be checked automatically using a dictionary or a more advanced high-performance LLM.
A human rater could be introduced into an automated system to serve as a tiebreaker when a group of LLMs disagree.
emergent_themes: The importance of informational parity between human and AI raters; discrepancies in available context (e.g., context sentences) can lead to different judgments.
The distinction between AI making categorical errors versus exhibiting differences in rater leniency is crucial for evaluating AI performance.
The conflict between dictionary definitions and colloquial language use presents a challenge for automated scoring systems.
The potential for unexpected inputs to cause 'jailbreak' events in LLMs, leading to illogical scoring decisions.
emergent_issues: The potential for LLMs to 'jailbreak' and provide illogical scores when faced with unexpected or out-of-domain learner responses (e.g., marking a comma as a correct translation).
The impact of subtle differences in the information provided to human versus AI raters (e.g., access to context sentences) can significantly affect scoring alignment.
LLMs may score grammatically incorrect but semantically related answers leniently, whereas human raters may treat these as clear errors, highlighting a difference in error evaluation.
