title: Exploring the Efficacy of ChatGPT-Based Feedback Compared With Teacher Feedback and Self-Feedback: Evidence From Chinese-English Translation
authors: Siyi Cao, Tongquan Zhou
summary: This study compares the effectiveness of three feedback types—self-feedback (SF), teacher feedback (TF), and ChatGPT-based feedback (CF)—on the Chinese-to-English translation quality of 45 advanced Master of Translation and Interpretation (MTI) students. Using BLEU scores for overall quality and Coh-Metrix for linguistic features (lexicon, syntax, cohesion), the study found that TF and SF resulted in higher overall translation quality than CF. However, ChatGPT feedback was superior in enhancing lexical capabilities and referential cohesion. Conversely, TF and SF were more effective for improving syntactic skills, particularly the use of the passive voice. The findings suggest that ChatGPT is a valuable supplementary tool for translation practice, complementing traditional feedback methods rather than replacing them.
APA_reference: Cao, S., & Zhou, T. (2025). Exploring the Efficacy of ChatGPT-Based Feedback Compared With Teacher Feedback and Self-Feedback: Evidence From Chinese-English Translation. SAGE Open, 1-18. https://doi.org/10.1177/21582440251369204

title: Can novice teachers detect AI-generated texts in EFL writing?
authors: Vanessa De Wilde
summary: This paper reports on a qualitative study that investigated whether novice English teachers were able to detect AI-generated writing and which strategies they used to do this. The results show that some novice teachers are quite good at detecting AI-generated texts, while others proved to have more difficulties. The teachers used both linguistic and content-related strategies to detect AI-generated writing. The results point towards the value of including this topic in teaching methodology courses in (initial) teacher training programmes.

title: Generative AI-assisted, evidence-informed use of L1 in L2 classrooms
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse, Yuwei Wan, Tsz Ying Ho, and Angel M. Y. Lin
summary: This intervention study aimed to raise preservice English language teachers' awareness of purposeful L1 use in L2 classrooms and to explore how generative AI tools like ChatGPT can support this practice. The study involved fifty-six preservice teachers in a Master of Education program in Hong Kong. Data were collected through pre- and post-intervention mixed-method surveys and follow-up group interviews. The findings indicate that explicit instruction significantly increased the teachers' intention to use L1 and their knowledge of evidence-informed strategies. Furthermore, the study identified that generative AI can assist teachers by providing linguistic knowledge, developing cross-language teaching materials, and acting as a personalized learning assistant for students.

title: Can my writing be polished further? When ChatGPT meets human touch
authors: Yoo-Jean Lee
summary: This study explores how 19 Korean EFL university students use ChatGPT in conjunction with human scaffolding (from teachers and peers) to improve their academic writing. Adopting the cognitive process model of writing as a theoretical framework, the research investigates the iterative process of planning, translating, and reviewing that learners engage in. Through think-aloud sessions and interviews, the study finds that guidance from the teacher and collaboration among peers were crucial for effectively using ChatGPT. This human-AI collaborative approach provided emotional reassurance and enhanced the learners' metacognitive awareness, emphasizing the importance of a well-orchestrated learning environment in the EFL writing classroom.

title: The impact of automated writing evaluation on writing gains
authors: Bart Deygers, Liisa Buelens, David Chan, Laura Schildt, Amaury Van Parys, Marieke Vanbuel
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of ChatGPT as an automated writing evaluation (AWE) tool for improving the English writing skills of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students. Over a nine-week quasi-experimental intervention, 105 first-year university students in Belgium were divided into two groups: a control group receiving only teacher feedback, and an experimental group receiving both teacher feedback and access to ChatGPT. The study focused on changes in syntactic and lexical complexity. Results showed that while the experimental group wrote significantly longer and more complex texts during the intervention, these gains were not sustained in a final writing task completed without ChatGPT. The study concludes that the primary factor for sustained improvement was instructional time, not the AI tool itself. It suggests that AI is most effective as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, human feedback, particularly for developing syntactic complexity, while its impact on lexical development is more limited without targeted instruction.

title: Charting New Waters: Exploring the Role of ChatGPT in Postsecondary Pathways Programs
authors: Rachel Toncelli, Ilka Kostka, Cristine McMartin-Miller, Lin Zhou, Balazs Szelenyi
summary: This chapter describes an exploratory, qualitative study on the integration of ChatGPT into postsecondary English language pathways programs for international students in the United States. Through an ethnographic approach involving five teacher-researchers and 82 students, the study investigated practical applications of ChatGPT across various language and content courses. Data were collected via a shared journal of teacher observations, collaborative lesson planning, and anonymous student surveys. The findings indicate that using ChatGPT within a student-centered framework fostered critical AI literacy, increased student engagement, and enhanced learning. While students perceived ChatGPT as a useful, personalized tool, they also recognized its limitations and the risk of overreliance. The authors reflect on their collaborative process, discuss the benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT, and provide practical guidance for educators on integrating AI into language teaching, emphasizing the importance of transparency, critical analysis, and building upon existing pedagogical practices.

summary: This study explores the use of ChatGPT for self-directed foreign language (FL) learning in out-of-class settings. Using a mixed-methods approach with survey data from 101 adult learners on social media, it examines how learners use the AI chatbot, their perceptions of its use, and whether these views differ by age and the language studied (more vs. less commonly taught languages). title: ChatGPT for language learning: assessing teacher candidates' skills and perceptions using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)
authors: Jose Belda-Medina; Vendula Kokošková
summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the critical skills and perceptions of 58 EFL teacher candidates regarding the use of ChatGPT for language learning. Participants engaged in collaborative writing and text refinement tasks in both their L1 (Spanish) and L2 (English), and then compared their work with versions generated by ChatGPT-4. The study used pre-, post-, and delayed surveys based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), along with focus group interviews, to gather data. Findings revealed that participants struggled to distinguish between human and AI-generated texts, often misattributing texts with a more complex style to the AI, regardless of language nativeness. While participants showed increasingly positive perceptions of ChatGPT's usefulness and expressed intentions to use it, they also raised concerns about accuracy, reliability, and the potential for over-reliance. The study highlights the need for explicit training in critical AI literacy within teacher education programs.

title: ChatGPT and the development of core language skills: An exploratory study of EFL college students
authors: Liqaa Habeb Al-Obaydi, Marcel Pikhart, Md Kamal Hossain
summary: This study explores the application of ChatGPT for developing core language skills (speaking, reading, writing, listening, communication) among 30 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) college students in Iraq and the Czech Republic. Over a six-week period, the research compared two approaches: using ChatGPT for content analysis through direct questions, and using it as an interactive guide and practice partner. Data was collected via interviews using a phenomenographic research design. The findings indicate that the content analysis method was ineffective, providing only generic recommendations. Conversely, using ChatGPT as an interactive partner provided significant support for skill development, with students showing highly positive attitudes, particularly for writing (100%), listening (87%), and reading (87%). The study concludes that ChatGPT is most beneficial when used for regular, long-term language practice in an interactive manner.

title: ChatGPT in foreign language lesson plan creation: Trends, variability, and historical biases
authors: Alex Dornburg, Kristin J. Davin
summary: This study assesses trends in prompt specificity, variability, and weaknesses in foreign language lesson plans generated by ChatGPT using zero-shot prompting. The researchers designed five prompts with increasing complexity and specificity, inputting each one 10 times to analyze the variability of the 50 generated lesson plans. The outputs were scored against criteria based on best practices and teacher licensure exam requirements. The findings indicate that while ChatGPT generally produced high-quality lesson plans, increased prompt specificity did not guarantee a corresponding increase in quality. The study also observed significant variability in outputs from the same prompt, with some generated content reflecting outdated pedagogical practices (e.g., reciting scripted dialogues) instead of current, research-based ones (e.g., a focus on communication). The results suggest that the AI model's training on historical texts may introduce biases toward teaching methods that are no longer considered effective, highlighting the need for teachers to critically evaluate AI-generated materials.
APA_reference: Dornburg, A., & Davin, K. J. (2025). ChatGPT in foreign language lesson plan creation: Trends, variability, and historical biases. ReCALL, 37(3), 332–347. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344024000272

title: Unpacking the Rejection of L2 Students Toward ChatGPT-Generated Feedback: An Explanatory Research
authors: Ziqi Chen, Wei Wei, Xinhua Zhu, Yuan Yao
summary: This sequential mixed-method study, grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), investigates the challenges and reasons behind L2 university students' rejection of ChatGPT-generated feedback on their argumentative writing. Data from 45 computer science students in Macao revealed that 45.9% of the AI-generated feedback was rejected, with a higher rejection rate for content-focused feedback (58.7%) than for form-focused feedback (41.3%). The primary reasons for rejection included misalignments between student expectations and the feedback received, the anticipated high workload required to respond to the feedback, mismatches with external references like teacher expectations, and other impeding conditions.

title: Investigating the Effect of Role-Play Activity With GenAI Agent on EFL Students' Speaking Performance
authors: Angxuan Chen, Jiyou Jia, Yuzhen Li, Lingyu Fu
summary: This study conducted a quasi-experiment at a Chinese university to investigate the effect of integrating a Generative AI (GenAI) agent into role-play activities for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students. A total of 53 students were divided into an experimental group (n=29) that role-played with a GenAI agent and a control group (n=24) that role-played with peers. The results indicated that while both groups significantly improved their speaking performance, there was no significant difference in the level of improvement between them. However, the experimental group showed significantly higher improvements in intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy compared to the control group. The findings suggest that GenAI-integrated role-play is a viable alternative to traditional methods, particularly for enhancing student motivation and self-efficacy.
APA_reference: Chen, A., Jia, J., Li, Y., & Fu, L. (2025). Investigating the effect of role-play activity with GenAI agent on EFL students' speaking performance. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 63(1), 99–125. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331241299058

title: Chinese EFL learners’ GenAI literacy in digital multimodal composing and self-regulated writing: chain mediation effects of needs satisfaction and creative self-concept
authors: Meilu Liu, Lawrence Jun Zhang & Timothy J. E. Neufeld
summary: This study investigates the psychological mechanisms underlying the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) literacy in Digital Multimodal Composing (DMC) on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' writing self-regulated learning (SRL). Using a chain-mediation model based on self-determination theory and exploration-exploitation theory, the research surveyed 634 Chinese EFL learners. Data was analyzed using structural equation modeling. The findings indicate that creative self-concept significantly mediates the relationship between GenAI literacy in DMC and writing SRL, whereas needs satisfaction does not have a direct mediating effect. However, a significant chain mediation effect was found for needs satisfaction followed by creative self-concept. The study suggests that GenAI literacy in DMC should be integrated into language learning syllabi to enhance students' writing skills.

title: Comparing Hong Kong secondary school students' perceptions of ChatGPT-assisted EFL writing
authors: David James Woo, Deliang Wang & Kai Guo
summary: This quantitative study investigates the perceptions of 107 Hong Kong secondary school students on using ChatGPT for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing. It compares three teaching approaches: process-based, genre-based, and prompt engineering only. The study assesses the impact of these approaches on students' motivation, cognitive load, and satisfaction across different academic achievement levels. Findings indicate that explicit writing instruction, particularly the genre-based approach, significantly enhanced motivation and satisfaction while reducing cognitive load compared to a prompt-engineering-only approach. Students from higher-achieving schools reported more positive outcomes. The study concludes that a genre-based, scaffolded approach is most promising for ChatGPT-assisted EFL writing, highlighting the need for differentiated instruction.

title: Comparing the effects of ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation on students’ writing and ideal L2 writing self
authors: Huawei Shi, Ching Sing Chai, Sihan Zhou & Scott Aubrey
summary: This study compares the effects of ChatGPT and Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems on university students' L2 English writing performance and their 'ideal L2 writing self'. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, 150 second-year Chinese university students were divided into a ChatGPT group, an AWE group, and a control group for an eleven-week intervention. Quantitative results from ANCOVA showed that the ChatGPT group significantly outperformed both the AWE and control groups in post-test writing scores. However, the ChatGPT group's 'ideal L2 writing self' was significantly lower than the AWE group's. Qualitative analysis of students' reflection papers revealed that while students recognized ChatGPT's powerful affordances, they also developed an over-reliance on the tool, leading to a perceived loss of creativity and agency. The study discusses pedagogical implications, suggesting a need to balance the use of such powerful AI tools with strategies that maintain learner autonomy.
APA_reference: Shi, H., Chai, C. S., Zhou, S., & Aubrey, S. (2025). Comparing the effects of ChatGPT and automated writing evaluation on students’ writing and ideal L2 writing self. Computer Assisted Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2025.2454541

title: Exploring the Impact of Affordance Theory on Motivated Learning Behavior in ChatGPT-assisted IDLE Contexts
authors: Yu Cui, Yaru Meng, Xiaowei Zhang, Lingjie Tang
summary: This study investigates the interplay of various factors in ChatGPT-assisted informal digital learning of English (IDLE) among 944 Chinese EFL learners. Using a quantitative approach with questionnaires and structural equation modeling (SEM), the research examined how perceived affordances, digital literacy, grit, and emotions (foreign language enjoyment and burnout) influence motivated learning behavior. The study, framed by affordance theory, found that learners reported moderate to high levels of all factors except for burnout, which was low. Key findings show that digital literacy mediates the relationship between perceived affordances and motivated learning behavior. Furthermore, digital literacy and foreign language enjoyment act as a strong serial mediation pathway. Conversely, neither grit nor burnout served as significant mediators in this context. The study highlights the importance of digital literacy and positive emotions in sustaining motivation in AI-driven learning environments.
APA_reference: Cui, Y., Meng, Y., Zhang, X., & Tang, L. (2025). Exploring the impact of affordance theory on motivated learning behavior in ChatGPT-assisted IDLE contexts. RELC Journal, 1-17. https://doi.org/10.1177/00336882251347978

title: Data-driven learning: From Collins Cobuild Dictionary to ChatGPT
authors: John Flowerdew
summary: This paper, a revised plenary speech, traces the evolution of data-driven learning (DDL) from its origins with corpus linguistics, exemplified by the Collins Cobuild Dictionary (Case Study 1), to its modern applications. It presents a second case study on a DDL workshop for PhD students' academic writing in Hong Kong, which used traditional corpus tools. The third case study replicates the workshop tasks using Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, analyzing their performance, affordances, and limitations. The author compares the deterministic, inductive approach of traditional DDL with the probabilistic, answer-providing nature of LLMs, concluding with a discussion on the future synthesis of both methodologies in language education.

title: Generating Genre-Based Automatic Feedback on English for Research Publication Purposes
authors: Stephanie Link, Robert Redmon, Yaser Shamsi, Martin Hagan
summary: This paper discusses the development and evaluation of an AI-mediated writing technology designed to support second language (L2) writers in English for research publication purposes (ERPP). The system leverages genre-based instruction (GBI) and a large language model (ELECTRA) to provide automated feedback on the rhetorical structure of research article introductions. The authors describe a streamlined workflow for training a neural network classifier using a large corpus of 40,000 research articles. They fine-tuned the model through an iterative process of automated classification and manual correction. The study reports on the high accuracy, precision, and recall of the network's classification, which surpasses previously reported results in genre-based automated writing evaluation. The authors demonstrate how this technology is integrated into a learning system called Dissemity, offering implications for tool development and GBI.

authors: Thi-Ngoc-Anh Duong, Hsiu-Ling Chen
summary: This study investigated how 47 high school EFL students in Northern Vietnam, divided into higher and lower proficiency groups, used a custom GPT-3.5-based chatbot (Writing Assistant Bot) for writing practice over 11 weeks. Using a mixed-methods approach with chat logs, writing tests, questionnaires, and interviews, the study examined usage patterns, writing performance, and perceptions. title: The Effectiveness of OpenAI GPT-Generated Definitions Versus Definitions from an English Learners’ Dictionary in a Lexically Orientated Reading Task
authors: Geraint Paul Rees, Robert Lew
summary: In metalexicographical research, experts have judged the performance of technologies such as OpenAI Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) in lexicographic production tasks as promising yet inferior to human lexicographers. It remains unclear whether this perceived inferiority limits the effectiveness of AI-generated lexicography in resolving practical language doubts. Accordingly, this study compares the effectiveness of AI-generated definitions to those from the Macmillan English Dictionary (MED) in resolving vocabulary doubts in a multiple-choice reading task designed to test lexical knowledge. It involves 43 L2 English users in the third year of an English studies degree at a Spanish university. Students provided with MED definitions performed better on the reading task than those without access to definitions. However, there was no significant difference between the performance of students with either MED definitions or without definitions altogether, and those provided with AI-definitions. The implications of these findings are discussed along with avenues for further research.
APA_reference: Rees, G. P., & Lew, R. (2024). The Effectiveness of OpenAI GPT-Generated Definitions Versus Definitions from an English Learners’ Dictionary in a Lexically Orientated Reading Task. International Journal of Lexicography, 37(1), 50-74. https://doi.org/10.1093/ijl/ecad030

title: Beyond Replacement: How Large Language Models Influence Dictionary Usage Patterns Among Chinese English Learners
authors: Rongyan Liu, Xiande Chen, and Yunfeng Xu
summary: This study investigates the influence of Large Language Models (LLMs) on the dictionary usage patterns of Chinese English learners. Using a mixed-methods approach with questionnaire surveys (n=608) and semi-structured interviews (n=17), the research finds that LLMs are not simply replacing traditional dictionaries but are reconstructing the language learning tool ecosystem. A clear functional division has emerged: learners use LLMs for complex tasks like translation and writing assistance, while traditional dictionaries are preferred for authoritative definitions and structured vocabulary learning. This task-oriented strategy is described as 'dictionaries for discrete knowledge acquisition, LLMs for integrated language application'. The study also identifies that tool adoption is stratified by demographic factors such as age, educational background, and English proficiency. Furthermore, it reveals a cognitive shift in how learners conceptualize language learning, highlighting a tension between instrumental utility and cultural acquisition. The findings suggest future directions for lexicography should focus on intelligent integration of authoritative content with AI capabilities and specialized, personalized tools.
APA_reference: Liu, R., Chen, X., & Xu, Y. (2025). Beyond replacement: How large language models influence dictionary usage patterns among Chinese English learners. International Journal of Lexicography, 00, 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1093/ijl/ecaf017

title: The Impact of ChatGPT on English for Academic Purposes (EAP) Students' Language Learning Experience: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective
authors: Jinming Du, Antonie Alm
summary: This qualitative study explores the perceptions of 24 postgraduate English for Academic Purposes (EAP) students in a New Zealand university regarding their use of ChatGPT. Using self-determination theory (SDT) as a framework, the study investigates how ChatGPT affects students' psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Through semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, the findings indicate that ChatGPT can support autonomy and competence by offering flexibility, personalized feedback, and a non-judgmental space for practice. However, its impact on relatedness is mixed; some students felt a sense of companionship, while others were concerned about reduced human interaction. The study concludes that while students see the benefits of ChatGPT, they also value human teacher interaction. It provides theoretical insights and practical recommendations for integrating generative AI into language education effectively.

title: Innovation Off the Bat: Bridging the ChatGPT Gap in Digital Competence among English as a Foreign Language Teachers
authors: Gulsara Urazbayeva, Raisa Kussainova, Aikumis Aibergen, Assel Kaliyeva, Gulnur Kantayeva
summary: This study investigates the impact of a guided, experimental implementation of ChatGPT on the digital competence of 24 in-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in Kazakhstan. Using a mixed-methods approach, the research assessed teachers' proficiency in integrating ChatGPT through a custom tool based on the TPACK framework before and after an eight-week intervention. During the intervention, teachers used researcher-designed prompts for various pedagogical tasks like lesson planning and creating assessments. Quantitative results showed statistically significant improvements in teachers' ChatGPT integration skills. Qualitative findings revealed that teachers perceived ChatGPT as beneficial for its creativity and ability to automate tasks, but also noted challenges such as the need to verify AI-generated content and its occasional repetitiveness. The study concludes that guided integration of generative AI can effectively enhance teachers' AI literacy and offers practical insights for teacher professional development programs.

summary: This exploratory case study examines how four university-level German language learners with diverse backgrounds (heritage and classroom learners) developed autonomy while integrating AI tools, primarily ChatGPT, into their self-directed learning. The study identifies key dimensions of autonomy in AI-mediated environments, including critical evaluation of AI output, evolving learner-AI relationships, and maintaining an L2 voice. summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the impact of AI-assisted learning, specifically using ChatGPT, on the academic writing skills of Chinese as a Second Language (CSL) students at a Chinese university. title: Enhancing EFL Writing Revision Practices: The Impact of AI- and Teacher-Generated Feedback and Their Sequences
authors: Thi Thanh Thao Tran
summary: This preliminary study investigates the impact of teacher-generated feedback (TGF) and AI-generated feedback (AIGF), as well as their sequencing (TGF-AIGF vs. AIGF-TGF), on the writing revision practices of 14 Vietnamese undergraduate EFL students. Using Google's Gemini, the study analyzed revisions in four essays across a 15-week course. Findings indicate that AIGF led to more revisions than TGF alone, and the combination of both yielded the highest revision frequency. AIGF was effective for surface-level issues (grammar, vocabulary), while TGF addressed higher-order concerns (content, organization). Although not statistically significant, the AIGF-TGF sequence resulted in slightly more revisions, suggesting that addressing surface-level errors with AI first allows for more effective teacher feedback on global issues later. The results support integrating AI and teacher feedback to enhance academic writing revisions.

summary: This study investigated the perceptions of 56 undergraduate English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students at a rural STEM university in Ecuador regarding the use of Generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, in academic writing. Through a survey, the research explored students' views on academic dishonesty, the motivations for using AI, and its perceived impact on their learning. Key findings indicate that students were more concerned about hindering their own writing skill development than about potential academic penalties. A majority of students believed that AI-generated text is easily detectable and considered submitting such work as academically dishonest. title: EFL secondary students' use of ChatGPT for writing task completion pathways
authors: David James Woo, Kai Guo & Hengky Susanto
summary: This study examines the content and sequencing of prompts used by English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary students to complete a writing task with ChatGPT without any prior instruction. Through a qualitative case study of four students, the research identifies six distinct types of prompts and varied 'prompt engineering pathways' that students developed through individual trial-and-error. The pathways ranged in sophistication and length (from five to 12 turns). Findings show that students did not use all available prompt types and each employed a unique combination, indicating a lack of strategic prompting skills. The study concludes that there is a significant need for explicit and personalized prompt engineering education in EFL writing classrooms to help students become more effective collaborators with AI writing tools.

summary: This qualitative study investigates the use of ChatGPT for academic writing among 43 Indian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners who have used the tool for over a year. title: ESP practitioners' perspectives on the efficiency of using artificial intelligence ‘ChatGPT' in needs analysis
authors: Tarek Assassi
summary: This study investigated the perspectives of English for Specific Purposes (ESP) practitioners on using ChatGPT for linguistic needs analysis, specifically for target and language learning needs in the context of aviation English. Addressing a gap in research, the study explored AI's potential to improve data accuracy and streamline the time-consuming needs analysis process. Using a qualitative approach, fifteen ESP practitioners, familiar with ChatGPT, were interviewed individually or in a focus group. They reviewed and compared needs analysis results generated by two methods: a traditional approach and an AI-assisted approach using ChatGPT, both based on Hutchinson and Waters' (1987) model. The findings revealed a positive reception for ChatGPT, with practitioners expressing confidence in its ability to accurately identify target situation requirements. They believed ChatGPT could mitigate common challenges like time constraints. However, they held reservations about the tool's effectiveness in identifying specific learners' language lacks compared to traditional testing methods.

title: Is generative AI ready to replace human raters in scoring EFL writing? Comparison of human and automated essay evaluation
authors: Arif Cem Topuz, Mine Yıldız, Elif Taşlıbeyaz, Hamza Polat, Engin Kurşun
summary: This study investigates the differences and relationships between scores assigned by two human raters (HR) and a Generative AI (GenAI), ChatGPT-3.5, on 210 essays written by 35 undergraduate English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The essays were evaluated using a five-factor analytic rubric. Findings revealed significant differences between the scores from the two HRs, and also between HR and GenAI scores, with GenAI consistently scoring lower. However, GenAI's scores were highly consistent across two separate evaluations (high intra-rater reliability), unlike the HRs' scores which showed weak correlation (low inter-rater reliability). A significant correlation was found between one HR and GenAI on all scoring factors, while the second HR showed correlation on only three factors. The study concludes that while GenAI demonstrates high reliability, its scoring differs from human judgment, suggesting its potential role as an assistant to reduce teacher workload, particularly for mechanical aspects of writing, rather than a full replacement for human raters.

summary: This study addresses the gap in understanding university learners' readiness for ChatGPT-based English learning by developing and validating a new instrument, the Learner Readiness for ChatGPT-assisted English Learning (LRCEL) scale. summary: This study investigates the relationship between the use of ChatGPT and the well-being of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in Iran, focusing on the mediating role of emotion regulation. Findings show that ChatGPT has significant potential for providing personalized learning support and enhancing cultural comprehension. title: Revisiting Integrated Model of Technology Acceptance Among the Generative AI-Powered Foreign Language Speaking Practice: Through the Lens of Positive Psychology and Intrinsic Motivation
authors: Chenghao Wang, Xueyun Li, Bin Zou
summary: This study expands the Integrated Model of Technology Acceptance (IMTA) to investigate how language learning emotions and willingness to communicate in various contexts influence the acceptance of Generative AI (GenAI) chatbots for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking practice. Using a questionnaire with 368 university students in China, alongside pre- and post-tests, the research found that willingness to communicate with GenAI positively impacts perceived usefulness and ease of use. Conversely, learners with higher communicative confidence found the chatbots less easy to use, and those experiencing language learning boredom perceived them as less useful. While GenAI improved speaking skills, particularly for lower-proficiency students, learners who prefer human interaction found the chatbots less engaging. The findings suggest that teachers should consider individual student differences and GenAI's limitations, advocating for a blended approach to create an effective GenAI-supported learning environment and highlighting the need for teacher AI competency.

benefits_affordances: GenAI chatbots effectively improved overall speaking skills, with significant progress observed from pre-test to post-test.
Lower-proficiency learners (A1-A2) experienced more substantial gains in fluency, coherence, pronunciation, and vocabulary compared to higher-proficiency learners.
Willingness to communicate with GenAI was a significant positive predictor of both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use.
Perceived usefulness (PU) was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention (BI), highlighting that learners adopt tools they find beneficial.
drawbacks: Learners with higher self-perceived communicative competence (SPCC) found GenAI chatbots significantly less easy to use, possibly due to higher expectations for conversational quality.
Learners experiencing foreign language boredom (FLB) were less likely to perceive GenAI chatbots as useful.
Learners more willing to communicate with peers in the classroom tended to perceive GenAI chatbots as slightly less useful, suggesting a preference for human interaction.

Higher-proficiency learners (B1-C2) showed minimal to no significant improvement in fluency, coherence, pronunciation, and vocabulary, suggesting a mismatch between the AI's content and their advanced needs.
study_limitations: The sample size was relatively small and from a single university, limiting generalizability.
The study did not explore a broader range of emotional variables, such as pride or anger.
The research focused on direct impacts, leaving potential moderating and mediating mechanisms (e.g., SPCC as a moderator) unexplored.
The experimental period of 13 weeks may be too short to assess the sustained impact of intrinsic motivations on technology acceptance and learning outcomes.

students: GenAI provides a psychologically safe environment for speaking practice, which can be particularly beneficial for lower-proficiency learners.
Acceptance and perceived utility of GenAI tools are highly dependent on individual differences, including emotional state, confidence, and preference for human interaction.
teachers: Teachers must recognize that GenAI is not a one-size-fits-all solution and should avoid indiscriminately pushing all students to use it.
Effective pedagogy requires teachers to use differentiated instruction, leveraging GenAI for personalized learning while understanding its limitations.
The importance of developing teachers' AI competence is underscored to enable them to integrate AI effectively and bridge the gap between AI capabilities and learner expectations.
institutions: N/A
other: Developers of GenAI chatbots should consider incorporating features like gamification, dynamic avatars, and real-time conversational feedback to increase engagement and motivate learners, especially those who experience boredom.

policy_guidance: Teachers should adopt a critical approach, integrating their own expertise with AI-assisted instruction to maximize benefits and create effective classroom outcomes.
Instruction should be differentiated to account for students' personalities, attitudes toward GenAI, and proficiency levels.
Teachers need a deep understanding of GenAI's limitations to support the development of higher-level English learners, whose needs may not be met by current chatbot capabilities.
emergent_themes: Compartmentalization of Communication: Learners appear to evaluate GenAI interactions differently from human interactions (whether face-to-face or digital), suggesting they perceive AI as a functional tool rather than a social interlocutor.

The 'Proficiency Paradox': While GenAI is effective for lower-level learners, its utility diminishes for higher-level learners, highlighting a critical gap in the ability of current systems to provide appropriately complex and nuanced linguistic input and interaction.

title: Structured or Semi-Structured? The Use of Reflection Journals in Postgraduates' Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Development in an L2 Academic Writing Context
authors: Danyang Zhang, Lanyu Wen, Junjie Gavin Wu
summary: This study examines and compares the effects of structured reflection journals (SRJs) and semi-structured reflection journals (SSRJs) on enhancing postgraduate students' Generative AI (GenAI) literacy in an L2 academic writing context. Based on frameworks from UNESCO and Digital Promise, the study developed a four-dimensional GenAI literacy framework. The GenAI literacy levels of 39 postgraduate students were assessed before and after an eight-week intervention involving four GenAI-assisted writing tasks and subsequent reflection journal entries. The results showed significant improvements in GenAI literacy for both groups across three dimensions (Operational Competence, Ethics and Security, and Critical Evaluation), with no significant statistical difference between the SRJ and SSRJ groups. However, a qualitative analysis of the journals revealed that SRJs, with their more detailed guiding questions, prompted deeper engagement with GenAI-related ethical rules and more thorough evaluations of AI-generated content. The study concludes by advocating for the integration of reflective practices into GenAI-assisted L2 academic writing to enhance students' critical evaluation skills and ethical awareness.

title: Giving Away the Immersive L2 Learning Experiences in GenAI-Mediated Contexts: The Contributions of Cognitive and Affective Factors
authors: Guanqiong Zhou
summary: This study explores the cognitive and affective factors that influence immersion in Generative AI (GenAI)-mediated second language (L2) learning. Based on the cognitive-affective model of immersive learning, control-value theory, and the technology acceptance model, the research examined how perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, enjoyment, and boredom impact immersion among 460 Chinese college L2 learners. Using structural equation modelling, the study found that perceived ease of use positively predicted perceived usefulness and enjoyment. Perceived usefulness, in turn, positively influenced immersion and enjoyment while negatively affecting boredom. Enjoyment was a positive predictor of immersion, but boredom had no significant effect. Mediation analysis showed that perceived ease of use indirectly influences immersion through the mediators of perceived usefulness and enjoyment. The findings offer practical implications for designing and implementing GenAI tools in L2 education.

summary: This study explores the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in informal digital learning of English (IDLE) practices. Using a mixed-methods approach combining an experiment with semi-structured interviews, the research investigates GenAI's effectiveness in improving the oral proficiency of college-level English learners. The study is framed by social cognitive theory and the Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) model within a holistic learning ecology. authors: Guangxiang Leon Liu, Ron Darvin, Chaojun Ma
summary: This study investigates the adoption and experiences of Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners using generative AI tools like ChatGPT for informal digital learning of English (IDLE). Using an explanatory sequential mixed-method design, the research combines a survey of 867 learners based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with interviews from 20 learners. The quantitative findings show that perceived usefulness, mediated by perceived ease of use, significantly predicts learners' intention to use and their actual use of these technologies. The qualitative data reveals three key themes: perceived usefulness emerges from hands-on experimentation, intention to use increases as learners negotiate the tools' affordances and constraints, and actual use involves employing AI chatbots as tutors or conversation partners. The study concludes that learners are creatively engaging with AI for IDLE, highlighting the need for developing AI literacies and suggesting implications for language pedagogy.

authors: Magdalena Pando, Maricela León, Caitlín A. Dougherty & Karla del Rosal
summary: This qualitative case study investigates the experiences of two elementary dual language teachers using ChatGPT for pedagogical planning. Framed by a teacher professional knowledge theoretical framework, the study analyzed the teachers' prompts and reflections from in-depth interviews. Four themes emerged: characteristics of dual language prompt engineering, teachers' evaluation of AI-generated content, a comparison of bilingual human and artificial intelligence, and teacher-identified affordances and constraints. The findings suggest a need for professional development in AI technologies for teachers in multilingual contexts and for developing prompt engineering skills.
APA_reference: Pando, M., León, M., Dougherty, C. A., & del Rosal, K. (2025). Exploring dual language teachers' experiences, perceptions and pedagogical implications of ChatGPT in emergent bilingual education. Bilingual Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.1080/15235882.2025.2478499

title: Exploring EMI teachers’ agency in addressing language-related challenges with ChatGPT: a multiple case study
authors: Wenyun Jia & Jack Pun
summary: This study adopts an ecological perspective of teacher agency to explore how three English-medium instruction (EMI) content teachers in a Chinese high school used ChatGPT to address language-related teaching challenges. Using data from GPT interaction logs and interviews, the study examines the factors influencing the teachers' agency. Findings show that teachers exercised agency by addressing language challenges, leveraging ChatGPT's affordances, and mitigating contextual constraints. The enactment of agency was dynamic and influenced by past experiences, social contexts, evaluations of ChatGPT, and future aspirations. The study highlights that teachers' initial and ongoing evaluations of the tool in response to their specific contexts play a crucial role in their engagement, informing how to facilitate effective teacher-AI collaborations in EMI settings.
APA_reference: Jia, W., & Pun, J. (2025). Exploring EMI teachers’ agency in addressing language-related challenges with ChatGPT: a multiple case study. Computer Assisted Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2025.2511061
research_h_q: How do high school EMI teachers exercise agency when using GPT?
What factors influence the ways in which high school EMI teachers exhibit agency when using GPT to address language-related teaching issues?

It can provide teachers with a sense of validation for their pedagogical ideas and approaches.

Outputs may not align with specific contextual needs, such as exam requirements, without careful prompting.
Generated materials, like glossaries, can be incomplete or insufficient for instructional purposes.

The retrospective examination of GPT usage might have overlooked some aspects of the teachers' agency exercise.

students: GPT-based activities were perceived to enhance knowledge retention and language skills (vocabulary, reading, speaking, writing).
Collaborative tasks inspired by GPT encouraged less proficient students to participate more actively.

teachers: Using GPT enabled teachers to actively address language-related challenges in their EMI classrooms.
Positive interactions with GPT boosted teachers' confidence and sense of professional competence.
The process prompted teachers to reflect on and adapt their existing teaching methods.
GPT's affordances helped validate and reshape teachers' professional identities, particularly regarding the integration of language and content teaching.
institutions: The findings provide insights for designing effective professional development programs on generative AI for teachers in EMI contexts.

policy_guidance: Professional development programs should be designed to help teachers navigate GPT's reliability issues and use it reflectively and confidently.
Training should introduce a wide range of GPT affordances and link them explicitly to EMI pedagogy.
Professional development should be personalized and responsive to specific classroom contexts and individual teacher needs.
Institutions should encourage a synergistic teacher-GPT relationship through iterative cycles of reflection, evaluation, adaptation, and implementation, supported by collegial collaboration.
emergent_themes: The dynamic and context-sensitive nature of teacher agency as an ecological phenomenon.
The interplay of iterational (past), practical-evaluative (present), and projective (future) dimensions in shaping teacher agency with AI.
The concept of 'developmental affordances', where teachers' real-time evaluative experiences with GPT shape their future agency.

emergent_issues: A teacher's initial evaluative experience (positive or negative) with an LLM can have a significant and lasting impact on their future agency and engagement, potentially overriding the general trend of increased acceptance with more exposure.
A significant gap can exist between a teacher's optimistic expectations of an LLM and its actual performance, leading to disillusionment and constrained agency.

There is a potential conflict between the student-centered pedagogical approaches often suggested by LLMs and the deeply ingrained teacher-centered learning cultures present in some educational contexts.

title: Exploring English as a Foreign Language Learners' Adoption and Utilisation of ChatGPT for Speaking Practice Through an Extended Technology Acceptance Model
authors: Bin Zou, Chenghao Wang, Yiwen Yan, Xiaoman Du, Yuan Ji
summary: This study investigates the factors influencing Chinese EFL learners' adoption of ChatGPT for oral English practice, using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Through a mixed-methods approach involving a survey of 212 learners and interviews with 12, the research found that perceived usefulness strongly influences attitude, which in turn predicts the intention to use. Facilitating conditions were a significant predictor of perceived ease of use. Qualitative findings highlight ChatGPT's effectiveness for simulating exams and dialogues, its convenience, but also its limitations, such as generic feedback and scenario-specific constraints, underscoring the need for user skill in prompt design and teacher guidance.
APA_reference: Zou, B., Wang, C., Yan, Y., Du, X., & Ji, Y. (2025). Exploring English as a Foreign Language Learners' Adoption and Utilisation of ChatGPT for Speaking Practice Through an Extended Technology Acceptance Model. International Journal of Applied Linguistics, 35, 689–704. https://doi.org/10.1111/ijal.12658

title: Exploring the use of ChatGPT-generated model texts as a feedback instrument: EFL students' text quality and perceptions
authors: Dunming (Jason) Lu, Yutian Zeng
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of using ChatGPT-generated model texts as a feedback tool for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing. It employed a quasi-experimental, pretest-posttest design with 104 Chinese high school students divided into three groups: a control group (no feedback), an experimental group receiving a teacher-written model text, and another experimental group receiving a ChatGPT-generated model text. The results indicated that both experimental groups significantly improved their writing quality in terms of content, organization, vocabulary, and grammar compared to the control group. The improvements between the two experimental groups were similar, suggesting ChatGPT-generated texts can be as effective as teacher-written ones. Students generally held positive perceptions towards the AI-generated models but expressed concerns regarding their potential lack of contextual relevance and stylistic unnaturalness.
APA_reference: Lu, D. (Jason), & Zeng, Y. (2025). Exploring the use of ChatGPT-generated model texts as a feedback instrument: EFL students' text quality and perceptions. Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.1080/17501229.2025.2525341
research_h_q: Does the use of ChatGPT-generated model texts as a feedback instrument significantly enhance mainland Chinese EFL students' text quality in rewritten essays?

The target learners are mainland Chinese high school Grade 11 students with B1 to B2 proficiency levels (CEFR). You need to write on the topic of whether environmental problems are too big for individuals to solve. Please adopt the argument that environmental problems are not too big for individuals to solve. Write at least 150 words.

drawbacks: Students reported that ChatGPT-generated texts could restrict their content development and creativity.

study_limitations: The study used only one model text, which may not provide sufficient input.
The one-shot experiment design may not capture the sustained, long-term effects of the intervention.
The findings' applicability may be limited as the study focused on a single argumentative writing task and prompt.
The assessment relied solely on holistic scoring, which could be supplemented by more nuanced measures.
Only a single, simple prompt was used, which may not reflect the full potential of advanced prompting techniques.

students: Can significantly improve writing quality by using ChatGPT-generated model texts as comprehensible input.
May become overly reliant on AI models, which could hinder their creativity and independent improvement.
teachers: Can use ChatGPT to efficiently generate high-quality model texts, reducing their workload as the sole feedback provider.

emergent_themes: Human-AI Collaboration: The study emphasizes a synergistic 'human-in-the-loop' approach, where teacher expertise is crucial for guiding and refining AI-generated content to meet pedagogical needs.

Comparable Effectiveness: Under conditions of a well-crafted prompt, AI-generated model texts can achieve a level of quality and pedagogical effectiveness comparable to those created by experienced human teachers.
Importance of Prompt Design: The quality and relevance of the AI-generated output are highly dependent on mindful prompt design that clearly articulates learning goals and learner context.
emergent_issues: Hindrance of Creativity: A major concern raised by students was that using a high-quality AI-generated model text could limit their own creativity and content development during the rewriting process.
Stylistic Unnaturalness: Students perceived the AI's output as formulaic, monotonous, and lacking the emotional depth and personal voice characteristic of human writing.

title: Exploring the dual impact of AI in post-entry language assessment: Potentials and pitfalls
authors: Tiancheng Zhang, Rosemary Erlam, Morena Botelho de Magalhães
summary: This paper investigates the use of Generative AI (GenAI) in post-entry language assessment (PELA) at the university level, using the Diagnostic English Language Needs Assessment (DELNA) at the University of Auckland as a case study. It presents two empirical studies: the first examines GenAI's capability to generate academic reading assessment texts and items, and the second evaluates a fine-tuned GPT-4o model for automated writing evaluation (AWE). Findings show that while GenAI is promising for content generation, it requires expert refinement for question complexity and subskill targeting. In AWE, the AI model's overall scores align well with human raters, but its feedback lacks detail. The paper conducts a SWOT analysis, highlighting AI's potential to enhance PELA's efficiency and scope, while also noting challenges like academic integrity and data privacy. It concludes by proposing a collaborative, human-centered model that integrates AI with human expertise to maintain assessment integrity and ethical standards.
APA_reference: Zhang, T., Erlam, R., & de Magalhães, M. B. (2025). Exploring the dual impact of AI in post-entry language assessment: Potentials and pitfalls. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, 45, 274–293. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190525000030

title: Exploring the perceptions of Chinese pre-service teachers on the integration of generative AI in English language teaching: Benefits, challenges, and educational implications
authors: Ji Young Chung, Seung-Hoon Jeong
summary: This study investigates the perceptions of 134 Chinese English pre-service teachers (PSTs) on integrating generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, into English language teaching. Using a quantitative approach, the research explores their familiarity with AI, its perceived impact on language learning, and its acceptance as a pedagogical tool. Findings show that PSTs recognize AI's potential to improve teaching efficiency, especially for grammar and writing. However, they also express concerns about over-reliance on AI, its negative impact on critical thinking, the authenticity of AI interactions, and ethical issues like data privacy and academic integrity. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for targeted professional development for educators to ensure a balanced and effective integration of AI in language education, preserving human interaction and cultural sensitivity.
APA_reference: Chung, J. Y., & Jeong, S.-H. (2024). Exploring the perceptions of Chinese pre-service teachers on the integration of generative AI in English language teaching: Benefits, challenges, and educational implications. authors: Lifang Bai, Yijia Wei
summary: This study investigates how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners notice, integrate, and perceive text reformulations generated by ChatGPT within a three-stage writing task (composing-comparison-rewriting). title: Exploring EFL students’ prompt engineering in human–AI story writing: an activity theory perspective
authors: David James Woo, Kai Guo & Hengky Susanto
summary: This study applies Activity Theory to investigate how 67 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) secondary school students in Hong Kong use prompt engineering with generative AI tools for short story writing. The students created their own AI tools using open-source models. The research analyzed students' AI tools, stories, and written reflections to identify the purposes behind their prompts. Three main themes emerged: a lack of awareness of purpose, overcoming writer's block, and developing or improving the story. The study also found correlations between these prompting purposes and characteristics of the students' activity systems, such as the sophistication of their AI tool, the quality of their story, and their school's academic achievement level. The findings suggest that educators should provide tailored instruction on AI use and that AI tool designers could incorporate differentiated guidance for users at different stages of writing.

title: Exploring interaction process, L2 motivation and intended effort in chatbot-mediated interactions: evidence from Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling
authors: Yunfei Du & Barry Lee Reynolds
summary: This study empirically examines the impact of chatbot-mediated interactions on learners' L2 motivational self system (L2MSS) and intended effort. 232 undergraduate students were divided into an experimental group (EG-CHAT) using the LLM-powered chatbot 'Doubao' for speaking activities, and a control group (CG) using a platform for structured practices like video watching and shadowing. A five-week quasi-experiment was conducted. Using ANOVA and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling, the study found that the EG-CHAT group showed significantly greater motivational changes, particularly in their 'ideal L2 self' and 'intended effort', compared to the CG. While both groups improved their L2 learning experience, there was no significant change in the 'ought-to L2 self' for either. LDA analysis of the EG-CHAT group's dialogue logs revealed that interactions were categorized into learning-related, class-related, and life-related topics, but were often superficial. The findings suggest that while LLM chatbots can enhance motivation, they require pedagogical scaffolding from teachers to foster deeper cognitive engagement.

title: Exploring EFL Teachers' Behavioral Intentions to Integrate GenAI Applications: Insights From PLS-SEM and fsQCA
authors: Muhammed Parviz, Francis Arthur
summary: This study investigates the behavioral intentions of 444 Iranian EFL teachers in higher education to integrate Generative AI (GenAI) applications like ChatGPT into their teaching. Using the UTAUT and AI-TPACK frameworks, the research employed a quantitative survey design, analyzing data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). Key findings indicate that performance expectancy and social influence are significant drivers for GenAI adoption. Conversely, a paradoxical negative relationship was found between teachers' AI-TPACK (a measure of deep technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge) and their intention to adopt GenAI, suggesting that greater awareness of the technology's complexities may act as a deterrent. The study identifies sociocultural and institutional challenges as major barriers and provides insights into the complex factors influencing technology integration in policy-constrained educational environments.

title: Facilitating student engagement through ChatGPT
authors: E. Meşe, Ö. Kuru & D. Atay
summary: This qualitative study investigates how utilizing ChatGPT in an online L2 writing course influenced the cognitive, behavioral, and emotional engagement and disengagement of tenth-grade students. title: Factors Influencing Learner Attitudes Towards ChatGPT-Assisted Language Learning in Higher Education
authors: Qianqian Cai, Yupeng Lin, Zhonggen Yu
summary: This study employs a mixed-method approach, combining structural equation modeling and interviews, to investigate the factors influencing higher education learners' attitudes towards ChatGPT-assisted language learning. Using an extended three-tier technology use model, the research finds that information system quality and hedonic motivation are more significant predictors of performance expectancy and perceived satisfaction than self-regulation. Behavioral intention was found to be a stronger predictor of learning effectiveness than perceived satisfaction or performance expectancy. The study also explores the mediating effects of these variables, highlighting that behavioral intention fully mediates the effect of perceived satisfaction on learning effectiveness. Despite limitations such as using an older version of ChatGPT, the findings offer implications for developers to focus on hedonic and informational aspects and for researchers to gain a more comprehensive understanding of learner attitudes.

Findings reveal diverse usage patterns and positive perceptions, highlighting the multifaceted role of digital resources in vocabulary acquisition, skill development, and language exploration. The study underscores the need for ongoing improvement in digital language learning tools and suggests avenues for future research, emphasizing long-term impact, personalized learning paths, emerging technologies, and socio-emotional aspects. title: Metaphorical conceptualizations of generative artificial intelligence use by Chinese university EFL learners
authors: Yi Yan, Wei Sun, Xiufeng Zhao
summary: This study explores the attitudes and perceptions of Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners towards Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in language learning. Using metaphor analysis, data was collected from 281 students from four universities in China who were asked to complete a sentence metaphorically describing GenAI. The analysis revealed a spectrum of attitudes, categorized into six metaphorical constructs: HUMANS, TOOL/MACHINE, BRAIN, RESOURCES, FOOD/DRINK, and MEDICINE. While many learners perceived GenAI as supportive and intelligent, others expressed concerns about over-reliance and the potential erosion of critical thinking skills. The findings highlight the necessity of considering learners' diverse views for the future integration of GenAI in language education and pedagogy.

title: Mobile language app learners’ self-efficacy increases after using generative AI
authors: Audrey K. Kittredge, Elise W. M. Hopman, Ben Reuveni, Danielle Dionne, Cassie Freeman, Xiangying Jiang
summary: This paper investigates the impact of generative AI-based features on the self-efficacy of language learners using the mobile app Duolingo. Across two studies with a total of 385 learners of French and Spanish, participants used AI features for conversation practice ('Roleplay') and on-demand grammatical explanations ('Explain My Answer') for one month. Using a pre-test/post-test survey design, the studies found that learners' self-efficacy for using the target language in real-life situations increased significantly. Learners who were new to the AI features (Study 2) showed broader and more significant gains in self-efficacy across various skills (speaking, grammar, understanding mistakes) compared to existing users (Study 1). A large majority of participants in both studies perceived the AI features as effective for learning and reported transferring their learned skills to real-world contexts.

title: Al vs. teacher feedback on EFL argumentative writing: a quantitative study
authors: Areen Alnemrat, Hesham Aldamen, Mohamad Almashour, Mutasim Al-Deaibes, Rami AlSharefeen
summary: This quantitative, quasi-experimental study investigates the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated versus teacher-generated feedback on the argumentative writing performance of 60 undergraduate EFL learners in Jordan. Participants, stratified by Intermediate-Low and Advanced-Low proficiency levels, were assigned to either an AI or teacher feedback group. They completed a pre-test writing task, received feedback, and submitted a revised post-test essay. The results indicated that while both feedback types led to significant improvements in writing scores, there was no statistically significant difference in gains between the AI and teacher groups. summary: This study compares AI-generated texts from ChatGPT with student-written essays, focusing on lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, and readability. summary: This study investigates how second language (L2) learners of languages other than English (LOTEs) use generative AI (GenAI) for writing and their perceptions of its ethicality. title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
authors: Cuiping Song, Yanping Song
summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the impact of using ChatGPT for AI-assisted language learning on the academic writing skills and motivation of Chinese English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students. The study involved 50 university students randomly assigned to either an experimental group using ChatGPT for writing tasks or a control group receiving traditional instruction over 12 weeks. Quantitative data from pre- and post-tests showed that the ChatGPT group had significant improvements in overall writing skills, including organization, coherence, grammar, vocabulary, and motivation, compared to the control group. title: EBA (Engaged but Amotivated) in AI-enhanced EFL learning: a qualitative study from a Chinese higher vocational context
authors: Lei Cao, Amelia Abdullah
summary: This study investigates the "Engaged but Amotivated" (EBA) phenomenon among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in a Chinese higher vocational college. Using Self-Determination Theory and a multidimensional engagement framework, the qualitative research explores how generative AI tools influence the motivation and engagement of low-proficiency students. Through classroom observations, interviews, and LMS log analysis over two semesters, the study found that students often exhibit 'performative participation'—completing tasks to meet institutional requirements without genuine intrinsic motivation. Key themes identified include engagement as compliance, motivational stagnation due to cognitive overload, and identity ambivalence where GenAI acts as both an enabler and an eroder of learner identity. The study cautions against equating visible engagement with meaningful learning in AI-mediated contexts and provides implications for pedagogy, AI system design, and teacher education.

title: From Experience to Adoption: Modelling EFL Learners' GenAI Continuance Through Linear and Configurational Approaches
authors: Liwei Hsu
summary: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly penetrates language education, understanding learners' continued intention to use this technology becomes crucial. This study examines EFL learners' continuance intention to use GenAI for language learning through PLS-SEM and fsQCA methodologies. Participants were undergraduate EFL learners (N = 383) from three universities in Taiwan, aged 18–24, with varying English proficiency levels (TOEIC 450–860 or CEFR A2-B2). Data were collected through an online survey comprising validated scales measuring technology acceptance constructs and personality traits using 5-point Likert scales. Analysis employed both partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results showed that three key dimensions – dependability, attractiveness and novelty – shape users' overall experience with GenAI, where dependability and attractiveness specifically align with users' initial expectations. Both expectancy confirmation and social influence predict learners' continuance intention. Openness to experience moderates these relationships positively for expectancy confirmation but negatively for social influence, indicating that individuals with high openness prioritise personal evaluation over social cues. As the first study to combine PLS-SEM with fsQCA in GenAI use research, it reveals complementary insights: while PLS-SEM identifies key predictors of continued use, fsQCA uncovers multiple pathways to adoption, with dependability and social influence as core conditions across configurations. This dual-method approach advances theoretical understanding of technology adoption by demonstrating how linear relationships coexist with complex configurational patterns. The findings provide practical implications for educational technology design, emphasising the need to balance system reliability and aesthetic appeal while accounting for individual differences in user personality traits.

authors: Yang Gao, Qikai Wang, Xiaochen Wang, Quan Quan
summary: This study investigates the beliefs of 298 Chinese EFL university teachers regarding the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) in language education, using the Expectancy-Value-Cost (EVC) theory. Through a quantitative survey and Latent Profile Analysis (LPA), the research identified three distinct teacher profiles: Low EVC, Medium EVC, and High EVC. The findings indicate that while teachers generally hold positive views on the value and potential of LLMs, they also recognize the associated costs and challenges. Significant differences in beliefs were found based on contextual factors such as school type, prior LLM experience, class size, teaching mode, and IT infrastructure. The study concludes with practical implications, emphasizing the need for institutional support, improved infrastructure, and targeted professional development to facilitate successful LLM integration.

authors: Ya Xiao, Danling Li & Kai Guo
summary: This study introduces a novel method using generative AI-powered non-player characters (NPCs) to enhance English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing in a digital storyline-based learning environment. Traditional storyline approaches are limited by static, pre-scripted NPCs, which restricts interactivity and personalization. The researchers developed an innovation in three stages: storyline design, AI-powered NPC development, and implementation in an EFL writing workshop. A pilot study was conducted with four undergraduate students, collecting data through questionnaires, chat histories, essays, and interviews. The findings indicate that AI-powered NPCs significantly increased students' situational interest and intrinsic motivation without adding to their cognitive load. This dynamic approach fostered engaging interactions beneficial for writing performance. The study is presented as the first to implement AI-powered NPCs in a game-based learning context for EFL writing, offering practical and theoretical insights for language education.

authors: Seongyong Lee, Jaeho Jeon, Jim McKinley, Heath Rose
summary: This study examines the use of ChatGPT in English Language Teaching (ELT) from a Global Englishes (GE) perspective, addressing the tool's pedagogical limitations in multilingual contexts where it often defaults to standard English. Using a Design and Development Research approach, the authors tested three models with varying levels of prompt engineering: a Basic model (single-step prompts), Refined Model 1 (multi-step prompting), and Refined Model 2 (using GE-oriented corpora and advanced prompt engineering). Thematic analysis revealed that Refined Model 2 showed significant improvements, offering affordances for GE-informed evaluation and communication. However, limitations such as defaulting to native-speaker norms and a lack of tailored feedback persisted. The findings emphasize the importance of using authentic data to improve the contextual relevance of GenAI outputs and highlight the pedagogical value of GenAI-teacher collaboration and teacher agency.

title: AI chatbot-assisted vocabulary learning: Relationships with self-regulation, motivation, and performance among Chinese private college students
authors: Chun Hao, Wei Xu, Huzaina Binti Abdul Halim, Mengyao Hao
summary: This study investigated the use of an LLM-driven AI chatbot, Doubao, for self-regulated vocabulary learning among Chinese private college students. An 8-week experiment compared an AI chatbot-assisted group with a control group using conventional methods. The results showed that the AI chatbot significantly improved vocabulary performance. summary: This study investigates how teacher presence affects student engagement with a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbot in a language learning environment designed with the First Principles of Instruction (FPI). Using a sequential explanatory mixed-method design, the study involved 60 university students in two groups: one with teacher presence (TP) and one with teacher absence (TA). Key findings indicate that students in the TP group reported significantly higher emotional and agentic engagement than the TA group. However, levels of behavioral and cognitive engagement were similar between the two groups. The study also identified six key features or roles of teacher presence in a GenAI-supported language learning context.

title: How to Design and Deliver Courses for Higher Education in the AI Era?
authors: Ahmad Samer Wazan, Imran Taj, Abdulhadi Shoufan, Romain Laborde, Remi Venant
summary: Technological breakthroughs in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) are challenging education. We argue that higher education will only cope with the era of AI when we reduce the reliance on textbooks and memorization, and take deliberate steps to integrate AI into the design and delivery of courses and exams. This chapter presents strategies based on the Delors report, demonstrating their application in cybersecurity, programming, English language teaching, and art. For course delivery, a dedicated Socratic chatbot, the AI Socrates Chatbot, was built and employed to offer personalized learning experiences. To evaluate the instructional design, data from seven exams where students were allowed to use ChatGPT was analyzed. The findings indicate that students' performance was not correlated with the level and way they used ChatGPT to answer exam questions designed around AI's limitations.

title: How good are LLMs in generating input texts for reading tasks in German as a foreign language?
authors: Anastasia Drackert, Andrea Horbach, Anja Peters
summary: This study investigates the potential of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT (versions 3.5 and 4), for creating high-quality input texts for German reading comprehension tasks at the B2/C1 CEFR levels. It compares AI-generated texts with benchmark texts from a high-stakes German exam (TestDaF) through computational linguistic analysis and evaluation by assessment experts. The findings indicate that while AI-generated texts are a valuable starting point, they require significant adjustments to match the quality of human-authored materials. Key differences were found in linguistic features; AI texts showed higher frequencies of nominalizations, greater lexical density, and more technical vocabulary, but lacked idiomatic expressions, illustrative examples, and passive constructions common in benchmark texts. The study concludes that expert refinement is essential for using AI-generated texts in language assessment.
APA_reference: Drackert, A., Horbach, A., & Peters, A. (2025). How good are LLMs in generating input texts for reading tasks in German as a foreign language?. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, 45, 222–252. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190525000066

title: Modeling generative AI acceptance, perceived teachers' enthusiasm, and self-efficacy to English as foreign language learners' well-being in the digital era
authors: Fangwei Huang, Yongliang Wang, Haijing Zhang
summary: This study investigates the effects of generative AI acceptance, perceived teachers' enthusiasm, and self-efficacy on the well-being of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. Based on a survey of 613 Chinese university students, the research employed structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships between these factors. The findings indicate that generative AI acceptance positively predicts both learners' well-being and their self-efficacy. Perceived teachers' enthusiasm was found to positively predict learners' self-efficacy but not their well-being directly. Furthermore, self-efficacy for receptive skills was identified as a mediator in the relationship between both AI acceptance and teacher enthusiasm and learners' well-being. Conversely, self-efficacy for productive skills did not play a mediating role. The study highlights the importance of both technological and human factors in AI-assisted language learning environments.
APA_reference: Huang, F., Wang, Y., & Zhang, H. (2024). Modelling generative AI acceptance, perceived teachers' enthusiasm and self-efficacy to English as a foreign language learners' well-being in the digital era. European Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/ejed.12770

RQ2: How does perceived teachers' enthusiasm affect EFL learners' well-being?
RQ3: What influence does self-efficacy have on EFL learners' well-being?

emergent_themes: The mediating role of self-efficacy: Self-efficacy for receptive skills acts as a crucial bridge connecting AI acceptance and teacher enthusiasm to student well-being.

Differential impact of self-efficacy types: The study distinguishes between the psychological impact of self-efficacy for receptive skills (which enhances well-being) and productive skills (which does not), revealing a nuanced relationship between confidence and well-being.

The evolving role of the teacher in the AI era: In AI-enhanced settings, the teacher's influence shifts from being a direct source of emotional support affecting well-being to a facilitator of student self-efficacy.

title: Measuring EFL learners' use of ChatGPT in informal digital learning of English based on the technology acceptance model
authors: Guangxiang Leon Liu, Chaojun Ma
summary: This quantitative, cross-sectional study investigates the acceptance and use of ChatGPT for informal English learning among 405 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners from Chinese backgrounds. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study used a questionnaire to measure Perceived Ease of Use (PEU), Perceived Usefulness (PU), Attitude (AT), Behavioral Intention (BI), and Actual Use (AU). Structural equation modeling revealed that PEU does not directly predict AT but does so indirectly through the full mediation of PU. Furthermore, AT positively predicts BI, which in turn is a strong predictor of AU. The findings validate a modified TAM for this context, highlighting that learners' positive attitudes and intentions, driven by the perceived usefulness of ChatGPT, lead to its actual use in self-directed language learning activities.
