title: Img2Vocab: Explore Words Tied to Your Life With LLMs and Social Media Images
authors: Kanta Yamaoka, Ko Watanabe, Koichi Kise, Andreas Dengel, Shoya Ishimaru
summary: This study introduces and evaluates Img2Vocab, a system designed for personalized vocabulary acquisition. The system uses learners' personal photos from Instagram, processes them with image recognition to extract keywords, and then uses a large language model (GPT-3) to generate contextual sentences containing new, relevant vocabulary. The goal is to connect new words with learners' prior experiences, which psychological studies suggest enhances learning. A within-subject experiment with 23 participants compared three conditions: learning with personalized images and generated text (C1), learning with generic images and text (C2), and learning with text only (C3). Findings show that while image-based contexts (C1 and C2) helped learners identify more difficult vocabulary (lower Zipf frequency) compared to the text-only context, the recall accuracy for words learned in the personalized context (C1) was slightly lower, though not statistically significant, suggesting these words were more challenging. Qualitatively, participants reported high engagement and found the personalized approach most helpful and enjoyable. The paper also discusses the system's privacy-centric design, ethical considerations of using personal data, and future directions for using advanced AI models for personalized language education.
APA_reference: Yamaoka, K., Watanabe, K., Kise, K., Dengel, A., & Ishimaru, S. (2025). Img2Vocab: Explore words tied to your life with LLMs and social media images. IEEE Access, 13, 20456-20471. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3533076

title: Implementation of AI-driven technology into education – a pilot study on the use of chatbots in foreign language learning
authors: Petra Polakova, Blanka Klimova
summary: This pilot study investigates the impact of a conversational chatbot on foreign language learning and learners' perceptions of its use. The study involved 58 university students in the Czech Republic, with B2 and C1 English proficiency levels, who participated in a one-month experiment. Using a mixed-methods approach combining pre/post-tests and a questionnaire, the research found that the use of the AI-driven chatbot led to a significant improvement in students' language skills. The questionnaire survey also revealed positive perceptions regarding the chatbot as a complementary learning tool, highlighting its potential to enhance language skills and its perceived usefulness in second language acquisition at the university level.

title: AcademiCraft: Transforming Writing Assistance for English for Academic Purposes with Multi-Agent System Innovations
authors: Zhendong Du and Kenji Hashimoto
summary: This study introduces AcademiCraft, a novel writing assistance tool for English for Academic Purposes (EAP) built on a multi-agent system (MAS) and large-language models (LLMs). Unlike commercial tools that often provide corrections without explanations, AcademiCraft corrects and refines academic texts while offering detailed explanations for its revisions to deepen user understanding. The tool features an open and replicable framework. Through rigorous benchmarks against leading commercial tools, AcademiCraft demonstrated superior performance in handling complex syntax, improving coherence, and providing accurate word choices, particularly for both native (L1) and non-native (L2) writers. The paper details the system's architecture, methodologies, and presents a comparative performance analysis.
APA_reference: Du, Z., & Hashimoto, K. (2025). AcademiCraft: Transforming Writing Assistance for English for Academic Purposes with Multi-Agent System Innovations. Information, 16(4), 254. https://doi.org/10.3390/info16040254

title: BPMN-Based Design of Multi-Agent Systems: Personalized Language Learning Workflow Automation with RAG-Enhanced Knowledge Access
authors: Hedi Tebourbi, Sana Nouzri, Yazan Mualla, Meryem El Fatimi, Amro Najjar, Abdeljalil Abbas-Turki, Mahjoub Dridi
summary: The intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and education is revolutionizing learning and teaching in this digital era, with Generative AI and large language models (LLMs) providing even greater possibilities for the future. The digital transformation of language education demands innovative approaches that combine pedagogical rigor with explainable AI (XAI) principles, particularly for low-resource languages. This paper presents a novel methodology that integrates Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) to create transparent, workflow-driven language tutors. Our approach uniquely embeds XAI through three mechanisms: (1) BPMN’s visual formalism that makes agent decision-making auditable, (2) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with verifiable knowledge provenance from textbooks of the National Institute of Languages of Luxembourg, and (3) human-in-the-loop validation of both content and pedagogical sequencing. To ensure realism in learner interaction, we integrate speech-to-text and text-to-speech technologies, creating an immersive, human-like learning environment. The system simulates intelligent tutoring through agents’ collaboration and dynamic adaptation to learner progress. We demonstrate this framework through a Luxembourgish language learning platform where specialized agents (Conversational, Reading, Listening, QA, and Grammar) operate within BPMN-modeled workflows. The system achieves high response faithfulness (0.82) and relevance (0.85) according to RAGA metrics, while speech integration using Whisper STT and Coqui TTS enables immersive practice. Evaluation with learners showed 85.8% satisfaction with contextual responses and 71.4% engagement rates, confirming the effectiveness of our process-driven approach. This work advances AI-powered language education by showing how formal process modeling can create pedagogically coherent and explainable tutoring systems. The architecture’s modularity supports extension to other low-resource languages while maintaining the transparency critical for educational trust. Future work will expand curriculum coverage and develop teacher-facing dashboards to further improve explainability.

title: Instructors' and learners' perspectives on using ChatGPT in English as a foreign language courses and its effect on academic integrity
authors: Manar Almanea
summary: This mixed-methods study investigated the perspectives of 24 university instructors and 135 learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in Saudi Arabia on the use of ChatGPT for learning and its implications for academic integrity. Over one trimester, instructors integrated ChatGPT into their teaching. Data was collected via questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. Findings indicate that both groups held positive attitudes towards ChatGPT, particularly for improving writing skills. However, significant concerns about academic integrity were raised, with learners admitting they might conceal their use of ChatGPT and use it to complete homework. The study identifies ChatGPT features that could facilitate misuse, such as generating unique responses and adhering to word counts. It concludes by discussing practical implications and strategies for mitigating AI-facilitated plagiarism, emphasizing the need for updated policies and pedagogical approaches.

summary: This phenomenographic study examined the perceptions of 30 research-active English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers from Iran regarding the potential benefits and drawbacks of using ChatGPT in second language (L2) learning, teaching, assessment, and research. title: Comparing Peer Feedback and Generative Artificial Intelligence Feedback in Japanese English as a Foreign Language Speaking Context: Impacts on Motivation, Engagement, and Writing Self-Efficacy
authors: Jerry Huang, Atsushi Mizumoto, Yung Lin Huang
summary: This study compares the effectiveness of peer feedback versus generative AI (GenAI) feedback, specifically from ChatGPT, on Japanese university students learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL). It examines the impact on their motivation, engagement, and writing self-efficacy for script-writing in preparation for speaking tasks. Over an academic year, 147 students first used peer feedback and then transitioned to GenAI feedback. Using surveys at three intervals, the study found that GenAI feedback significantly increased students' 'ideal L2 self' (a component of motivation). While writing self-efficacy improved with peer feedback, it remained high but did not increase further with GenAI. Students also reported significantly higher affective and behavioral engagement with GenAI feedback compared to peer feedback, though cognitive engagement levels were similar. Qualitative data revealed students appreciated GenAI for its immediate feedback and suggestions but were concerned about over-reliance and the lack of human interaction. The study concludes that GenAI can be a valuable complementary tool in EFL instruction, enhancing motivation and engagement, but requires careful implementation, including well-designed prompts and instructor guidance.

title: The Predictive Effects of Sociobiographical Variables, English Learning Confidence, and Digital Competence on AI-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English (AI-IDLE)
authors: Guangxiang Leon Liu, Xian Zhao
summary: This study investigates the factors that predict Chinese university students' engagement in AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE). Using survey data from 1,012 English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) learners and employing hierarchical regression analysis, the research examines the predictive power of sociobiographical variables, English learning confidence, and digital competence. Digital competence and the number of digital devices owned are also strong predictors, though their effect sizes vary. Ethnicity was found to be a statistically significant but practically limited predictor. summary: This study investigated the development of 11 Iranian EFL teachers' cognitions regarding the use of ChatGPT for L2 writing instruction and feedback during a professional development (PD) program. authors: Jiang Renfeng, Yang Gang, Shen Qi
summary: This study investigates the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) tools on the autonomous motivation of Chinese university students learning English, framed by Self-Determination Theory (SDT). summary: This study investigated the effects of integrating ChatGPT into genre-based instruction (GBI) on the argumentative writing performance, willingness to write (WtW), and perceptions of first-year EFL English majors in Taiwan. title: Engaging Multimodal Literacy Through Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Case Study From an English as Second Language Writing Classroom
authors: Xiao Tan, Ruonan Zhao
summary: This study, grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics, investigates how two English as a Second Language (ESL) students utilize Generative AI (GenAI) in a multimodal writing assignment. It explores which semiotic metafunctions (ideational, interpersonal, textual) the students focused on when creating AI-generated images for a photo essay and how they perceived their own development in multimodal literacy. The findings indicate that the two students had different understandings of the role of images in storytelling. One student (Keshav) primarily focused on ideational meanings (representing events and characters), while the other (Yang) attended to both ideational and interpersonal meanings (engaging the audience). However, textual meanings (composition and layout) were largely overlooked by both. The study provides empirical evidence on GenAI use by ESL students and offers insights for designing multimodal tasks.
APA_reference: Tan, X., & Zhao, R. (2025). Engaging multimodal literacy through generative artificial intelligence: A case study from an English as second language writing classroom. International Journal of Applied Linguistics, 0, 1-15. https://doi.org/10.1111/ijal.12852

title: What Drives University Students to Use ChatGPT for Translation? Disciplinary and Experiential Influences
authors: Lulu Wang, Simin Xu, Kanglong Liu
summary: This study investigates the factors influencing university students in Hong Kong to adopt ChatGPT for translation tasks, guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Based on survey responses from 308 translation and non-translation majors, the research uses structural equation modeling to analyze the data. The findings indicate that performance expectancy is the primary driver for adoption, followed by facilitating conditions. Effort expectancy and social influence were not significant overall. The study also reveals that prior experience and academic discipline are key moderating factors. Novice users are influenced by both performance and social factors, while experienced users prioritize performance alone. Translation students focus mainly on performance benefits, whereas non-translation students are also influenced by the availability of institutional support. The study concludes that educational strategies for AI integration must be tailored to different student groups and highlights the need for institutions to provide secure AI tools and for developers to consider user-centered design.

title: Learners’ Acceptance and Use of Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Generated Content in AI-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English
authors: Chenghao Wang, Yiran Du, Bin Zou
summary: This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigates the acceptance and use of multimodal AI-generated content (AIGC) among Chinese EFL learners in AI-mediated informal digital English learning (AI-IDLE). Using the Integrated Model of Technology Acceptance (IMTA), the study analyzed survey data from 706 learners and interview data from 20 learners. Quantitative findings show that perceived enjoyment significantly influences behavioral intention, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use. Perceived usefulness and ease of use jointly mediate the relationship between enjoyment and behavioral intention. Qualitative analysis reveals that learners creatively use and transform multimodal AIGC to enhance understanding, retention, and engagement. Despite challenges like cultural mismatches, cognitive load, and technical issues, these positive experiences motivate continued use. The study highlights the importance of both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in AIGC adoption and provides insights for innovative practices in AI-IDLE.

title: Beyond Linguistic Proficiency: Emotional, Cognitive, and Cultural Pathways of Generative AI in EFL Well-Being—A Technology-Humanities-Culture Synthesis
authors: Yanyu Yang, Suhua Yao
summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the dual impact of generative AI (GenAI) on the holistic well-being of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in a non-Western context. Employing a 'technology-humanities-culture' approach that synthesizes Seligman's PERMA model, Oxford's EMPATHICS framework, and critical cultural theory, the research analyzes data from interviews, diaries, observations, and AI system logs from Chinese non-English majors. The study identifies three key pathways through which GenAI mediates well-being: emotional scaffolding (anxiety alleviation vs. alienation), cognitive optimization (self-efficacy vs. homogenization), and cultural immersion (engagement vs. simplification). Based on these findings, the paper proposes the 'GenAI-EFL Well-being Model' to advocate for ethical AI integration in language education, emphasizing a shift from instrumental efficiency to holistic learner flourishing through adaptive algorithms, localized cultural content, and hybrid teaching methods.

title: Integrating AI-powered tools in EFL pronunciation instruction: effects on accuracy and L2 motivation
authors: Safaa M. Abdelhalim, Raniya Abdullah Alsehibany
summary: This study investigates the effects of integrating AI-powered tools, specifically ChatGPT and the ASR-based system SpeechAce, into structured EFL pronunciation instruction. Using a sequential mixed-methods design with 71 undergraduate female EFL learners in Saudi Arabia, the research examined impacts on pronunciation accuracy (segmental and suprasegmental features) and L2 motivation. Quantitative results indicated significant improvements in segmental pronunciation (phoneme accuracy at word and sentence levels) and motivation (Current L2 Self and Learning Effort). However, gains in suprasegmental features like word stress were limited. Qualitative findings from student interviews supported these results, highlighting positive perceptions of the AI tools for providing real-time feedback, enabling personalized practice, and increasing engagement. The study concludes that AI tools are pedagogically viable for enhancing pronunciation instruction in formal EFL settings, particularly when integrated into a hybrid model with teacher guidance.

summary: This study investigated the efficacy of using Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL) strategies in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing. The researchers developed an LLM-supported Cognitive Academic Language Learning Model (CALLA-LLM) and tested it against a traditional CALLA model in a randomized controlled trial involving 65 elementary school students over five weeks. title: Integrating large language models with corpus-based language pedagogy: an approach to collocation use in L2 writing instruction
authors: Chuang-Qi Chen, Zhenlei Huang, Xindong Ye, Hui Jin
summary: This study investigated the effectiveness of combining large language models (LLMs) with corpus-based pedagogy (CBLP) for teaching lexical collocations in English writing. The researchers developed and implemented a Corpus-Based Language Pedagogy with Large Language Models (CBLP-LLM) framework. In a five-week experiment, 70 sophomore students were divided into an experimental group using CBLP-LLM and a control group using traditional CBLP. Data collected before, immediately after, and one month after the intervention showed that the CBLP-LLM group had significant improvements in writing performance, lexical quality, and motivational beliefs, alongside a reduction in cognitive load. title: Interacting with ChatGPT in essay writing: A study of L2 learners' task motivation
authors: Javad Zare, Ahmad Al-Issa, Fatemeh Ranjbaran Madiseh
summary: This study investigated the impact of ChatGPT 4.0 on the motivation of L2 learners to write English argumentative essays. Conducted at a public university in a non-English-speaking country, the research employed an experimental, mixed-methods design. The findings indicated that interacting with ChatGPT 4.0 had a significant positive and lasting effect on learners' motivation. However, a notable decline in motivation during the delayed post-intervention phase suggests a need to balance the use of AI as a support tool with the development of independent writing skills. The study identified several factors contributing to the initial increase in motivation: learners' perceived improvement in their essay writing abilities, the supportive learning environment fostered by ChatGPT acting as a tutor, positive interactions with the tool, and enhanced meta-cognitive awareness of their specific writing challenges.

title: Investigating students' uptake of teacher- and ChatGPT-generated feedback in EFL writing: a comparison study
authors: Shaoyan Zou, Kai Guo, Jun Wang & Yu Liu
summary: This study investigates and compares the uptake of feedback from teachers and ChatGPT among 20 Chinese undergraduate EFL students in the context of argumentative writing. Through analysis of essay revisions and a questionnaire survey, the research assesses students' engagement with, and the accuracy of their revisions based on, the two feedback sources, while also exploring their perceptions and preferences. Findings indicate that students demonstrated higher engagement and achieved greater accuracy with teacher feedback, particularly for content and language issues. However, ChatGPT's feedback on organization was more successfully integrated by students. Despite a general preference for teacher feedback, students recognized the unique strengths of ChatGPT, suggesting its potential as a complementary tool to create a more integrated and effective approach to EFL writing instruction.
APA_reference: Zou, S., Guo, K., Wang, J., & Liu, Y. (2025). Investigating students' uptake of teacher- and ChatGPT-generated feedback in EFL writing: a comparison study. Computer Assisted Language Learning. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1080/09588221.2024.2447279

study_limitations: Feedback was categorized as only actionable or unactionable, without considering the impact of feedback explicitness.

summary: This study examines the relationship between writing anxiety in English second language learners and their intention to use ChatGPT as an automated writing evaluation tool. title: Enhancing L2 Writing Skills: ChatGPT as an Automated Feedback Tool
authors: Gökçe Kurt, Yavuz Kurt
summary: This qualitative study explores the perceptions of Turkish pre-service English teachers on using AI-powered ChatGPT as an automated feedback tool for L2 academic writing. Through focus-group interviews, the study compared ChatGPT feedback with traditional peer and teacher feedback. The findings indicate that students perceive ChatGPT as a valuable tool with affordances like practicality, interactivity, and adaptability, providing high-quality, detailed feedback. However, they also noted constraints such as occasional inconsistencies, dependence on prompt quality, and the risk of overreliance. The study concludes that ChatGPT can be a valuable supplement to, but not a replacement for, human feedback, and recommends a complementary approach that integrates AI, peer, and teacher feedback, supported by appropriate training in AI literacy.

title: Exploring YouTube content creators' perspectives on generative AI in language learning: Insights through opinion mining and sentiment analysis
authors: Mazhar Bal, Ayşe Gül Kara Aydemir, Mustafa Coşkun
summary: This study analyzes the content, comments, and transcriptions of 66 YouTube videos published between December 2022 and October 2023 to understand the perspectives of content creators on using generative AI for language learning. Using opinion mining and sentiment analysis, the study found that most videos focused on speaking and writing skills, with less attention to listening and reading. The sentiment was predominantly optimistic and analytical, suggesting a positive view of generative AI as a tool for language learning. A clustering analysis identified four main themes: 'language development and practices,' 'basic expression skills,' 'intercultural communication skills,' and 'language structure and meaning.' The findings indicate that creators see generative AI as a promising tool for developing practical communication skills, and these insights can inform the creation of AI-supported language learning materials.

title: Exploring large language models for L2 metaphonological awareness tutoring
authors: Kacper Łodzikowski, Jarosław Weckwerth, and Kamil Malarski
summary: This observational study evaluates the feasibility of using a custom GPT-4-based AI Tutor for second language (L2) metaphonological awareness training. The tutor was piloted in an English phonetics and phonology course for first-year university students in Poland. Through two novel homework assignments, the study analyzed learner interaction logs, reflections, and survey data. Findings indicate that while most learners found the AI Tutor's personalized explanations helpful, the overall sentiment was mixed due to the model's tendency for confabulation (hallucination). Despite these challenges, the pilot showed the potential for LLMs to foster active, self-regulated learning. The study recommends designing improved LLM-based learning environments, promoting AI literacy, and conducting further experimental research on the long-term effects of AI tutors.
APA_reference: Łodzikowski, K., Weckwerth, J., & Malarski, K. (2025). Exploring large language models for L2 metaphonological awareness tutoring. Journal of Second Language Pronunciation, 11(1), 46-75. https://doi.org/10.1075/jslp.24030.lod

RQ3: How do learner interaction patterns and perceptions reflect the role of the AI Tutor in shaping the learning experience, particularly in promoting active and self-regulated learning?

prompts_used: Objective: You are an expert in educational technology research and qualitative data analysis. Perform a sentiment analysis on a dataset obtained from a pilot study. Study context: This research explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) for enhancing metaphonological awareness in second language (L2) learners. The study aimed to: 1) Assess LLMs' capabilities on course content (English phonetics and phonology); 2) Design and pilot 2 novel homework assignments that learners completed with an LLM-based tutoring system (AI Tutor); and 3) Collect learner feedback on the pilot. The pilot was embedded in the first couple of weeks of a 9-month English Phonetics and Phonology course at a Polish university, engaging first-year students through both in-person and online modalities. The course emphasised practical activities and independent study, supported by a mix of traditional and AI-enhanced tools. Participants, primarily B1+ level English learners without much prior experience with LLM-based tools, interacted with the AI Tutor built on GPT-4. Two distinct homework assignments were designed to exploit the AI's capabilities and limitations. The first homework activity focused on leveraging the AI Tutor's capacity for personalised one-to-one tutoring. First, the learners read a coursebook chapter and answered questions, ranging from articulatory description of English consonants to more conceptual topics, such as differences between phonemes and allophones. Then, they asked the same questions of the Tutor, compared its answers with their own, and engaged in a dialogue to clarify any misconceptions. Finally, they answered three questions to reflect on the Tutor's helpfulness. The second homework activity was consciously designed to elicit situations in which students critically evaluate the AI Tutor's output to notice that it is helpful but not infallible. The teacher provided each learner with an incorrect allophonic transcription of a word. The learners needed to discuss with the AI Tutor which elements of the transcriptions were correct and which were not. Second, the learners were asked to work with the AI to produce allophonic transcription of three other words (each learner received a different set). Task: You are now analysing the learner's reflections on the [first/second] homework activity (one learner per row). Provide a tab-delimited output that contains four columns: learner_id: As per the original data. sentiment_classification: Classify the overall sentiment of reflections as Positive, Negative, or Neutral. sentiment_rating: Reflect the intensity of sentiment by assigning a numerical rating on a scale from 1 (very negative) to 10 (very positive), with 5 indicating neutral sentiment. sentiment_ analysis: Within a limit of 300 characters, identify key aspects influencing the overall sentiment. Analyse these in the context of L2 learning, phonetics and phonology, and AI-assisted education, emphasising their impact on sentiment. Be precise and informative, yet use simple words. After providing the output, stop. Don't add any comments. Data: [...]
learning_perceptions: Perceived utility: Students had mixed perceptions, with some finding the tool useful only with prior knowledge, while a majority (81%) viewed it as a supplement rather than a replacement for the coursebook.

Perceived accuracy: Students' perception of accuracy was varied and task-dependent, with all learners reporting at least one incorrect response and some describing the AI's contradictory answers as 'bipolar'.

Trust: The non-judgmental nature of the AI was appreciated and created a safe environment for asking questions, suggesting a degree of trust in the interaction style, though not always in the content accuracy.
Self-reported performance: Learners self-reported gains in understanding of all five course topics covered during the pilot, particularly phonemes and allophones.

benefits_affordances: Provided personalized explanations and analogies that aided conceptual understanding.
Engaged learners in active and self-regulated learning by facilitating constructive and interactive learning activities.
Created a safe, non-judgmental environment for asking questions and collaboration, which can be beneficial for anxious students.
Served as a useful supplement to traditional course materials, bridging the gap between static coursebook information and personalized help.
drawbacks: The AI Tutor had a propensity for confabulation, providing incorrect or inconsistent answers, particularly for tasks requiring logic or advanced domain knowledge.
Inaccuracies and complex explanations from the AI created challenges for learners and potentially increased their extraneous cognitive load.
The AI's performance was particularly weak in tasks involving phonetic transcription.
The AI's tendency to change its stance on rules was perceived as 'bipolar' by a student, indicating a lack of reliability.
study_limitations: The generalisability is limited due to the observational nature of the study and the small convenience sample.
The positive perceptions of the AI Tutor may have been influenced by the novelty effect of the technology.
The study relied on student self-reports for learning gains rather than pre- and post-intervention assessments of metaphonological awareness.

students: Gained access to a 24/7 personalized learning tool that fostered active and self-regulated learning.
Experienced both the benefits of personalized analogies and the confusion from AI inaccuracies, highlighting the need for critical engagement.
Benefited from a non-judgmental learning environment for asking questions.
teachers: The study provides a model for designing novel homework assignments that leverage both the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs to promote critical thinking.
Highlights the need for teachers to actively promote AI literacy and guide students in using these tools effectively and critically.
institutions: Demonstrates the technical and pedagogical feasibility of integrating custom LLM-based tutors into university-level courses.
Underscores broader systemic challenges for technology integration, such as the need for sufficient instructor training and ensuring equitable access.

policy_guidance: Teachers should be encouraged to experiment with building their own AI tutors using commercially available platforms and simple prompt engineering.
Learners must be trained to engage with LLMs as tools for critical analysis, rather than as infallible sources of information.
Educators should create prompts and activities grounded in domain-specific pedagogical best practices.
Researchers should experimentally measure the efficacy of LLM-based interventions, focusing on variables like explanation style and response length on student engagement and outcomes.
emergent_themes: Tension between learner preference for concise, authoritative coursebook answers and the dynamic, detailed, and sometimes convoluted interactions with the AI.
The AI tutor's role as a 'third participant' in the learning ecosystem, alongside the teacher and peers.
The pedagogical strategy of intentionally designing activities that leverage an LLM's known limitations (e.g., transcription errors) to foster critical evaluation skills in students.
emergent_issues: A fundamental limitation of LLMs, being textually grounded, may be their inability to accurately model physical phenomena like phonetic processes, a problem that better datasets may not solve.
Inaccurate AI responses can increase learners' extraneous cognitive load, as they must expend additional effort to verify and correct the information provided.

title: L2 students' barriers in engaging with form and content-focused AI-generated feedback in revising their compositions
authors: Chen Ziqi, Zhu Xinhua, Lu Qi, Wei Wei
summary: This study investigates the revision strategies and barriers L2 writers face when using ChatGPT for corrective feedback on argumentative essays. Forty-five undergraduate computer science students were tasked with seeking feedback from ChatGPT and revising their work. The findings, analyzed through the lens of the Technology Acceptance Model, revealed that students rejected or ignored approximately 38% of the AI-generated feedback, with a significantly higher rejection rate for content-level suggestions (e.g., evidence) compared to form-level corrections (e.g., grammar). The barriers were categorized into two main themes: 'inconvenience to use' (feedback overload, general descriptions instead of specific error highlighting, repetitive comments) and 'unusefulness' (misinterpretation of the author's intent, lack of clarity and examples, extraneous feedback). The study suggests pedagogical strategies to mitigate these barriers and enhance students' feedback literacy in AI-assisted learning environments.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Feedback for Second Language Intelligibility: An Exploratory Intervention Study on Effects and Perceptions
authors: Kevin Hirschi, Okim Kang, Mu Yang, John H. L. Hansen, Kyle Beloin
summary: This study investigated the effects and perceptions of AI-generated feedback on second language (L2) English intelligibility. Ninety L2 learners were divided into three groups: one receiving visual and narrative (ChatGPT-like) feedback, one receiving visual-only feedback, and a control group with no feedback. The intervention was an online, self-paced course focusing on segmental and suprasegmental features. Pre- and post-intervention speaking tasks were evaluated by raters. Results showed that while visual feedback alone improved prominence production, only the group receiving both visual and narrative feedback significantly improved in prosodic features (prominence and thought groups) and overall intelligibility. However, this same group reported the lowest perceptions of the feedback's helpfulness, particularly for segmental accuracy. The study suggests that AI-generated narrative feedback can be effective for improving L2 pronunciation but highlights a disconnect between learning gains and learner perceptions, indicating a need for refinement in AI feedback systems.
APA_reference: Hirschi, K., Kang, O., Yang, M., Hansen, J. H. L., & Beloin, K. (2025). Artificial intelligence-generated feedback for second language intelligibility: An exploratory intervention study on effects and perceptions. Language Learning, 75(S1), 204–241. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12719
research_h_q: RQ 1: To what extent does visual and visual+narrative AI-based feedback on English intelligibility impact learner production of specific pronunciation features (pauses in thought groups, prominence, and segmental accuracy)?

RQ 3: How do learners perceive the usefulness of such feedback?

prompts_used: Please analyze my speech recording for issues that might interfere with intelligibility. The first section should be “Prominence Analysis" and discuss which words were prominent as compared to which words should be prominent. The second section should be "Speech Rate" and discuss any function words that were longer than appropriate or content words that were too quick. The third section should be "Thought Groups" and discuss if pauses marked were in appropriate parts of the phrase. The fourth section should be “Phonemic Analysis" and mention only the most severe phonemic errors in content words. Please keep your responses for each section to 150 words or less and use bullet points.
duration: The intervention consisted of four 15-minute lessons and four practice sessions, with an average of 4.3 days between pretest and posttest.
learning_perceptions: Usefulness of feedback: Learners rated the helpfulness of the feedback on a 5-star scale. The group that received narrative feedback and showed the most improvement consistently gave lower usefulness ratings, suggesting a misalignment between perceived helpfulness and actual learning gains.

benefits_affordances: The combination of visual and narrative AI feedback significantly improved learners' production of prominence and thought groups, as well as their overall intelligibility.
Visual-only feedback was effective for improving prominence production in scripted tasks.
The study provides evidence that AI-based feedback can be a useful tool for L2 pronunciation improvement, particularly for suprasegmental features.
drawbacks: Learners who received the most effective feedback (visual+narrative) perceived it as less helpful than the other groups.

There was no measurable improvement in segmental accuracy for any group, and the narrative feedback for the segmental lesson received the lowest helpfulness rating, suggesting issues with its perceived accuracy or utility.
study_limitations: The intervention duration was short, which may have limited the training effects, especially for segmental production.
The study did not include a delayed posttest to assess the long-term durability of the improvements.
The study did not investigate how learner characteristics like L1 background and proficiency level interact with the effectiveness of AI feedback.
The statistical models may have been underpowered to detect between-group differences due to the complex factorial design and uneven rater assignment.

students: The study supports the use of AI tools for pronunciation training to improve intelligibility, but highlights that sustained engagement is likely necessary for success.
teachers: AI-generated feedback can serve as a supplemental tool for pronunciation instruction in large classes or for self-paced practice where teacher feedback is limited.
Teachers should guide learners on how to use AI tools, balancing them with human feedback and cautioning against overreliance.
institutions: N/A
other: For researchers, the findings confirm that AI-generated feedback can be effective but requires further refinement. It highlights the need for more research into designing and fine-tuning AI systems specifically for L2 learners' needs.

policy_guidance: N/A
emergent_themes: Misalignment of learning gains and learner perceptions: The group that benefited most from the intervention perceived the feedback as the least helpful, raising questions about how to design feedback that is both effective and positively received by learners.

Primacy of suprasegmental features for intelligibility: The short-term intervention led to improvements in intelligibility primarily through gains in suprasegmental features (prominence, thought groups), while segmental accuracy remained unchanged.
emergent_issues: Pedagogical usability of technical representations: The use of a technical phonological alphabet (ARPAbet) in feedback, while accurate, may have confused learners unaccustomed to it, hindering uptake.

Technical robustness across contexts: The performance and accuracy of AI models for feedback can be inhibited by variations in users' L1 backgrounds, microphone quality, and background noise, posing a challenge for real-world application.

title: Exploring the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Facilitating Assessment of Writing Performance in Second Language Learning
authors: Zilu Jiang, Zexin Xu, Zilong Pan, Jingwen He, Kui Xie
summary: This study examined the robustness and efficiency of four large language models (LLMs), GPT-4, GPT-3.5, iFLYTEK and Baidu Cloud, in assessing the writing accuracy of the Chinese language. Writing samples were collected from students in an online high school Chinese language learning program in the US. The official APIs of the LLMs were utilized to conduct analyses at both the T-unit and sentence levels. Performance metrics were employed to evaluate the LLMs’ performance. The LLM results were compared to human rating results. Content analysis was conducted to categorize error types and highlight the discrepancies between human and LLM ratings. Additionally, the efficiency of each model was evaluated. The results indicate that GPT models and iFLYTEK achieved similar accuracy scores, with GPT-4 excelling in precision. These findings provide insights into the potential of LLMs in supporting the assessment of writing accuracy for language learners.

title: Large Language Model-Driven Dynamic Assessment of Grammatical Accuracy in English Language Learner Writing
authors: Timur Jaganov, John Blake, Julián Villegas, Nicholas Carr
summary: This study explores the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to scale up Dynamic Assessment (DA) for grammatical accuracy in English language learner writing. The researchers developed DynaWrite, a modular application that uses LLMs to provide dynamic, graduated feedback. title: Leveraging LLM-based chatbots for interactional grammar feedback in L2 writing: opportunities and challenges
authors: Dongkwang Shin, Jang Ho Lee
summary: This study explores an innovative use of LLM-based chatbots for providing interactional grammar feedback in L2 writing, guided by the principles of Dynamic Assessment within a Vygotskian framework. The research involved 89 second-year pre-service teachers in South Korea who participated in a workshop to build their own grammar feedback chatbots. They then used these chatbots to receive feedback on their English essays. The findings indicate that such chatbots have significant potential as a feedback tool, offering advantages like contextual interaction and progressive feedback explicitness. While the chatbot was seen as a valuable, complementary resource to human teachers, the study also highlights challenges, particularly the difficulty participants faced in prompt engineering. The authors conclude that while promising, effective use of such tools requires systematic training for users.
APA_reference: Shin, D., & Lee, J. H. (2025). Leveraging LLM-based chatbots for interactional grammar feedback in L2 writing: opportunities and challenges. Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching. https://doi.org/10.1080/17501229.2025.2549037
research_h_q: RQ1. What are pre-service teachers' experiences with building an LLM-based grammar feedback chatbot and evaluating the accuracy of its feedback?
RQ2. How do pre-service teachers compare LLM-based chatbots with human instructors regarding grammar feedback, and what are their preferences?

teachers: other (training participants on chatbot development)

prompts_used: Check grammatical errors and awkward phrasing as the user types, and provide step-by-step feedback based on the sample feedback file in the Knowledge section.
Number each sentence in the user's text and include the number and sentence together in your feedback.
Present erroneous sentences one at a time and give the user a chance to find and correct the errors.

If the user can't find the error, or if the user's correction is incorrect, tell the user explicitly what the error is in grammatical terms, and if the user's correction is still incorrect, present the corrected sentence.
When asking the user to identify and correct errors, and when explaining corrective feedback, please chat in Korean language, except when referring to target sentences in the input text.

Once again, if you give the user a sentence and ask him/her to correct the error and he/she doesn't know, don't mention the correct wording, just tell him/her that there is a mistake and to correct it. For example, if there is an error in the number of matches, don't mention the correct wording, but hint that there is an error in the number of matches and correct it. If the user doesn't revise the error correctly after a second chance, explain it in detail and point out the correct wording.

Give the user at least 2 chances to correct the error, with a few more hints if he/she fails. Even if you've provided corrective feedback after two unsuccessful attempts to correct the error, if additional errors remain or the user has questions, provide additional feedback and ask for feedback on whether the user wants to move on to the next error sentence after making sure you've explained enough.
After providing feedback on the first incorrect sentence, present the next incorrect sentence and follow the same procedure for providing feedback.

Overall, the error feedback phase consists of providing an opportunity for error recognition and correction, providing a brief description of what the error is in grammatical terms if error recognition or correction fails, providing an opportunity for correction (without mentioning the corrected expression), and then explicitly providing the corrected expression if correction still fails. If the user says he/she doesn't know, don't give him/her the answer right away, but give him/her another chance to correct grammatical errors as described above.
When the feedback and correction activity for the last erroneous sentence is complete, present the final corrected version of the text.
learning_perceptions: anxiety: Participants felt less anxious receiving feedback from a chatbot compared to a human teacher, as the chatbot shows no frustration or tiredness.
satisfaction: Participants were generally satisfied with the chatbot's feedback.
other (perceived difficulty): Over half of the participants found the process of building a grammar feedback chatbot to be difficult or very difficult, primarily due to drafting effective prompts.
other (perceived accuracy): More than half of the participants rated the chatbot's feedback as accurate or very accurate.

other (preference): A slightly higher proportion of participants preferred human teachers (52.8%) over chatbots (40%) for grammar feedback, valuing the subtlety, reliability, and personalization from humans.

drawbacks: Building a well-functioning chatbot is challenging for users, especially drafting effective prompts.
Chatbots may provide inconsistent or inaccurate feedback, making them less reliable than human teachers.
Chatbots lack the ability to explain subtle grammatical nuances that human teachers can.

title: Exploring ChatGPT literacy as predictor and moderator in enhancing informal digital learning of English (IDLE): a partial least square analysis
authors: Xiaomeng Li, Lei Mee Thien
summary: This study investigates the role of ChatGPT literacy within the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework for Chinese learners of English as a foreign language (EFL) in informal digital learning contexts. summary: This study explores the affordances and challenges of integrating the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tool ERNIE Bot into the L2 writing feedback process, using a usefulness theoretical framework. title: MODALITY OR AUTHENTICITY? The Role of Authentic versus Al-Generated Texts in Language Learner Engagement
authors: Michele Back, Kyra Kabulis
summary: This mixed-methods action research study investigates the impact of AI-generated texts versus authentic texts on student engagement in two intermediate L2 French secondary classrooms in the United States. The study compared student engagement across four tasks: reading an authentic text, reading an AI-generated text, watching an authentic video, and watching an AI-generated video with text-to-speech audio. Data was collected through classroom observations and informal student discussions. Findings indicate that text modality (audiovisual vs. written) was a more significant factor for engagement than text authenticity (human vs. AI-generated). While students found audiovisual materials more engaging overall, they could distinguish AI-generated content by its repetitive and clichéd nature. The study concludes that while authentic texts remain valuable, AI-generated materials, particularly when presented in engaging modalities, can serve as effective and practical tools for language teachers.

title: Pre-service Language Teachers’ Task-specific Large Language Model Prompting Practices
authors: Benjamin Luke Moorhouse, Tsz Ying Ho, Chenze Wu, Yuwei Wan
summary: Since the emergence of ChatGPT, a type of large language model (LLM), there has been interest in how these tools can support language teachers’ professional practices and assist them with professional tasks, e.g., lesson planning. The current study explored how pre-service language teachers interacted with LLMs to assist them in improving lesson plans, and the knowledge and skills involved in these task-specific prompting practices. Data was collected from 25 pre-service teachers enrolled in a Master of Education in English Language Teaching program at a Hong Kong university. Analysis was performed on their submitted assignments, which included a revised lesson plan, a typed pedagogical rationale for the modifications, the logs of their interactions with the LLMs and reflections on the use of LLMs. The findings revealed a three-stage decision-making process among the teachers when interacting with AI to improve lesson plans. These were task identification, iterative prompting, and task implementation. Our findings also suggested that for teachers to engage effectively with LLMs they need pedagogical content knowledge, LLMs knowledge, and prompting skills. This study has implications for teacher professional development in enhancing prompt practices and the effective use of LLMs for accomplishing professional tasks.

title: ChatGPT, a partnering tool to improve ESL learners’ speaking skills: Case study in a Public University, Malaysia
authors: Jayanthi Muniandy, Mahiswaran Selvanathan
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness and challenges of using ChatGPT as a tool to enhance English as a Second Language (ESL) learners' speaking skills within a flipped classroom setting at a Malaysian public university. Using a mixed-method design with a sequential explanatory approach, the research collected data from 40 ESL learners through questionnaires and focus group interviews. The findings indicate that ChatGPT positively impacts learners' speaking skills by improving vocabulary, grammar, and confidence, and is perceived as easy to use, useful, and motivating. title: Opportunities and challenges of using artificial intelligence in language education: Perspectives from Vietnam
authors: Cristina A. Huertas Abril, Tú Anh Hà
summary: This study explores the attitudes and perceptions of Vietnamese in-service language teachers towards Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Language Learning (AIALL). Using a qualitative approach with semi-structured interviews involving eight teachers, the research investigates the perceived advantages, disadvantages, problems, and risks of integrating AI in language education. The findings indicate that while teachers hold generally positive views, appreciating AI's potential to save time, reduce workload, and enhance learning, they also express significant concerns. These concerns include the degradation of students' cognitive skills like critical thinking and creativity, the potential for overreliance and academic dishonesty, threats to data privacy, and the risk of job replacement. The study concludes by highlighting the need for official guidance, training, and policy from institutions and policymakers to ensure the safe and effective implementation of AI in language education in Vietnam.

title: Willingness to communicate with artificial intelligence (AI)? insights from tracking EFL learners' perceived acceptance and chat output
authors: Jian-E Peng, Weijun Liang
summary: This study investigated the interactions between 12 English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) learners in Macau and ChatGPT over a ten-week period. Drawing on a post-humanist perspective and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), it explored the dynamic relationship between the learners' Willingness to Communicate (WTC) with ChatGPT and their acceptance of the tool, measured by perceived ease of use (PEU), perceived usefulness (PU), and attitude toward using (AT). Data were collected through weekly questionnaires containing both closed and open-ended items, as well as screenshots of the learners' chat interactions. Thematic analysis of the qualitative data revealed that ChatGPT fulfilled four main roles: an opinion/advice giver, a language learning helper, a content knowledge provider, and a factual information supplier. Overall, learners held positive perceptions of the tool. Using change point analysis and moving window correlation analysis, the study found that some learners experienced significant changes in their WTC, PU, and AT over time, and uncovered varied and dynamic correlations between these variables. The findings provide new perspectives on the concept of WTC with AI and highlight the complex interplay between learners' WTC and their acceptance of such tools.

title: Perceived supports, achievement emotions, and engagement in multimodal GAI chatbot-assisted language learning: a sequential mixed-methods study
authors: Xueqing Wu, Rui Li
summary: This study employed a sequential mixed-methods approach to investigate the relationships between perceived supports, achievement emotions (enjoyment and boredom), and learner engagement among Chinese EFL learners interacting with a multimodal generative artificial intelligence (GAI) chatbot. Quantitative data from 499 learners and qualitative data from semi-structured interviews were analyzed. The findings indicate that learners experienced high autonomy but felt they lacked competence support. Perceived supports positively influenced both engagement and enjoyment, while enjoyment was found to be a significant mediator in the relationship between perceived supports and engagement. Conversely, boredom did not have a significant impact or mediating role. The study suggests integrating emotionally enriching experiences into GAI chatbot design to enhance learner enjoyment and engagement.

title: Evaluation of AI-generated reading comprehension materials for Arabic language teaching
authors: Ahmed Allaithy & Mai Zaki
summary: This study investigates the effectiveness of five AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Co-Pilot, JAIS, and Diffit) in generating Arabic reading comprehension materials for intermediate-level learners. Using a framework of text analysis, error analysis, and usability assessment, the study evaluates the linguistic quality and pedagogical suitability of the AI-generated content. The findings reveal significant linguistic challenges across all tools, including the overuse of nominal sentences, verb misuse, pronoun errors, and the influence of English syntax, resulting in unnatural expressions. Despite these issues, the tools showed potential for creating diverse question types. The paper concludes that rigorous quality control and human oversight are necessary when using AI for Arabic language education, offering insights for educators, curriculum developers, and AI designers to improve the efficacy of these tools.

title: The Role of Supportive Environments in Shaping EFL Teachers' Adoption of ChatGPT
authors: Nguyen Hoang Mai Tram, Vu Tran-Thanh
summary: This study applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), extended with factors of supportive environments (social influence and facilitating conditions), to explain English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers' intention to adopt ChatGPT for teaching. Through a quantitative survey of 176 Vietnamese EFL teachers, the research found that teachers regularly used ChatGPT for creating exercises, lesson planning, professional development, and other tasks. The results highlight that supportive environments are crucial for acceptance. Social interaction strongly influenced both perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while facilitating conditions only influenced perceived ease of use. The study confirms the core TAM relationships, where perceived ease of use and usefulness positively affect attitude, which in turn predicts the intention to continue using the tool. The findings offer valuable insights for educators, institutions, and policymakers on creating effective strategies for integrating AI tools like ChatGPT into educational settings.

title: EFL Writing Teachers' Agency in Response to AI Emergence from an Ecological Perspective
authors: Hoang Le-Khanh, Khoa Do, Vu Tran-Thanh
summary: This chapter reports a qualitative study on the agency formation of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing teachers amidst the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Teacher agency holds significance in educational discourse as agency supports educators' professional growth and enables them to adeptly navigate the dynamics of educational environments and enhance student outcomes. Data were collected from computer-assisted live personal interviews with seven Vietnamese experienced teachers. Using the ecological model framework (Priestley et al. in Teacher agency: an ecological approach, 1st edn. Bloomsbury Academic [1]) and a thematic analysis process (Braun and Clarke in Qual Res Psychol 3:77–101 [2]), the study uncovered a complex relationship between EFL teachers and AI tools like ChatGPT. Results show the teachers' reluctance to accept AI due to adherence to traditional pedagogies, lack of clear AI integration guidelines, and concerns over AI's accuracy and potential misuse. The findings suggest that, in AI's early integration stage, teachers' professional agency evolves independently of AI influences, viewing AI as a supplementary, non-disruptive tool in language education. Implications for teacher education and training are discussed.

title: Pedagogical Restructuring of Business Communication Courses: AI-Enhanced Prompt Engineering in an EFL Teaching Context
authors: Debopriyo Roy
summary: This chapter presents a case study on integrating prompt engineering into a business communication course for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. It explores how using ChatGPT, in conjunction with Google Search, can shift pedagogical focus from language mechanics to fostering critical thinking, problem-solving, and an entrepreneurial mindset. The study investigates how students can be guided to construct layered, logical arguments and produce professional documents through project-based learning. It argues for a pedagogical restructuring where the emphasis is on asking pertinent questions and engineering effective prompts, rather than on the direct production of text. The principles are demonstrated through a series of complex assignments completed by a graduate student, highlighting the complementary roles of AI and traditional search engines in a constructivist learning environment.

summary: This study investigates the factors influencing the adoption of ChatGPT among English for Specific Purposes (ESP) learners in business communication courses in India. Using a model based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), the research surveyed 526 students from two private Indian universities. The study highlights the need for targeted training, transparent policies, and AI literacy initiatives to foster responsible integration of ChatGPT in education.

title: Reconceptualizing Self-Directed Learning in the Era of Generative AI: An Exploratory Analysis of Language Learning
authors: Belle Li, Curtis J. Bonk, Chaoran Wang, Xiaojing Kou
summary: This exploratory study investigates the integration of ChatGPT in self-directed language learning (SDLL) by analyzing the experiences of 19 language-learning YouTubers. Through thematic analysis of interviews and video content, the study proposes a reconceptualization of the self-directed learning (SDL) framework for the era of generative AI. The new framework, an extension of Song and Hill's (2007) model, incorporates learners' personal attributes like technology readiness and self-efficacy, an autonomous-adaptive learning process, and the influence of a broader learning context that includes social and ethical elements. summary: This qualitative case study explores the perceived threats of Generative AI (GAI) to the personal agency of 53 Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) master's students in Vietnam, who are also teachers. summary: This study investigates the impact of ChatGPT on the engagement and motivation of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) university students. title: A multi-stage interactive writing task for the assessment of English language writing proficiency
authors: Andrew Runge, Sarah Goodwin, Yigal Attali, Mya Poe, Phoebe Mulcaire, Kai-Ling Lo, Geoffrey T. LaFlair
summary: This paper details the development and validation of an innovative, multi-stage interactive writing task for the Duolingo English Test. The task uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze a test taker's initial written response to a prompt, identify themes they did not discuss, and then present a customized follow-up prompt for them to elaborate on. Through a series of five experiments, the study evaluates the impact of prompt phrasing, the accuracy of LLM-based theme detection, and the overall validity and fairness of the task. Results indicate that the interactive design aligns writing assessment more closely with real-world writing processes, that a fine-tuned theme-detection model can effectively minimize asking students to repeat content, and that scores remain consistent regardless of the specific follow-up prompt. The study provides evidence that LLMs can be integrated into high-stakes assessments to enhance construct validity while maintaining fairness.

title: To resist it or to embrace it? Examining ChatGPT’s potential to support teacher feedback in EFL writing
authors: Kai Guo, Deliang Wang
summary: This exploratory study investigates ChatGPT's potential to support English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in providing feedback on student writing. The researchers compared feedback generated by ChatGPT with that of five experienced EFL teachers on 50 argumentative essays written by Chinese undergraduate students. The comparison focused on the amount and type of feedback across three areas: content, organisation, and language. The study found that ChatGPT produced significantly more feedback than teachers, with a more balanced distribution across the three areas. The types of feedback also differed, with ChatGPT favoring directive and praise-based comments, while teachers used more informative and query-based feedback. Additionally, the study examined the teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT's feedback, revealing both positive aspects (e.g., capability in assessing content, specificity, potential to reduce workload) and negative concerns (e.g., lengthiness, readability for students, irrelevance). The authors conclude by suggesting a collaborative model where teachers leverage ChatGPT's strengths while mitigating its weaknesses to enhance feedback on student writing.
APA_reference: Guo, K., & Wang, D. (2024). To resist it or to embrace it? Examining ChatGPT’s potential to support teacher feedback in EFL writing. Education and Information Technologies, 29(7), 8435–8463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-023-12146-0

authors: Fatih Karataş, Faramarz Yaşar Abedi, Filiz Ozek Gunyel, Derya Karadeniz, Yasemin Kuzgun
summary: ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence application, has emerged as a promising educational tool with a wide range of applications, attracting the attention of researchers and educators. This qualitative case study, chosen for its ability to provide an in-depth exploration of the nuanced effects of AI on the foreign language learning process within its real-world educational context, aimed to utilize ChatGPT in foreign language education, addressing a gap in existing research by offering insights into the potential, benefits, and drawbacks of this innovative approach. The students were introduced to ChatGPT through learning experiences over a span of four weeks by the researcher as a language teacher. The findings suggest that ChatGPT positively affects students' learning experiences, especially in writing, grammar, and vocabulary acquisition, and enhances motivation and engagement through its versatile and accessible nature in various learning activities. These insights contribute to understanding the utility and constraints of employing ChatGPT technology in foreign language instruction and can inform educators and researchers in developing effective teaching strategies and in designing curricula.

summary: This study employed the Hedonic Motivation System Adoption Model (HMSAM) to investigate the adoption of ChatGPT among English as a Second Language (ESL) learners. summary: This study explores the factors influencing the acceptance of ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence chatbot, for English Language Teaching (ELT) among Iranian EFL (English as a Foreign Language) teachers. summary: This study investigates the impact of using ChatGPT to assist English as a foreign language (EFL) college majors in revising essays. Through a prospective, double-blinded, paired-comparison study involving 44 students, it was found that ChatGPT-assisted revised essays received significantly higher scores than the original versions. A key finding was that students with lower initial scores experienced the greatest score increases, which raises concerns about fairness in evaluation and assessment. title: Examining the moderating effect of motivation on technology acceptance of generative AI for English as a foreign language learning
authors: Yi Zheng, Yabing Wang, Kelly Shu-Xia Liu, Michael Yi-Chao Jiang
summary: This study investigates the factors influencing English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' acceptance and use of generative AI tools, grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Through a survey of 620 Chinese undergraduates, the research uses structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships between UTAUT2 constructs (like performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence) and SDT motivation in predicting behavioral intention and actual use of AI. The findings show that most UTAUT2 factors and SDT motivation significantly predict learners' intention to use AI. Notably, SDT motivation also acts as a significant moderator, influencing the relationships between facilitating conditions, effort expectancy, social influence, and learners' behavioral intentions and use. The study concludes that understanding the interplay between technology acceptance factors and intrinsic motivation is crucial for the successful integration of generative AI in language education.

title: Exploratory study on the potential of ChatGPT as a rater of second language writing
authors: Dongkwang Shin, Jang Ho Lee
summary: This study investigates the potential of ChatGPT as an automated writing evaluation (AWE) tool for second language (L2) assessment. A custom chatbot, built on GPT-4 using the 'My GPTs' feature, was developed to rate 50 English essays written by Korean secondary-level EFL students. These AI-generated scores were then compared with the ratings from two experienced in-service English teachers. The findings, based on intraclass correlation coefficients, indicated a strong similarity between the human and ChatGPT scores. However, a more detailed analysis using the multifaceted Rasch model revealed that ChatGPT's ratings deviated slightly more from the expected model than the human raters' scores. The study concludes that while ChatGPT shows significant potential as an accessible and supplementary AWE tool that can assist L2 teachers, its ratings may require further calibration to align more closely with human evaluation standards.
APA_reference: Shin, D., & Lee, J. H. (2024). Exploratory study on the potential of ChatGPT as a rater of second language writing. Education and Information Technologies, 29, 24735–24757. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-024-12817-6

title: Teaching EFL students to write with ChatGPT: Students' motivation to learn, cognitive load, and satisfaction with the learning process
authors: David James Woo, Deliang Wang, Kai Guo, Hengky Susanto
summary: This mixed-methods study investigated the experiences and perceptions of 21 secondary school EFL students in Hong Kong using ChatGPT for a writing task in a workshop setting. The study focused on their motivation, cognitive load, and satisfaction. Data were collected through pre- and post-workshop questionnaires and think-aloud protocols. Findings showed that while student motivation to learn about ChatGPT was already high and only increased slightly, they experienced a high cognitive load, particularly during the prompt engineering phase. title: The effects of generative AI usage in EFL classrooms on the l2 motivational self system
authors: Jerry Huang, Atsushi Mizumoto
summary: This study investigated the impact of incorporating ChatGPT into an instructor-led university writing class in Japan on students' motivation. Using a mixed-methods approach with a control (n=45) and treatment (n=35) group, the study measured changes in students' Ideal L2 Self, Ought-to L2 Self, and L2 Learning Experience based on Dörnyei's L2MSS framework. Findings showed that students who used ChatGPT maintained significantly higher levels of motivation in their Ideal L2 Self and L2 Learning Experience compared to the control group, whose motivation declined. The Ought-to L2 Self was not significantly affected. Qualitative data indicated students found ChatGPT appropriate and useful for writing, though some raised concerns about overreliance and academic integrity. The study concludes that instructor-led integration of AI can sustain student motivation in mandatory language courses.
APA_reference: Huang, J., & Mizumoto, A. (2024). The effects of generative AI usage in EFL classrooms on the l2 motivational self system. Education and Information Technologies, 30, 6435–6454. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-024-13071-6

title: Chinese university teachers' engagement with generative AI in different stages of foreign language teaching: A qualitative enquiry through the prism of ADDIE
authors: Xiaohua Liu, Yangyu Xiao
summary: This study conducted in-depth interviews with 17 university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in mainland China to investigate how they integrate generative AI (GenAI) into their teaching processes. Using the ADDIE model (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) as a framework, the research found that GenAI tools were predominantly used in the 'development' stage for creating teaching materials and activities. authors: Madina Bekturova, Saule Tulepova, Altnay Zhaitapova
summary: This study explores how Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) students in Kazakhstan perceive the usefulness and ease of using ChatGPT for academic writing, and how these perceptions influence their intention to continue using it. Using a modified model combining the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM), the researchers surveyed 334 TEFL students from two universities. The quantitative results from an exploratory factor analysis showed a strong direct relationship between perceived ease of use, usefulness, satisfaction, and continuance intention. Students who found ChatGPT useful, easy to use, and were satisfied with it were more likely to intend to use it in the future. However, qualitative analysis of open-ended survey questions revealed significant student concerns regarding ChatGPT's reliability, potential for plagiarism, and the risk of losing their own writing skills. The study highlights the need for enhanced accuracy and reliable information from the AI tool.

summary: This study introduces and validates the 'ChatGPT Usage Scale for Foreign Language Learners,' a tool designed to evaluate how university students in foreign language departments use AI chatbots. title: Exploring student perceptions of language learning affordances of Large Language Models: A Q methodology study
authors: Ke Li, Lulu Lun, Pingping Hu
summary: This study uses Q-methodology, a mixed-methods approach, to investigate Chinese undergraduate students' perceptions of the language learning affordances of Large Language Models (LLMs). By having 26 students rank statements about LLMs' potential and limitations, the study identified three distinct viewpoints: 'prudent skeptics,' who are concerned about the absence of a human element and question LLMs' learning benefits; 'enthusiastic embracers,' who are optimistic about the personalized learning opportunities LLMs offer; and 'conservative adopters,' who acknowledge the supplementary role of LLMs but emphasize the user's ability to ask effective questions. The findings highlight the importance of scaffolding, AI literacy, and individual differences in integrating LLMs into language education. While the study's generalizability is limited by its methodology, it provides a nuanced understanding of student perceptions to inform curriculum, pedagogy, and policy.

authors: Simin Xu, Yanfang Su, Kanglong Liu
summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the cognitive, affective, and behavioural engagement of Master's students in translation with ChatGPT-generated feedback. Through a translation-and-revision experiment, surveys, and interviews, the study found that students exhibited high cognitive engagement, investing considerable effort in the revision process, though they sometimes struggled with vague feedback. Affectively, students were moderately satisfied, appreciating the feedback's potential but also expressing disappointment with its generic nature. Behaviourally, students' actions were influenced by cognitive and affective factors, leading to selective uptake of feedback and self-initiated corrections. title: The mediating effects of needs satisfaction on the relationship between teacher support and student engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots from a self-determination theory (SDT) perspective
authors: Yan Li, Thomas K.F. Chiu
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots, such as ChatGPT and ERNIE Bot, are documented to influence student learning experience and student engagement. However, factors affecting student engagement in GenAI chatbots learning context are less understood. Self-determination theory (SDT) suggests student basic needs satisfaction-autonomy, competence, and relatedness— are associated with student behavioral, cognitive, emotional and agentic engagement. Teacher support-autonomy, structure, and involvement– derived by the three SDT needs. Hence, this study aims to clarify how factors (i.e., teacher support, student needs satisfaction) affect student engagement in this GenAI context in second language (L2) education. It examines the mediating effect of needs satisfaction on the relationship between teacher support and student engagement with a chatbot Data was collected from 364 university students through a questionnaire. The participants learned English as second language with ERNIE Bot under teacher support for four sessions. Our results revealed that needs satisfaction could partially mediate the relationship between teacher support and student behavioral, cognitive, and agentic engagement. They also suggest that needs satisfaction fully mediates the relationship between teacher support and emotional engagement. These suggests that GenAI chatbots better emotionally engage students in language learning than teachers do. One possible explanation for this is that students found learning with chatbots to be enjoyable and stress-free in L2 education. The results suggest teachers should take AI chatbot’s affordance and student feeling into account for emotional engagement when using GenAI chatbots. We suggest future studies should include additional factors such as personality and peer support.

title: Evaluating the performance of ChatGPT and Claude in automated writing scoring: Insights from the Many-facet Rasch model
authors: Rui Jin, Mingren Zhao, Chunling Niu, Yuyan Xia, Hao Zhou, Na Liu
summary: This study evaluates the automated writing scoring (AWS) performance of two Large Language Models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Claude, using zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies. The Many-Facet Rasch Model (MFRM) was used to analyze 117 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) essays written by Chinese university students, which were graded by four human raters and four LLM-prompting combinations. The findings indicate that LLMs were more severe but also more consistent in their scoring than human raters. Few-shot prompting resulted in better alignment with human raters compared to zero-shot prompting. Notably, none of the LLM configurations showed evidence of gender bias. The study concludes that while LLMs are promising supplementary tools for educational assessment, they require further optimization to ensure fairness and accuracy, particularly regarding scoring severity.

summary: This qualitative study explores the experiences of 47 secondary school teachers in Malta who use generative AI for teaching the Maltese language. Grounded in sociocultural theory and constructivist principles, the research used semi-structured interviews to understand how teachers employ AI for tasks like text generation, interactive storytelling, and personalized feedback. Findings indicate that teachers perceive AI as beneficial for improving student proficiency, engagement, and motivation, particularly through immediate and tailored feedback. However, they also raised concerns about student overreliance on technology, the need for teacher training, and other context-specific challenges. The study highlights the potential of generative AI for differentiated instruction in a minority language context and identifies areas for future research, such as the measurable impact of AI on student outcomes.

summary: This qualitative study explored university students' perceptions of using Generative AI (GenAI) in translation practices at a Sino-foreign cooperative university in southern China. title: "Brave New World" or not?: A mixed-methods study of the relationship between second language writing learners' perceptions of ChatGPT, behaviors of using ChatGPT, and writing proficiency
authors: Li Dong
summary: This mixed-methods study investigates the relationship between L2 writing learners' perceptions of ChatGPT, their usage behavior, and their writing proficiency (complexity, accuracy, fluency). Data was collected from 215 Chinese university students through surveys and writing samples, with a follow-up focus group of four students. The study, framed by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), found that performance and effort expectancy positively influenced students' intention to use ChatGPT, while social influence had a negative effect. Facilitating conditions and behavioral intention predicted actual use. Notably, ChatGPT usage was found to significantly predict only the complexity of students' writing, not accuracy or fluency. The qualitative findings revealed students' need for teacher support and guidance. The study emphasizes the importance of human agency and the role of educators in guiding the critical and ethical use of AI writing tools.
