title: Enhancing second language speaking assessment: Integrating large language models for Finnish and Finland Swedish proficiency scoring
authors: Ekaterina Voskoboinik, Anna von Zansen, Nhan Chi Phan, Yaroslav Getman, Tamás Grósz, Mikko Kurimo
summary: This study investigates the use of large language models (LLMs) to improve automated speaking assessment (ASA) for less commonly taught languages, specifically Finnish and Finland Swedish, where learner data is often scarce and imbalanced across proficiency levels. The researchers explored two main approaches: 1) using LLMs to generate synthetic speech transcripts to augment training data for traditional machine learning models (BERT), and 2) using LLMs (GPT-4 and Llama 2) to directly score learner transcripts through zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting. The findings indicate that augmenting datasets with LLM-generated data improves scoring accuracy for underrepresented proficiency levels. Furthermore, direct scoring with LLMs, particularly using a few-shot approach, proved to be a practical and scalable alternative, achieving performance comparable or superior to traditional models without requiring extensive training data or parameter updates. The study also confirms that using automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts instead of manual ones does not significantly degrade scoring performance, paving the way for fully automated, real-time assessment systems.

title: Exploring Engagement, Self-Efficacy, and Anxiety in Large Language Model EFL Learning: A Latent Profile Analysis of Chinese University Students
authors: Qikai Wang, Yang Gao, Xiaochen Wang
summary: This study explores the engagement, self-efficacy, and anxiety of Chinese EFL university students using Large Language Models (LLMs). A questionnaire assessing five dimensions (behavior, cognitive, and emotional engagement; self-efficacy; and anxiety) was administered. Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) identified three distinct student profiles: (1) Enthusiastic Explorers (high engagement, low anxiety), (2) Adaptable Learners (moderate engagement, low self-efficacy), and (3) Ambitious-Anxious Pioneers (high engagement, high anxiety). The findings highlight the diverse ways students approach LLMs for English learning and provide insights for educators to optimize the use of these tools.

title: Who is most likely to accept AI chatbots? A sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of personality and ChatGPT acceptance for language learning
authors: Changrong Du, Mi Tang, Chenghao Wang, Bin Zou, Yinan Xia & Yiran Du
summary: This study examines the role of personality traits in university students' acceptance of ChatGPT for language learning, using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach. Structural equation modelling based on responses from 233 students in China showed that perceived ease of use significantly predicted perceived usefulness, which in turn influenced attitude and behavioural intention. Among the Big Five traits, conscientiousness positively predicted both perceived usefulness and ease of use; openness and agreeableness positively influenced perceived usefulness; while extraversion and neuroticism significantly affected perceived ease of use in positive and negative directions respectively. The qualitative phase, based on interviews with 15 students, explored how and why these personality traits shaped learners' perceptions and behaviours. Thematic analysis identified key mechanisms such as goal-directed routines (conscientiousness), exploratory curiosity (openness), emotional reassurance (agreeableness), and uncertainty sensitivity (neuroticism). These findings highlight the importance of considering personality in the design and implementation of AI-assisted language learning.

title: What Motivates Second Language Majors to Use Generative AI for Informal Learning? Insights From the Theory of Planned Behavior
authors: Hanwei Wu, Zhangkun Dong
summary: This study investigates the factors influencing second language (L2) majors' intention to use Generative AI (GenAI) for informal learning, using the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) as a framework. Data was collected from 668 L2 majors in various Chinese universities via an online questionnaire. Using structural equation modeling, the study found that subjective norm and attitude positively predicted behavioral intention, whereas perceived behavioral control did not. GenAI literacy was a significant predictor of intention, both directly and indirectly through attitude. External beliefs also positively influenced subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, and attitude. Demographic factors such as gender and age were found to have no significant impact on the model's constructs. The study concludes with implications for integrating GenAI into L2 education.

H5. External beliefs significantly and positively predict subjective norm.
H6. External beliefs significantly and positively predict perceived behavioral control.
H7. External beliefs significantly and positively predict attitude.

title: Investigating EFL teachers' use of generative AI to develop reading materials: A practice and perception study
authors: Jieting Jerry Xin
summary: This study explored how three English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers perceived and used ChatPDF, a generative AI tool, to develop materials for reading lessons. Data was collected through teacher-AI dialogues, created artefacts (original and finalized materials), and semi-structured interviews. The findings indicated that teachers primarily used ChatPDF for text modification, task design, and seeking pedagogical suggestions, relying on their pedagogical content knowledge. The study identified a 'D-R-E-A-M' pattern (determine needs, render prompts, evaluate suggestions, adjust prompts, make final decision) in the teachers' workflow. While teachers acknowledged the tool's advantages in efficiency and idea generation, they also noted limitations such as unreliability and inability to process multimodal content. The results offer pedagogical implications for both EFL teachers and teacher educators on leveraging generative AI for materials development.

title: Unleashing the power of perceived enjoyment: exploring Chinese undergraduate EFL learners' intention to use ChatGPT for English learning
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Lei Mee Thien
summary: This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model by incorporating perceived enjoyment as an intrinsic motivation to investigate factors influencing Chinese undergraduate English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students' intention to use ChatGPT. Using a quantitative survey design with 432 students from two Chinese universities, the study employed partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) for data analysis. The findings revealed that effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence, and perceived enjoyment were all positively related to students' intention to use ChatGPT. Notably, perceived enjoyment was found to mediate the relationships between the other three factors and the intention to use the technology. The study highlights the significant role of intrinsic motivation, particularly in the high-pressure, exam-oriented context of Chinese higher education, and provides insights for developers and educators on designing engaging AI-based language learning tools.

title: Personalized L2 argumentative writing Instruction through GenAI-enhanced corpus-based language pedagogy: an intervention study
authors: Javad Zare, Fatemeh Ranjbaran Madiseh
summary: This study investigates the use of Generative AI (GenAI), specifically GPT-4O, to personalize L2 argumentative writing instruction within a Corpus-Based Language Pedagogy (CBLP) framework. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods experimental design, the study compared an experimental group, which received personalized feedback and tailored writing support generated by GenAI analyzing their own essays, against a control group receiving traditional instruction. Quantitative results from IELTS writing tasks showed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher scores in both short-term and long-term assessments. Qualitative analysis of follow-up interviews revealed that the intervention's effectiveness was attributed to customized feedback, an interactive learning experience, a supportive (non-judgmental) attitude from the AI, and immediate, easy access to assistance. The findings suggest that integrating GenAI with CBLP is a potent approach for enhancing L2 writing pedagogy.

title: The Influence of Natural Language Processing on EFL Speaking Skills: Investigating Learner Adaptability, Language Accuracy, and Fluency
authors: Jing Zhang, Qiaoyun Liao, Lipei Li, Jingyi Luo
summary: This study investigates the independent effects of three Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools—AI chatbots (ChatGPT), machine translation (Google Translate/DeepL), and automatic summarization (SMMRY/QuillBot)—on the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking skills of adaptability, accuracy, and fluency. Using a 12-week pretest-posttest randomized controlled trial with 436 EFL learners, the research compared three treatment groups and a control group receiving traditional instruction. The findings indicate that the chatbot treatment group achieved significantly higher gains in all three measured skills compared to the other groups. The study concludes that interactive, scaffolded practice with AI chatbots is most effective for holistic speaking skill development, while machine translation is best for vocabulary and summarization for coherence. The results are framed within sociocultural theory, the input hypothesis, and nonlinear dynamic language learning theory, providing pedagogical recommendations for integrating NLP tools in language education.

title: To revise or to recommend: an exploratory sequential mixed method study on GenAI formative feedback on Reading assessment in secondary schools
authors: Ziqi Chen, Wei Wei, Katherine Cao & Jessica To
summary: While evaluation-based feedback has been widely advocated in language assessment research for its perceived utility, this study examined and compared the effectiveness of three types of GenAI formative feedback within secondary education reading assessments. This study employed an exploratory sequential mixed methods design, guided by the Student-Feedback Interaction Model. Six teachers evaluated GenAI formative feedback provided to 516 Year 9 students on constructed-response reading tasks. Feedback types included: (1) answer revisions, (2) reading strategy recommendations, and (3) additional task recommendations. Qualitative data were collected from post-evaluation interviews. Contrary to prevailing feedback research that positions recommendation as more impactful than revision, MANCOVA tests reveal GenAI revision feedback was rated significantly more effectively than recommendation feedback across classical, fiction, and technical writing reading genres. Qualitative data from post-evaluation interviews revealed key limitations of GenAI's recommendation on reading strategies and tasks: (1) repetition and copied materials; (2) limited development of knowledge transfer; (3) irrelevance to high-stakes exams; (4) generic and non-contextualized recommendations; and (5) overly complex language for lower proficiency students. This study provides the first empirical evidence demonstrating that GenAI formative feedback proves more effective for answer revision than strategy recommendation. It advances genre-specific insights by revealing GenAI's greater efficacy in classical literature tasks compared to fiction or technical texts. Practically, the research proposes a feedback-literate GenAI integration model that addresses five limitations of recommendation-based approaches (including repetitiveness, transferability gaps, and exam misalignment), offering educators actionable principles to implement AI tools critically while maintaining pedagogical intentionality.
